title: A fantastic addition to any fountain pen collection, my go-to over my Waterman
text:
At first glance, this pen is very attractive, and has a lovely form. What's under the hood, however, is a true fountain pen collector and connoisseur dream.

The pen can be fully disassembled for easy maintenance, so that is a wonderful feature all on its own. The nib and housing can be changed to accommodate a change in point to EF, F, M, B, or Stub. The nib itself is firm, yet still flexible enough that this amazing stub nib creates a calligraphic line with gentle pressure. The piston fill can be fiddled with to increase or decrease the flow of ink to the nib per your particular tastes as well, allowing for a more bold, or a more refined line. Unlike my Waterman, this pen NEVER leaks. I use this pen fairly exclusively, and I am able to go two weeks with heavy writing and note taking without needing to refill, because the capacity in the ink chamber is that high!

The stub nib is extremely smooth out of the box, which some love, but I need the sensory feedback of a little texture to the nib, so a little experience has told me that a superfine grit paper provides enough texture to the nib for the feedback to be perfect for me. This stub is now, IMHO absolutely perfect. I have a 25 year collection and history with fountain pens, from newest innovation to vintage classics, and while I love them all, this is still my favorite after purchasing it just shy of two years ago. I would put the performance, balance, and full specs against any pen in my collection, and almost any other pen on the market today. At this cost, this pen is a steal, and I'm frankly surprised that they make a profit on it.

title: I had to remove one star for sturdiness and for receptivity to fountain ink
text: I write with a fountain pen (piston type). This was purchased as a journal to track my certification studies. I really needed this to be able to be carried daily, AND to not need to blot the ink before I turn the page. I've used the pen on many paper types, and while this is receptive and certainly smooth, it holds the ink at the surface for longer than some of the other journals I've used. I think it would be better suited for the $15-19 price point, unless they can improve the porosity of the paper without compromising the smooth texture. It can be done, and has been at the price point I have indicated.

title: Won’t be purchasing HP printers again. :(
text: Where do I start. Pros; easy to install, and can find them everywhere. Cons; way too expensive for the volume of product, cartridge stops working because sensor says it’s empty when it still has product in it, cartridge can’t be refilled, ONLY replaced (inconvenient AND bad environmentally -  why not just sell us the ink kits), cartridges last half the time of competitor’s like Cannon and Edson, and printer won’t print ANYTHING if one color is out - not even in black and white.

title: I'm amazed that it's living up to the hype.
text: I wanted the smaller size, so that it would be useful as a daily planner and goals tracker, but I was worried that it might be tougher to write in due to how much smaller it is. Thank goodness that's not the case! I am pleased to report that this is a planner that really does make good on it's promise. The concept behind *this* planner is that large long-term goals can be achieved by breaking them down incrementally. The Penguin planner is an excellent option for short-term goals, but the Clever Fox is definitely designed for clarifying and achieving long-term plans in a fluid, and dynamic way. As with any change in habit, keeping up with the things you need to do is key to getting the job done, this planner helps you lay it all out, and helps you learn - in real time - where the log jams show up.

title: Precise and well balanced
text: This is a very fine writing tool, and everything you'd expect from German workmanship. My pen arrived with the extra fine nib, which I enjoy, and two cartridges of Lamy ink (blue and black). Being something of an ink snob, and also developing a decisive taste in fountain pens, I found this slightly-higher than entry point priced fountain pen to rival the ease and fluidity of my old Monte Blanc. I have used the refillable cartridge (purchased separately), with varying inks, and have found it's performance to be consistent right down to the last drop of ink. Not a drop of ink had leaked, and I have had the pen for a bit now. The feel of the pen is very nice, it has a similar feel to an architectural pen or pencil in that it is designed to give control to the user, and the weight of the metal gives substance to that feeling of control. The extra fine nib does have a bit of drag to it, but that is because it truly has a very fine line, almost rivaling that of the head of a pin, and the ink is meted out very evenly. All in all, I can highly recommend this pen to those who desire control and consistency in their instrument.

title: Excellent value and performance
text: Pilot makes an amazing, yet low cost, fountain pen. Of all the pens I have owned, from the expensive Mont Blanc, to the medium ranged Lamy, this little humble pilot pen is my go-to. The barrel feels substantial, without being heavy and fatiguing. The nib is a joy, thin to my tastes, with an almost impossible to miss sweet spot. With the right ink, there is almost no fatigue because the nib *glides* along the paper. In comparison to both Lamy and Mont Blanc, the Pilot nib somehow writes a thinner line. The grip isn't quite as comfortable as the Lamy I own, but far more comfortable than the MB. If you are a new convert to fountain pens, this one will spoil you. If you're an old veteran, you will greatly appreciate the performance in such a reasonably priced gem.

This puts the tray under the bar without even being in the lowest position. It would be far too low for a normal sitting desk. My desk converts between sitting and standing so I just had to adjust the height a bit for each setting.

A bonus is that my chair actually fits the desk better. The desk didn't go quite low enough for my chair, but with the tray, the keyboard sits lower and I can adjust the chair to where I need it--not just as high as it can go.

text: Super happy with this purchase. I have had a lot of dissatisfaction with other company that sell kaweco on Amazon but this was a great purchase. Super smooth for a fine fib. Now looking for other colors and nib sizes 👏🏻

title: Disappointed
text: So I love kaweco. I have several. This was super appealing. But the description was lacking so I was suspicious. It states is a kaweco AL sport but the description states plastic.  AL means aluminum and the price was in the al range. The nib says “wide” then later written B. Well it’s a BB. It was also crooked. The vent didn’t align with the feeder and it was cut slightly lopsided.  I’m not sure what’s going on here but this is going back.

title: Wanted to love it
text: Heard great things about this brand, really wanted to love this pen. But. It was not smooth across the paper. The balance of weight was a little funky. For the price I shouldn't complain but I just didn't enjoy it.

title: disappointed
text: I heard great things about the brand. Unfortunately, I was disappointed in the material and craftmanship, returned it. Not worth the price.

title: Favorite pen ever.
text: Looking for a pen that : doesn't smudge, dries fast, doesn't ghost much, causes less hand cramps, works on a variety of papers???? This is it! My go to pen. Perfect in every way.

title: Maybe it's me
text: I know this is discontinued but i love this pen for art. Bought it twice both times nib maligned. Returned.

title: Great little pen
text: These metropolitans aren't as smooth as Lamy or Kaweco but are durable and write well, can't complain.

title: Ok-ish
text: I heard great thing about these pens, but ultimately returned it. Very scratchy across the page. But seems like it would otherwise hold up well.

title: Didn't love it
text: I had high hopes for this case as so many people recommend it. However, the material was very thin and didn't seem to have aligned seams. Also the zipper was a bit finicky. I returned it.

title: Love Lamy
text: Great little pen from Lamy. They always hold up well. No complaints.

title: Great for Line and Wash watercolor
text: Nice crisp thin line for watercolor work. Love this pen. Holds up longer than microns

title: Work great on black paper
text: These are perfect for black paper. Show up really well. Good for drawing, doodling. They do take a while to dry but I have no complaints

title: favorite fountain pen for watercolor
text: Love this pen with the matching ink for watercolor work. VERY permanent

title: Nice color
text: This is my first fine nib Kaweco, usually use medium nibs. Like the color, fine nib isn't quite as buttery as the medium but writes well. Always love the brand

title: Pretty good
text: Like it. Smooth. Lots of nib creep.

title: So so
text: These are ok.  They’re relatively damaging to whatever you clip them to. So if it’s art or a journal etc it will leave marks. I ended up giving them to my sister...

title: Love it
text: Love.  Thick pages.  Hold up.  No bleed through.  Perfect

title: funny and convenient
text: Nice, funny cards that are perfect for my family. The humor's a bit raunchy, but it works, plus, now I don't need to bother going out to get a card at the grocery store every month.

title: Great little pen
text:
I love this pen. Beyond reason. It's a smooth, even writer, and it's got good flow, even with drier inks. My only complaint is with the squeeze converter, but I've taken to just refilling the cartridges with bottled ink, and that gives me the ink capacity I need. Plus, it looks like a much nicer pen than it is, and the color is fun while still looking at home in my school or office.

I've got it inked up with Monteverde's Olivine, which is a nice dark green that contrasts beautifully with the light green of the pen body, and matches the darker green by the collar. Diamine Meadow would probably be a perfect match for the pen body color, though, if you want to go that route.

title: This is the second time I've had to review this
text:
Vine doesn't seem to have posted the first one. So long story short, I didn't like it. It's poorly thought out, full of typos, and physically flimsy.

Shame you can't read the original; it was actually pretty detailed.

title: Good set
text: If this set fits the way you think about your budget, then it'll work well for you.  It's also pretty, which is a plus in a field of dead boring budget fillers.

title: Does what it's supposed to
text: Decent quality, fits the notebook, good price.

title: Love it!
text:
Possibly the best electric pencil sharpener I've ever used. It pulls the pencils into the sharpener blades, creates a beautifully sharp point on virtually every pencil I've tried (regular graphite, charcoal, sanguine and sepia, and colored pencils) and then ejects it. No over-sharpening, no mess (nice, big shaving receptacle), and no batteries or plug-in needed. It's rechargeable and a charge lasts quite a while.

My only concern is finding replacement blades for the sharpener. I'm still not quite sure what sort is needed. I found ZMOL replacements here on Amazon, but they don't seem to look like what's in my sharpener. You'll probably have to do some homework, as I will. But not to worry because according to the information I've read you can sharpen 1000+ pencils before needing to change.

title: Nice tool
text:
But I would have preferred something with more comprehensive money management inserts. There are twelve budget sheets, one for each month, and 8 envelopes for cash, receipts, etc. So far so good, but the budget sheets are just lists where you can note date, amount, what the entry is, and balance. If you use them for both income and out-go, you'll end up with a messy looking list of numbers that can be hard to navigate, and really not customizable at all. Because of this I ordered some A6 budget inserts that let me divide up money in from money out, and make notes on cash on hand and so forth.

The planner itself is nice looking though, and seems sturdy, so it will last you for a while, and the price is quite reasonable, IMO. It just needs a little something extra.

title: Poorly planned planner
text:
This is an 18 month/72 week planner. Do you see the problem? No? Well I didn't either until I started using it. There are only enough weekly scheduling pages in each month for 28 days. And we all know that there's only one month in the year with only 28 days, right? (And even then, every 4 years, that changes.) So what do you do with the leftover days? And how do you deal with a month that starts on a Thursday or Friday and leaves you with 3 or 4 leftover days? Because the book is bound, there's no shuffling in new pages for the overflow. You're stuck with leftover days and nowhere to deal with them.
And TBH, even the physical look of the planner left something to be desired. The spine is so loosely bound that the pages hang out past the covers. It's not horrible, it just doesn't look nice.

I see that everyone else seems happy with their planner, so who knows? Maybe you'll find a way to deal with the extra days problem. I just dumped it and went back to my trusty A6 planner binder that I can use year after year with new inserts.

title: Exactly what I needed
text: I needed something convenient to keep business items that might need action.  I can keep this close to my desk with current bills, health information and the like, and use my filing cabinet for longer-term records.  It's easy to use and holds a lot of material.

title: Exactly what I need
text: I tend to compartmentalize, so this was just what I needed to file information on my recent health issues.  Each pocket holds a reasonable number of documents, and it comes with enough tabs for each pocket.  The only thing I don't like is that the paper tabs have a glossy surface making it harder for the ink to dry.`I turned them inside out.  Easy peasy.  Ultimately I think this is well worth the money for anyone who needs easy access to their documents.

title: I like this set!
text: First, be aware that the bulk of the pens are black.  You get a handful of colored ones, but mostly you're going to be dealing with a whole lot of black pens.  That said, they're decent pens.  They hold a lot of ink, write smoothly, and while they're a bit slim, they're not bad to hold.  For the money you could do a lot worse.

title: Plain old post-it notes are cheaper and actually better.
text: The adhesive on these is so-so at best.  It's nice having a fun little container for your arrows and notes, but is it worth the money?  I don't think so.

title: Well... no
text:
I'm adding a third star because the company responded almost immediately to my review with very thorough comments touching on my concerns. I suspect that they would be highly responsive to any questions or complaints from customers, so while my initial experience wasn't optimal, I think this is a company that can be relied upon to do the right thing.
___
I was really looking forward to having a lightweight file container that could handle hanging file folders, lock, and be easily carried. So did I get that? Um... yes and no. I got a lightweight file container that can easily be carried (Unless it's holding files, but obviously paper is going to make it heavier.) But can it handle hanging folders. Well, yes unless you actually want to zip it closed and lock it. The lid will not fit over the box if the folders are hanging folders. Believe me I tried any number of times to close it, and I did get one side zipped, but then the zipper handle wouldn't fit into the lock.

So the bottom line here is that you can have a file container that you can zip and lock, or you can have one that holds hanging folders. You can't have both.

Oh, and the instructions don't tell you how to actually lock the box. Once you program in your new combination, zip up the lid and press the zipper handles into the lock notches. Click click.

title: A little pricey but a nice notebook
text: I think these are mostly intended for teens and tweens, but I find they're handy for household things.  You know, a place to make a note about what you're going to make for dinner on Tuesday, or what time your HVAC guy is coming by to service the furnace.  It's neat and compact, and for a touch of whimsey comes with some nice stickers.  Life doesn't always have to be staid and dull, does it?

title: Friendly
text: All practical concerns fall by the wayside when you start adding stickers to your journals and planners.  Why?  Because they add a whimsical dimension to things, a statement, a "look at me!" touch to your writing/record keeping that makes everything seem fresh.  These stickers -- and it's a generous assortment -- are practical, sure, but they're charming and fun, and they'll make you smile as you add them to your notes, or as you read them over.  So break out of the pen-scratch mode and add a bit of vigor to your planners with these stickers. They might even help you hold onto memories that simply writing things down won't accomplish.  I think they're worth the price, and believe me, I've seen a lot of sticker sets that don't begin to live up to that ideal.

title: Nice pens
text: They're nice little pens, good color, and yes they are fast-drying.  Unfortunately  they also seem to dry up pretty quickly.  I've used the blue one twice now and it's laying down a sketchy line as if it's trying to run out of ink.  I can't imagine that's possible, so I keep pumping on the point, and it does improve for a while.  It could just be one bum pen, or some other factor I haven't yet figured out.  Still, for the price, the set is a nice one.

title: Perfect size for my card
text: Nice, heavy-duty sleeve for my vaccination card, keeps it safe and pristine in my purse.  Also comes with perforations on the top so you can put it on a lanyard.  I'm not generally called upon to show my card very often, but this will certainly be a help for those times when I do need to.

title: Beautiful journals
text:
I'm a blank book junkie, I freely admit it. I've used Moleskine, Leuchtturm, and many others, and I think that these give you more bang for the buck than any of the others. It seems like a lot to invest upfront, but $6 per journal is a very reasonable price. You can certainly split the lot with friends, but if you're like me, you'll find uses for most if not all.

They have a lot of the high-end features: ruled, numbered pages; elastic closure and pen holder, table of contents, expandable pocket in the back, and a good, solid cover. The pages seem sturdy, and so far I've had no problem with bleed through. As a blank notebook junkie, I can recommend these unreservedly.

title: This is a deal
text: An all-in-one for such a low price?  Sold!  though I confess I was skeptical after my last HP printer turned out to be such a difficult beast.  But the 2755 installs easily, connects quickly and does a fantastic job printing quickly and cleanly.  Good copies as well.

title: Not as good as I'd hoped.
text: I wish I liked this lap desk better.  There's a lot about it to like; the silicon strip that keeps my laptop from moving around on the desk, the ridge that keeps it from sliding off, and the phone divot. It's also lightweight and comes with a carry handle.  All that said, I still have problems with it.  The way its constructed and filled means that it sits flat.  There should be more filling toward the back to tip the lap desk forward a bit.  As it is, the whole thing rocks back and forth when I move my legs.  It's under-filled, as well, which means that the computer isn't up high enough for me to work comfortably. To get it where I need it to be, I have to put it on top of another cushion that both raises and tips it toward me.  I hate being the naysayer on this, but there are things that need improving.

title: Lovely
text: This is a nice notebook.  It feels good in my hand, and writing in it is pleasant.  It's very giftable if you can bring yourself to give it up.  Nice for your favorite writer, chef, or journaler.

title: I love this printer
text:
I'm thrilled to have a printer I can use with my phone, but more than that, the ease of connecting it to my laptop is like nothing I've experienced before. Usually there's so much faffing around you have to do to get a printer to talk to anything, but with this one, I told my computer "Go look for it" and it showed up immediately, and printed perfectly from the get-go.

Print quality is good, and I love that I can print from so many different sources. The footprint is small, too, an improvement over the behemoth I used to have. Many thanks to HP for such a user friendly printer.

title: Does exactly what it should
text: Adheres well, good magnetic force. Terrific for refrigerator magnets or a little guerilla art.

title: Cheap
text: I appear to be the single naysayer, so take what I write with a grain of salt. But I found this to be cheaply made, and unreliable. Keyboard slides around too much, silicone bars pop off. (Why are they not permanently affixed?) It's okay but not what I'd hoped.

title: These are really nice
text: These folders are nice and sturdy.  They hold a LOT of paper for me.  So far I haven't inserted them in a three-ring binder, but I'm considering making a binder for all my household manuals.  The folders are attractive as well, with nice black and white graphics, and brightly colored interiors (well two, the third has a black interior.) Nice selection for home or school.

title: Nice set
text: Good colors, comfortable.  Pilot is always reliable.  I wish they were a bit broader and more flexible, but you can't have everything.  And the broad-tip black pen is great for lettering.  There's a simple lettering guide in the package as well.

title: As with all things 3M, good stuff
text: This is good tape.  I can't say I think it's hugely better than regular Scotch tape, but it does disappear when you smooth it down, and it is strong.  It's reasonably priced for what you get, so why not go with the stronger disappearing tape?

title: Nice notebooks
text: These little notebooks are perfect for tucking into a pocket or purse.  The pages are lined, and there are 48 per book, with thick paper covers. The insides of each cover are printed with spaces for personal information in the front, and information on time zones and unit equivalences in back, along with something odd about pulse points.  The only problem that I see is that you'd have to find a gold, silver or white pen to fill in all the personal information on both the black and dark blue notebooks. Regular ink will not show up.  Not a big deal but a bit of an oversight.  Good price for three.

title: Yup, they dissolve all right.
text: They're not kidding when they say these things are dissolvable.  An empty jar of mine sat in the sink overnight, and the label was gone the next morning.  So like gremlins, don't get them wet!  And don't handle the sheets with damp hands.  Other than that, they're pretty much like normal labels, though lighter weight than average, and translucent.  They stick to glass or metal, so wherever you want to slap your label on a mason jar, it'll adhere well.

title: Fun set of pens
text:
I'm a sucker for pens. Many stationery items, actually, but pens in particular, and this set is a nice, well priced one with eight ultra micropoint pens in candybox colors. Gel pens have a smooth writing feel which is why I've come to like them, and even an ultra micropoint will write without noticeable drag. The colors are nice, brightish pastels, but don't be fooled by the word "green." That pen is turquoise, which has only a 3rd cousin relationship to green. Still, they're a great addition to my writing tools where different colors help me keep my thoughts and ideas organized.

And they're fun. I love signing checks or contracts, or addressing envelopes in violet or pink, or some other unexpected color. Why not, right? Have some fun with these pens; knock yourself out.

title: Lovely planner but hugely over-priced.
text:
I love planners. I love tarting them up with stickers and washi tape, and clippings, so when I saw that this one encouraged all those wonderful, silly behaviors, I was hooked. Which is a good thing because this planner is absolutely not portable unless you don't mind carrying pounds of stuff in your bag. It's a desktop planner.

For me, it's a pretty useful one. I get month-at-a-glance which is always valuable, and a generous page for each weekday, weekends share a page. There is space for appointments, notes, menus, to-do lists, and on Sunday, a prep list for the coming week to remind you of the regular maintenance you need to do to keep your planner current and useful. It's O-bound which is nice because that gives you a lot of room for tucking things between pages. It has reinforced corner hard covers, and a pocket inside the front cover. There's also a page of stickers to get you started with embellishing your pages. Generic stuff, as you'd guess. Overall this is a nice, well thought out planner.

However, and this is a biggie, I have shopped for and bought any number of planners over the years, and one thing I can tell you is that a nearly $60 price tag for a dedicated (one year only, non-refillable) planner is way too pricey. I have paid far less for far more, and been quite happy with the design and functionality I got, particularly when you consider that many of my planners have been refillable, and used until they fell apart,or until another comely planner caught my eye. (Yes, I'm fickle; I have have a roving eye for stationery items.) For this kind of money, I'd want more than one page of "Yay, go me, attagirl, rah rah rah" type stickers, and a single pocket inside the front cover. What about the back cover, folks? Why not one there. And why not a moveable page keeper type thing, so that you can go directly to the current page? All of those things are grace notes, sure, but they're useful grace notes and would go a long way toward justifying the cost of this thing.

Will I use this? Yes. Do I think I will find it useful? Yes. Would I ever buy another? Not at this price. Drop it by $25 and it would be reasonably priced. By $30 and it would be a great deal. But for $58? Nope, sorry. Simply not worth it as it stands.

title: Wonderful invention, especially if you have hand or wrist problems
text:
I have bad carpal tunnel problems, and find it difficult to hold books for long periods of time, so I've been unable to read hardcovers at all, and only smallish paperbacks. I rely on an e-reader for the most part, and that's fine, but I have a big library of books, and I want to read them. Finally someone clued me in to the existence of The Book Seat, and I love it. It takes a bit of getting used to but it's well-designed to hold your book in just the right position for hands-free reading. You can also use it to hold your tablet or e-reader, so no matter what your format of choice, you're covered. It has a pouch on the back for, well, whatever, reading glasses, a pencil or pen, a candy bar, a charging cable. And it also has a loop that I use to hang it from my headboard when I'm not using it, so it's always right there with me when I want to read in bed.

Finally, someone has given me back my ability to read hard copy books. Woo hoo!

title: They are what they are, cheap pens.  But they're fun cheap pens.
text: I've bought two sets of these pens.  The first I loved, they seemed to last forever.  The second set, not so much.  But when I consider the price I paid and what I got for that price, I think it's still worth it, and would buy them again.  They're fun for however long they last, and useful to color code my notes to myself.  Don't treat them roughly, and don't expect them to last as long as your Bic, and you should be fine.

title: Huge footprint, good quality
text:
First off, this thing is huge. No really, I mean HUGE. It's taken me some time to find a place where I could actually set it up and test it. It's also persnickety, as most printers are, and sometimes whoopses the network settings. I just keep hitting "Retry" and eventually it says, "Oh yeah, there it is." It's messy to fill, and it's kind of loud. Basically it's a bit like having a baby dragon on the desk; it takes up a lot of space, does what it wants to do, and makes alarming noises.

However, the print quality is excellent on most things. It's not a printer for art prints as far as I can tell, but I'll cover that in a bit. First standard useage. Print is crisp and dark. Simple images are good, not fuzzy, or at least not so fuzzy that it really matters. Pages print quickly and cleanly, though I did have one glitch which I still haven't figured out, though it may have something to do with the art print I was trying to make.

I wanted to test the quality of image printing so I chose a digital painting I'd recently finished. (It's always a good idea to test the color profile before you send it out to be printed. No surprises then.) The printer didn't seem to be doing much of anything. There were the usual alarming noises, but no printing noises. Ten minutes later, I canceled the job and the paper came though with about a quarter of the image printed. This told me a couple of things: First, when it's printing something like an image, it's not noisy at all, and the alarming noises are the guts rumbling as things move through them. Second, it takes for-freaking-ever to print out even an 8x10 image. Granted, it was high resolution. Third, for all the time it spent dithering over the image, the quality wasn't what I'd hoped. The line was a little soft so the quality of the image was disappointing, not terribly, but not as good as I would have hoped based on the high quality of the other things I'd printed out. The colors were off but that isn't a huge thing, it happens. What you see on the page and what you see on the screen are rarely the same. However, the very next thing I printed was fubar'd. Everything printed on one line. I'm not sure what happened there, and have to retry that same file to see what happens next.

The quick start guide is fine, the user's manual is not as enlightening as I would hope. So here's a couple of tips: Take the quick start guide seriously when it tells you to take precautions as you fill the tanks. Careful as I was, my hands still ended up covered in ink. As I said above, it's messy to fill. And on first fill, don't assume that if you've filled the tanks up to the line, that you've done the right thing. In fact I don't know what those lines are for. When I tried to get the inks to charge, the printer kept telling me "Nope, not going to happen." Finally I got to to tell me to fill the tanks to at least half their capacity. It looked like they were three quarters filled, but I thought "What the heck?" and just squirted what was left of the ink into their respective tanks. And that did the trick. Don't trust that fill line.

Setting up the network was not easy, but I never have had a printer that didn't balk at network connections. I expected a problem, so was not surprised. That it did finally connect, and only dropped the connection a couple of times was actually a happy surprise. Setting up the Scan to Cloud was a snap. Honestly, the process was so well thought out that all I had to do in most cases was say, "Yup, please let this scanner send you stuff."

On the other hand, Google Cloud Print setup is daunting. It generates a warning in Chrome, and is confusing enough that I decided not to bother with it. I also didn't bother to set up the Fax function because I never fax anything.

I think if I'd realized how big it was I'd never have requested the opportunity to review it, but all things considered it's worked out fairly well. I don't think it would be my first choice of all-in-one printer for that reason, but overall it's a fast, high-quality printer. If you need a powerhouse like this, I think it's a good deal.

title: My new favorite notebook
text:
I'm a fan of Moleskine notebooks and have been for a long time now, but they can be pricey. Recently I came online to look for planners and found the Leuchtturm notebooks. While I didn't choose one as a free-form planner, I did decide to order one as a book for notes on a long-term writing project.

I'm so happy that I made that choice since I find I like the Leuchtteurms better than Moleskines! Not only did I get far more pages than I'd get in a Moleskine, but they are better organized with space for a title and date at the top of each one, page numbers at the bottom, and a table of contents in which you can keep track of your notes. As with Moleskine, there's an elastic band to keep the book shut when not in use, but there's also a pocket in the back in which to keep loose papers.

The Leuchtturms all come with a sheet of labels. There are labels for the spine, which makes it a good choice if you plan to shelve your notebooks at some point, and labels for the front cover. The only thing even remotely negative thing I can say about these labels is that the ones for the spine are a bit difficult to center, and will peel up along the edges or at the ends. I've fixed this by putting a strip of transparent tape over them.

The pages are good and thick, and fountain pen friendly, so you don't have to worry about a lot of bleed through. Really, these things are just grand.

title: Absolutely lovely
text:
A dear friend found this on my wishlist and sent it to me for my birthday this year, and I have been using it almost non-stop since it arrived. It's not only lovely to look at, it writes like a dream. I had a bit of trouble getting the cartridge in at first, but then I actually read the instructions and figured out what I was doing wrong. I mean, who knew that instructions were useful?

All joking aside, this pen is so lovely to use. I've used the Pilot disposables and while they're fine and they write well, this pen is just head-and-shoulders above them. The line is smooth and the ink flows perfectly, no skips, no blobs. And the pen feels good in my hand. Never underestimate the importance of hand feel with a pen. It's like mouth feel with food, when it's wrong you simply won't enjoy the experience no matter how nice everything else is.

The truly amazing thing is that you get all this in an affordably-priced pen. No, it's not one of those pens that makes you weep to behold. It's pretty though, and unless you're a collector or you're looking for something status-y, I honestly question the sense in paying more than about $25 for any pen. But then you wouldn't be looking at this review if either of those things applied. Rather you're looking for a fountain pen that will touch a chord for you, a pen that will make you feel more authentic somehow, a pen that harks back to a time when writing things by hand was the norm, when authors hunkered down in their rooms and produced their novels in longhand, and hostesses wrote out invitations in their best cursive. A time when people actually wrote thank you notes as opposed to texting things like "Thnx, UR teh roxxors." Not that I have anything against texting, mind you, I do a lot of it. It's just that sometimes you want to take the time to do things the old fashioned way.

So yeah, this pen? Teh Roxxors.

title: Really nice desktop planner
text:
I have to say that I've rarely been disappointed by the AT-A-GLANCE line of planners. They're usually well thought out, with good, clean designs, and ample room for your assignments, meetings, and the like. This particular planner is no exception to the high quality of AAG products. It's a handsome book with a cover that feels a bit like soft leather. It feels nice in the hand. The design is not fancy, just thirteen months (July 2015 through July 2016) and pages for Contacts and Notes, with reference and event calendars, a holiday list (rather comprehensive) and time zones and area codes for the US

You get a two-page month-at-a-glance view, plus two-page weekly views which gives ample room for anything but the most detailed diary entries. It's full size at approximately 8.5"x11", and so is more of a desk calendar than a carry-along. The unfussy color scheme is beige and white which makes it suitable for anyone or any situation.

This isn't one of those planners where you can keep your entire life in one place. I had one of those. You lose it, you have to start over as someone else. This is just a nice, neat, ultimately disposable planner for the academic year.

title: Nicely thought out design
text:
I really like this portfolio. It's well thought out with ample room inside for folders, brochures, and even a small tablet. It has a pocket which, to my surprise, fit my Firephone with its somewhat bulky case, and there is ample room for other bits and bobs that you might need in a meeting. It comes with a refillable pad of recycled paper.

It seems pretty sturdy. The zipper is large and easy to open and close, and the stitching looks solid, though time and use will tell, of course. The highest praise I can give is that I think it's worth the price.

Disclaimer: I was sent this product in exchange for an honest review.

title: Tiny but useful
text:
Disclaimer: I was sent this product in exchange for an honest review.

Let me be upfront here: I'm not going to talk about passports because that's not why I chose this bag for review. I chose it because I like small bags. The one I carry on a regular basis is only a bit bigger than this. But I can fit all my credit cards and cash in the front zippered pocket, my glasses and lipstick in the top pocket, and my cell phone -- which is not small -- in the clear pocket, and I'm good to go. I can also clip my carabiner through the pen loop on the side, and carry my keys on the bag. This gives me everything I need for a dinner-and-movie night or a quick trip out to the store. The strap is long enough that it can be used cross-body, making it hands-free, or can be shortened, and the end tucked into the bag to make a hand strap.

Let me be clear: There's not a lot of space to spare when I put my things in this purse. I'm not going to take this to work, on a day-long shopping trip, or use it when I'm traveling except to hold a passport, tickets, and a few other small things I need to have handy. If you want a truly small purse that's no-frills (except for the color, which is lovely) then this bag may be for you. title: A very nice pen for the money
text:
Short: My Pilot MR writes well. It's large but not huge. It looks fancy but not tacky.

Longer:
I wound up buying a Pilot MR "Animal" White Tiger (medium nib) as well as a Pilot MR Retro Pop Red (fine nib) along with two Parker Vector (medium nib) fountain pens, which are in the same $10-$15 price range. The Retro Pop has an anodized aluminum-like finish, and the Animal has a glossy lacquer-like finish. Both seem pretty scratch-resistant. I really like how both of my Pilot pens write, and I think they should fit the bill for anyone who wants something that stands out more than a typical pen, but isn't huge and too flashy.

I like my Parker Vectors, too, but given the choice I'd take the Pilot MRs. They write more smoothly, look like a higher-end pen, and came with an ink cartridge and converter. On the other hand, the Vectors are more understated, smaller and easier to pocket, and they're less prone to having little ink droplets escape the nib when capped. The Pilot MR medium nib draws a slightly finer line than the Parker Vector medium, but it could be a difference in ink viscosity. I'll be using both as everyday pens, but I'll be making more effort to take good care of the Pilots and in the future I'm more likely to keep collecting Pilot pens.

First, the paper is smooth - if you're like I was until recently and never paid attention to paper you write on - and you write a lot or enjoy writing, try Clairefontaine notebooks or stationary. Do try their paper. Smooth. No bleed-through. No show-through. I keep thinking of reasons to write - it's that nice. (Fountain pen friendly, too) Second, the spiral bound notebook itself is the same really high quality as the paper.  I had my doubts so I ordered one. Just one. I'm not a "verified purchaser" and have no connections with the seller or Clairefontaine. I'm blown away by how well this notebook is made! It's not stiff or uncomfortable to carry - just the opposite. Somehow Clairefontaine figured out how to make an attractive, well-designed, easy-carry spiral notebook that won't come apart and won't get hung on everything you're wearing and carrying.  Especially for college students or adults wanting a spiral-bound notebook.

I'll give the Metro another go, but sadly I'm not chancing this style in a Fine pt again, even though it's a really gorgeous pen.

Happy ending!

title: Barely magnetic, can't use standard dry erase markers
text:
Standard dry erase markers are not particularly effective on this surface, even bold, new chisel tips. You just cannot see the marks with dry erase markers very wel. I had a handful of wet-erase overhead transparency markers, and these work great, however. Those clean up with a damp paper towel, but not the same as dry erase, if that's the effect you're going for.

I purchased three of these for my office to mount vertically, side by side, with a few inches between. Two of the three had rounded corners, and one had squared corners. If you get multiples and this is aesthetically important to you, beware.

The magnets they included (two pink ones per board) do stick to the board, but since the glass is fairly thick and there's just a thin sheet of metal in the back, most magnetic things (marker/eraser holder, regular refrigerator magnets) don't stick. You will need to find very strong magnets if you want to use the surface for that purpose.

title: Easy to Use/Beginner Friendly
text:
Widely considered the go to beginner fountain pen and for good reason. I've purchased two of them, medium and fine point. They are both easy to use and came with a black ink cartridge (not intended to be refilled but can be done with a blunt syringe).

What to know before buying:
-The medium is quite wide especially with normal paper, the ink is prone to feathering. For this reason I would recommend the fine nib to start.
-You need ink to refill the pen, one cartridge lasts a little while but doing a lot of writing I used it up in less than a week.
-It comes with a converter but you will need fountain pen specific ink to use it - India ink will ruin the pen

Overall great price and lives up to the hype.

title: Do you know what “high quality” paper means?
text:
Yes the paper is very “high quality” but let’s take a look at what that means:

High quality doesn’t necessarily mean thick or heavy. Or fully opaque. This is high end paper in that it is well-made, and it’s a sheet that’s thick enough to write on both sides, thin enough for the journal to lay flat and to fit a lot of pages in the book. The coating repels ink enough for it to not bleed through, but not so much it never dries. These are difficult properties to balance and Leuchtturm does it well, hence the expense.

Cheaper journals exist with thicker heavier papers without a coating, which ink bleeds through in nothing flat because they “wick” ink.

Rhodia also has high end paper which is different - not better or worse. It is thicker, and the Journal has fewer pages as a result. Its coating repels ink more so there is less chance of bleeding or ghosting but more smearing.

If you have a pen that scratches the paper and damages the coating you’ll get bleed through. If your ink is wet and dark it’ll “ghost”. That’s not a sign the paper is poor quality but that - if you can’t handle ghosting - this paper isn’t for you.

I get bleeding with fine point fountain pens because they scratch the coating and damage the paper. Surprisingly I get *less* bleeding with a broader nib that runs really wet, and A Noodler’s Bulletproof ink, probably because the pen sets the ink on top of the coating where it dries. Ghosting is most minimal with Pigma Micron pens. Ghosting is also something people often get over, once they write on the other side. Or they don’t and they buy another journal.

They are well bound. I’ve worked in printing and this type of binding is appropriate to the application and the most lasting. It’s also expensive to execute especially with numbered and dotted or lined pages. The pockets, cover, and ribbons hold up better than cheaper brands and the inclusion of stickers that really stick well - not just one but an assortment - is not cheap.

I’ve tried tons of competitors and it’s only Leuchtturm that hold up well and provide the features I need (numbered pages, index, pocket, elastic, ribbons, lots of colors). I have these in every size and use several a year. I have one on my desk at work I’ve used to collect work knowledge for 2 years, I use it several times a day, and it looks like new. I have another two I’ve been using heavily for 2 years for genealogy research. I go through 1 every 6 months for my Bullet Journal. Even some having gotten wet didn’t cause much damage (again, coated paper, good binding).

So. The price is appropriate. The product works as designed and then some. The details do make a difference, as they say, and are very well done. As long as your personal preference is toward more pages per journal and better laying flat, and to less smearing, and you can handle ghosting, you’ll find lots of use and tons of pens that work well.

title: Some Pluses some Minuses
text:
So it's fun to trash talk Leuchtturm and all, and with Bullet Journaling taking off, and Alibaba so easy to access, there will be many entries into the field who try to one-up the leader. A friend got this for me and it's what it claims to be (hence the four stars, when in the field of similar journals I think it's a 3 star product suitable for very few). For a number of reasons I passed it along and bought another Leuchtturm.

Paper quality is hard to quantify, and reaching for a higher number in gsm is about all a customer has. All this really says is how much the paper weighs. I've had 120gsm coloring book paper bleed with markers that don't bleed in Leuchtturm 90gsm paper because Leuchtturm and Rhodia are coated to be ink resistant.

That being said if your number one complaint is ghosting (where you can see the image a little but the ink hasn't actually penetrated the page), this may be better for you than Leuchtturm or Rhodia. Personally I find it more visually distracting that this has such dark dots compared to what I'm used to. I'll take ghosting over that. And I like being able to see thro the page a tiny bit to copy the previous layout.

Ghosting bugged me a little too the first day of Bullet Journaling but once you write on the next page you don't see it and most people aren't bothered by it in the long run. It's the trade off for having a book that lays flat with zero coaxing and zero pressure on the binding. It's also how you keep a book slim with lots of pages.

I personally don't care for the paper in this, because feathering is the thing that makes me crazy. My Bullet Journaling routine also requires a back pocket in the journal, and a professional grown up appearance which I feel is lacking with the cute embossing. I also prefer making my own pen log and don't care for this index.

So. Go for it if you like the outside pattern and heavy paper is more important than anything else. Journals are a very personal choice. I'm going to stick with that other brand because "I ain't afraid of no ghost" and the other features from the slimness to the pocket to the professional exterior are what I need.

I haven't had an opportunity to put them to the test and don't expect to, in the way I use my Bullet Journal (a Leuchtturm). I may migrate ongoing collections to them, like recipes. It seems it's the type of paper that I've found holds up well to fountain pens that don't scratch the paper too deeply (in a hand that doesn't press too hard), Pigma Micron markers, Tombow brush pens, and the like.

You'll probably like these if you want a place to take notes or journal just in a linear way, and never refer back except by date. I'd recommend them to everyone for an "appendix" to a Bullet Journal, for ongoing collections, if only they had page numbers.

To keep costs down, I imagine, you can tell someone printed large sheets of just dots and sliced them into books. So - we have inconsistent margins, a little crookedness to the rows ... also the dots are larger and darker than the Leuchtturm so more intrusive.

I mention Leuchtturm only as a point of reference, for this probably isn't intended to compete.

If you're looking for something like a composition book that's basic and well made, this will work. Anyone who does Bullet Journaling or DIY planners and wants to collect information and write things they may refer back to probably should opt for something different.

title: Not the same as pictured
text: I have the Neon pack of these markers. They are awesome on my white Quartet glass whiteboard. The neon markers have to be shaken, then primed before the first use by depressing the nib until it is saturated. The neon Quartet dry erase markers work wonderfully, so I wanted to buy these additional colors. The picture shows the markers are the same kind that needs to be shaken and primed before use (above the word Marker, in the picture, it says 'SHAKE'/'PUMP') and the bottoms of the markers are clear and you can see the liquid in them. The markers I received do not say 'SHAKE'/'PUMP', they do not have a nib that needs priming, and the bottoms of the markers are made of an opaque plastic, rather than the clear plastic which exposes the liquid as in the picture.  They performed mediocre.  The blue, black and green markers were just fine, but the red marker was very weak - not bold at all.  The reason it was so important for me to have the markers that need to be primed like the neon colored markers, is that I wanted a marker that would perform as well as the neon. The neon markers are more like a paint-marker and write very bold, even on the white glass board.  I will try ordering from a different supplier. text: I've been using these pens since 2007 and while I've tried other pens more and less expensive, I always go back to Microns. Something about the way they formulate the ink is special. Sakura's inks are the darkest and most fade resistant of all the inking pens I've used. Whether they smear depends on the paper you;re using. It doesn't smear on copy or cardstock, but it can smear on smooth papers like marker or smooth Bristol. It also doesn't bleed through. I would not recommend these for general writing as the nib can be quite thin and break under heavy writing. They are excellent for drawing, sketching, drafting, and inking. There is some degree of smearing on marker paper if you color over them with marker. I find that prismacolor markers smear more than copic markers. Erasing over the lines can also lighten the ink on smooth papers, not so much on bond paper. Microns can last a long time if you remember to cap them when not in use and store hem in a dry dark place.

title: Great pen at a great price
text:
I have a large collection of fountain pens, new and antique, cheap to “what was I thinking?”, and have used fountain pens since I was in elementary school, 55 years ago, so I tend to be picky.

This pen is an excellent buy. I prefer extra fine nibs, but as these pens are from Japan (their nibs write much finer lines than their Western equivalents), I opted for a fine point. It was a good choice, laying down a line a bit finer than American or European extra fine nibs, smooth as silk, with good ink flow right out of the box. The pen is about 3/4 of an inch shorter than the Pilot Metropolitan and noticeably lighter, but doesn’t feel at all flimsy. The cap posts nicely while using and feels good in the hand. The slate grey is a nice, understated color - grey with a blue undertone - not drab.

This would be an excellent “everyday” pen, particularly if you don’t want something large in a pocket or bag. At this price, it would be a solid choice as a pen for someone who is ready to step up from disposable fountain pens but doesn’t want to spend a fortune. I would recommend buying the Pilot CON-40 converter as well, as this pen comes with only one cartridge and no converter. The only possible drawback I can see is the size - a person who has large hands or is more comfortable writing with a larger and/or heavier pen may find this too small. Other than that, very highly recommended.

title: Good Starter Pen
text:
I wanted an affordable entry into the fountain pen hobby and this fits the bill.

It comes in a plastic case with a clear window, which offers a nice touch for the price point.

I ordered a medium nib and I wrote about 20 pages in an A5 journal before the cartridge ran out of ink. The included squeeze converter lasted 17 pages in the same journal. I noticed no skipping. It did not write immediately out of the box so I squeezed the cartridge a bit and that immediately solved the issue, which never recurred.

The grip section feels a tad small in my large hands so I ordered another pen once I found I enjoyed fountain pen writing. I do not regret this purchase for one second because I wanted to test the waters with an inexpensive option and this pen served its purpose well.

I strongly endorse this product for fountain pen beginners.
