text: I'd prefer a slightly lighter color of blue, but this looks good. I especially appreciate that the ink dries quickly enough that I don't smear it around - a real problem for the left handed. I use this with a Metro fine nib and it is my go-to writing combo.

title: Smooth writing, even for a lefty
text: I have been a fountain pen user on and off for decades. I decided to give these Pilot MR/Metropolitans a try as I'd read good things about them. IMHO, fine nibs are the only way to go. This is a terrific pen, and the retro colors and designs look great and makes them easy to find on a cluttered desk. I bought a second one in a different color and take it with me when I know I'll need a pen. I bought some of the blue cartridges and like them even better. It is a bargain, buy one... maybe two.

title: Amazing!
text:
Pros: People give me room to sit on the subway when I pull this out; Burnt edges suggest this was pulled from a good old fashioned book burning; Perfect for recording my manifesto, spells I'm trying out, and secret rites; Binding is not tight enough to effectively press small to medium sized insects
Cons: Plain front cover - I wish there were customization options (e.g., Bosch panel) or custom text (preferably in the Fraktur font); Burnt smell fades over time

title: Poor zippers
text: I expected these to be like some similar bags I had purchased on Amazon. However, the zippers on these are quite poor.

title: Works with a Micron-style pen
text: I had hoped it would be work with these pens but wasn't sure if it would be big enough. It is, and all the pieces appear to be pretty well constructed.

title: Opaque, good color variety
text:
These are standard for Gelly Roll Moonlight. Gelly Roll quality (very nice), and like the other Moonlight pens, they are opaque and matte. They are not dimensional like the Souffle, and they do not have the slight sheen and plastic-y feel when dry. They are not permanent, so they don't layer well, especially as the texture is so different from the other lines of Gelly Roll.

These are good pens, and I love the color variety. These more neutral colors can be hard to find, and it really fills out the set. The one criticism I have of the colors is that like other Gelly Roll lines, it does not have a red. Sakura, please listen: we need a red! But yes, they are good and I will buy them again.

title: The paper is waterproof, but the writing isn't.
text: If you want your notes to stay on the page, you'll need to use a permanent marker.

title: High quality build
text:
I will say it takes a little coordination (or practice and muscle memory, for the uncoordinated like me); but punching the holes without it generally takes more skill. This helps you keep track of what you're doing by having very regular measurements for spacing your holes.

What really impresses me is the build quality of the whole set. The large "screws" that hold it together while you're punching are plastic, but they are sturdy and do a good job of holding everything securely. And the awl or "pointy tool" as I've heard it called by some, stands up to some wear. I've gone through several others of different brands that looked as strong but weren't, in the time that I've had this one just plug away. It's still sharp after several years of use, and the metal is still as strong and straight as it was when I got it. The tip hasn't bent, either. The handle is well glued, and there is no wobbling to it.

My only frustration is that I've lost one of the screws and I don't know how to replace it.

title: Cute
text: It's really cute, but I worry about it being a little waxy.

title: They do what they're supposed to.
text: What can I say? They are paperclips and they work as they should.

title: Almost identical to the Ikea ones.
text: I hang these as pencil cans on the side of a rolling cart, and they work very well this way. The curve of the plastic is a little different and makes it harder to open to slide onto the cart side than the actual Ikea one I have there; but once there, I don't notice any difference. They are well-made and handy.

title: They work as expected.
text:
I mostly use one pocket pen holder (the rest are for backup or when another use arises), but have tried the clip holders as well, and both work well. They have a snug, reliable fit, and I trust my pens in them. The one that I use is on an iPad case, and holds two off-brand styluses. I could probably fit a third if I had reason to, but it would be a less comfortable fit. Both of my styluses have clips, so I clip them onto the fabric of the pocket and they are very secure. The only difficulty is that the fabric isn't stiff at all, so the clips don't slide on smoothly.

I am very happy with this purchase and highly recommend it. The one piece of advice I would give is be careful where you adhere them because they can make it lumpy to hold or set down while the case is open.

title: They really motivated my son to read.
text: My son was having trouble with understanding what reading was for, so he was making no progress. These books made the difference. They are easy for the very earliest beginning reader, and they are clear and written in a sensible order. I bought mine elsewhere and they were bigger than these. Unfortunately, I think these considerably smaller books are harder for young eyes to focus on. Still, they are worth it.

title: Beautiful, vibrant ink!
text: This "brilliant red" is a lovely warm red.  It flows well in the two pens I loaded with it, and I find it very easy to write with.

title: They aren't fancy, but they're cute and the work.
text: I like the pretty colors, but what really attracted me to these binder rings is that when they close, there is no bump. I made a junk journal with them and I like that it can open all the way or fold open all the way. A bumpy hinge would have made it more awkward, and wouldn't have looked as good. Even without a hinge, they are surprisingly easy to use, because the plastic is so flexible.

title: Good paper storage for tight spaces.
text: The design is clever and they work as expected. They are not super sturdy, but not flimsy either, and if used as intended, they should last OK. The only downside for me is that they really aren't practical for any size paper other than letter size or close to it. But letter size must be put in very neatly or it covers up the tabs. Overall I am pleased with them.

title: You'll be addicted.
text: I love these pens so much I keep on buying them. The ink goes on so smooth and the translucent shine is perfect for so many purposes the Glaze pens never go on streaky. Sheer fun to use.

title: The best I've tried.
text:
So far, I think I've bought six of these. Two got lost, two were damaged by hyperactive kids, and on one, the shavings compartment hinge broke. It's possible that that was due to a hyperactive kid, too, though.

I've used several models of Kum pencil sharpeners, and I have liked them all. This is my favorite, though, because 1, it has a catcher, 2, the blades in this one are carbon steel, and 3, I just love the long line sharpening.

The only drawbacks are, for me, not all that important. The casing, and particularly the plastic shavings holder, could be stronger. The pencil pointer holes are a nice extra, but I find the built in pointers on the ends of most of my 2mm clutch pencils to be a better fit. I don't consider either of these things a dealbreaker.

title: Wow. I am impressed.
text:
I am startled at the weight this can hold! This rack probably weighs 20 lbs and I had tried everything I could think of to get it to stay put. It hangs from a hook but swings out wildly if not secured. This stuff not only secured it but is holding it up. The book is now just a security measure.

I found that to make it effective, it works best if you push it into the surface you are adhering it to... Like, really mash it. It works better with time, too. That is nice because it helps you to unstick it if it gets stuck to itself, and allows for repositioning.

title: Some of my favorite pens
text:
I just love my souffle pens, enough that I have them on subscribe and save.
The ink is opaque and fairly permanent, with a slightly chalky texture when dry. The flow is lovely. The nib allows it to come out at a steady rate, and although it is controllable, it feels like it's just flowing. It had a high surface tension, and doesn't really absorb into the paper, so it gives the impression of puddling; that is how they get their dimensional quality.
A few things to be aware of: if you go over water soluble ink, it will pick up a little bit of the color. It is difficult to layer over it because of the chalky texture. After they are opened (the protective wax tip removed) if they are not used for a while the ink in the tip will dry out, but scribbling on some scratch paper will usually fix it.

title: The high quality I expected
text: This ink is as beautiful as I expected. It is not an ink that changes color depending on how much is laid down, but it does darken with heavier application. It flows quite well with my medium nib but is not so wet that it gets difficult to handle with anything but a fine nib. I have not tried it with anything but medium and fine, but it works nicely with both.

title: Good value, mixed results
text: I bought these for three kids who are very tough on things. Two are still intact into the second semester, which is a record, but one of them was destroyed in the first week. They seem to be a good value.

title: Much sturdier than other inexpensive clipboards
text: The clipboards themselves are surprisingly good. They are thick and hard, much more so than other inexpensive clipboards I have bought. The only real complaint I have is with the retractable hanging bit. Some of the holes are at an odd angle, making them difficult to hang from small hooks, and I wish they slid out more tightly so they wouldn't slide down quite so easily while being hung. If I ever need a large number of clipboards again, I would buy these again.

title: Awesome selection of colors
text:
I'm happy with these dots, and I love the color selection. They stick well, too.
The only downside, and the reason I didn't give it a 5, is that they are glossy-coated, which makes them hard to write on. Even permanent marker needs to be marked more than once for it to get dark. I would give them 5 stars if they were more papery.

title: Buying again. Will buy again.
text: Basically I need two kinds of everyday writing pens: a thin tip and a comfortable, smooth pen, usually broader. The .7mm medium tip Inkjoy Gel Pens are perfect for my smooth, broader writing. I hate scratchy pens, and almost all ball points offer more resistance than I like. Most other colored gel pens are impractical for normal writing. These are perfect. They glide on the paper, and write on more surfaces than ball point or rollerball. The comfort grip makes them even nicer to use. The color selection, even in the smaller packs, is good. It covers a good range. The larger packs have more colors, which is nice, though some of them have repeats of the most popular colors. This is the second pack I've bought, and I am certain I will buy many more.

title: Easy to customize, and easily refillable.
text:
I was pretty excited about this. I ordered in two sizes, and am very pleased. I got them in A4 and B5 sizes. If you aren't familiar with size numbering, A4 is standard notebook size and B5 is, I believe, a European size standard. It is about the size of a composition book.

As a junk journal artist, I am always on the lookout for new styles of book and binding, and this is unlike anything I've seen before. It is much sturdier than a spiral notebook, and obviously more customizable. You can buy paper already cut to fit in the book, or you can use a special hole puncher to use your paper of choice. The hole puncher is not difficult at all, but if you prefer the convenience, the paper is easier.

Pros:
* It is pretty easy to use. Just take a pen or similarly shaped object, stick one end down inside the first few rings, and then lift the other end. You can "zip" down the rings from there.
* Because it has so many rings, unlike an ordinary binder with two or three notebook rings, the paper is more firmly set in the notebook.
* It takes up less room than a standard binder, so is more portable.
* It looks better than either a binder or a spiral notebook, especially as you can customize your cover according to your taste. It looks more "book-like," too.
* Unlike many other refillable notebooks that look similar, the holes in the paper are not slit for insertion, making the paper and cover much more secure.
* You can remove and refill pages as needed.

Cons:
* At the time of this review, Amazon does not carry a larger ring unless you buy the pre-filled notebook, so you can fit a limited number of pages.
* I suspect you have a limited number of openings before the plastic weakens and doesn't fit together as well. Although it's reasonably strong, it could be stronger. I'm not sure how much stronger, though, because it might reduce flexibility for opening.
* The size selection, so far, is limited. I would love to see A5 available.

All in all, I am very excited about this product. I am waiting for the pre-filled one to arrive to use for my next bullet journal. I can't wait!

title: They are just like they look.
text: They are exactly what they are supposed to be. We are using them as reward tokens, and they work well for the purpose.

title: Best I've tried.
text: I've tried so many brands, and each one had serious limitations, especially not enough adhesive. This is the only one I have found that works right, works well on most paper surfaces, and doesn't jam up. My only disappointment is that it is disposable, not refillable. I don't like filling landfills unnecessarily. Also, I wish they made a dot version.

title: Works consistently well
text: It's obviously one of the lowest price shredders, so don't expect luxury features; but it works well, and has never given me any trouble. It can handle up to 6 papers at a time,but it does better with three or less. It works better than the last shredder I had, which was a name brand.

title: Clever circle making tool.
text:
This is a tremendously helpful tool for making accurate circles. the smaller circles on the inside you can achieve by using it as a stencil/template. Then if you look closely, you will see a row of tiny holes. Those are for the bigger circles. You put your pen or pencil inside the one that is indicated by the size you want, and swivel the clear plastic part within the green frame, while holding the frame still. It's a very clever design, and works pretty well.

The difficult parts, though, and the reason I only gave it four stars, are that it's hard to get a smooth circle in the smaller sizes of the swivel sizes, and it is difficult to hold down. It can be a little awkward to use on a non ideal, flat surface, such as inside a journal. It is still useful enough that I highly recommend it.

title: Excellent point.
text:
Why get a long point sharpener? One reason is that it takes a little longer to get dull, and makes better use of the lead. Even more, though, you have more control over your strokes. You can do larger areas with the side of the lead, preserving the tip for the places where you need a sharp line. If you have high end pencils, this can be a good savings. You want the pencils to last as long as possible.

The long point from this sharpener is lovely, and the blades are sharp and precise. This pencil sharpener is a little different from the twisty ones you remember from school. It has two holes, but they are not for two different sizes of pencils. Rather, the first hole is for shaping the wood and the second is for shaping the lead. This is what enables it to get such a long point.

Kum pencil sharpeners already have a strong reputation with strong, sharp titanium blades. I had one already that I liked a lot, but it didn't have a shavings catcher so I thought I would upgrade, especially when I saw this long point sharpener. I was not disappointed. I was a little confused because the sharpener arrived in a box that is apparently the same box used for an almost identical sharpener that also comes with a pencil pointer in the side for 2mm lead holder leads. The box indicated it, but it wasn't the case. (No problem, I hadn't ordered one with the lead pointer, so I had no reason to expect one.)

The one thing to be aware of is that it can't do miracles on a pencil that doesn't have the lead right in the middle. Some of my Prismacolors are unevenly leaded, and it was impossible to get those sharp in this sharpener. The fault is really with the pencil, though, not the sharpener. A pencil that is not evenly filled will always be hard to sharpen. (Derwent Colorsoft and Faber Castell Polychromos are similar quality colored pencils but more centered.) I've included a photo of pencils sharpened with this sharpener alongside some that are not yet sharpened.

title: Works OK, but frustrating
text:
It works, but it is awkward in several ways. Mostly, it's because of the rotary action. It's not just a matter of of getting used to it, though it's part of it. Here are some of my issues :
- It's clumsy to get your lead into. You have to put in, and it will go into an upper part. Then you have to wiggle and change your angle until the lead reaches the lower part, where the grinder is.

-It takes longer than the simpler twist style.

- You can't see your lead at all, so you have to guess when it's sharp, check the lead, then go through the whole irritating process again if it isn't.

- Even when your lead is in the grinder you must hold it at a very specific angle. Too close and the lead doesn't touch the grinder. Too far, and the tip breaks.

- It is non-intuitive. Rubbing a lead in a circle around a grinder is unnecessarily complicated compared to to simply twisting either a lead holder or a sharpener.

Like I said, it works. If you really like rotary pointers you might like it. But frankly, I consistently get better results even with the dinky pointers built into the end of my super-cheap, made-in-China, no-brand clutches.

title: My favorite pens for using in my bullet journal.
text:
These are marketed for coloring, and they are good for the fine details in the Johanna Basford books. My main reason for buying them, however, was for bullet journaling. I like using different colors to encourage myself to keep up with using my planner, and also to help me visually differentiate between different parts of a page. They help me to be a little more organized.

What I like about them:
* The wide variety of colors, all of which are vivid and strongly pigmented.
* The fine line is good for writing in small spaces.
* The nib is smooth and writes comfortably. This is the main reason I prefer these over the Stabilo .88, which I find to be scratchy.
* The box is well designed to keep the pens in. It's not a super special strength or anything, but it keeps them organized and easy to remove and replace in the same spot.
* They are good for multiple uses both practical and artististic.
* I have experienced almost no ghosting or bleeding, on paper that other pens of similar type have bled through.
* Even on super smooth paper, they write flawlessly. Roller balls and the like sometimes have trouble on very smooth papers, but these will write on just about anything.

title: Good pens for a good price
text:
I will start by saying that I got these (a 30 pack) at less than half price on a lightning deal, or I might have waited longer to buy them. That said, they are pretty good pens. I will start with the basics: they flow well and have a good variety of colors. Almost all of them are glitter or metallic.

The good:
* They all flow well. About half of them needed a good shake to get started, but that's typical for pens that have been in storage. Once they started, they kept going.
* They feel good. They are a good weight, they have a good .7 nib size, and the nibs roll smoothly. The grip is comfortable.
* The colors are a good variety. I was especially pleased to find three reds, as I find reds lacking in most brands. There is a warm red, a cool red, and a wine red. Five of the neon colors look neon to me, but the other two were still nice colors. The blues in each group are especially vivid.
* The case is high quality. The pens snap into place and it looks like it will last, as it is sturdy. I recommend keeping them in the case, or it may be hard to tell glitter from metallic at a glance. They come organized in a sensible order.
* They appear to be almost completely waterproof. This is important for me, because I do mixed media art journaling, and I don't want my writing to smear if I cover it with a wet medium.

The bad: Well, not bad, but less than optimal...
* I wish there were more than three regular colors (non metallic, non glittery.)
* Coverage is a little splotchy. Not bad, but not as good as Gelly Roll.
* Non opaque. Some of the neons are slightly opaque, but mostly they will not work well on dark colors.
* Little bleeding, but significant ghosting. (This was sampled on cheap printer paper. Obviously they will ghost less on better paper.)

My conclusion: These were definitely worth the Lightning Deal price, and are probably worth the full price, too. I like having colors that Gelly Roll doesn't have, and although they are not the best gel pens I've used, they are pleasant and reasonably high quality.

Update: I've had these for a couple of years now. They were in storage for a while. I am impressed that they did not dry out. A few of them are finicky now, and need shaken to bring the ink down, but they still work.

title: Labels don't have to be ugly.
text: These labels are simple but attractive, and the kraft paper is less glaring than white. They are good for labeling food jars and such, but I use them in my bullet journal. I think they give it a classic touch. And of course, they are Avery and meet the usual Avery quality standards.

title: Attractive pen that writes well.
text:
A beautiful fountain pen that many people recommend for an excellent "starter" pen. The Retro Pop collection is, I believe, part of the Metropolitan collection, but with little bits of decoration near the nib/cap. I got this in red to put red ink in, and you can get many colors to keep multiple ink colors in pens at once.

I will warn that the ink (as with other Pilot fountain pen ink I've used) bleeds like crazy. It is the only ink I have found that will bleed through ClaireFontaine paper. You have the option of using a different ink from the start, or you can use it with the expectation of only using one side of the page. Even with the enclosed ink being this wet, it's not a deal breaker for me, as I really like the pen a lot. I will be buying more in other colors.

title: Good for matching pen color to ink color
text: These fountain pens work well enough, and it's nice to have an assortment of colors so that you can match the barrel color to the ink color. They are definitely student grade, though and feel too light to hold. They also look like student grade. They are pretty good starter fountain pens, at a very good price.

title: Pretty bookmarks
text: These magnetic bookmarks are very handy. They are less heavy than some others I've used in the past, which is helpful when turning pages. The magnets are strong enough to hold fairly well, but not strong enough that two bookmarked pages are likely to stick together. I would like it if they were even a little less heavy, but I don't know if that's even possible. All in all, they are a fantastic value while being aesthetically pleasing. I use them in my bullet journal, and they serve a second purpose as well: acting as a tab. The set is big enough that you can use multiples at a time.

title: A beautiful color
text: This ink is stunning - and I mean stunning. It's somewhere between a purple and a rich blue, maybe more on the blue side. It is a standard ink, meaning it has the ordinary qualities: it is not waterproof or archival, which means it isn't fade resistant but is easier to clean from a fountain pen than a waterproof or semi waterproof.

title: Decent pen, but not flex.
text: A very attractive pen, and it writes nicely. It isn't a flex nib, though.

title: Holds a heavy load of 9x12 paper tablets and pads.
text: I originally got one of these when I was student teaching several years ago. It worked well, so I bought another one recently. This time it is to organize my art papers and pads by type. Most of my pads are 9x12, and the pockets can hold 2-3 books/tablets each. It is heavy, but the pockets are strong enough to handle it. The only negative is that it did not come with hooks. I didn't have any hooks small enough to go through the grommets, so I attached binder rings to the grommets and hung them from some over the door hooks, and it's working great. I should mention that the hooks were missing from the last one I bought too (we used clear packing tape that time). I don't know if they were missing or just not part of the package, but it's something to be aware of.

title: Surprisingly high quality.
text:
I really didn't expect these little notebooks to be great. I just figured they'd do the job. I wanted to insert them into my "fauxdori" and they were the right size, with dot grid. Boy, was I surprised. The quality is far better than any of the more expensive journals I've bought. The binding is glued, but appears quite sturdy. It does not lay flat, but if you break it in, it will lay fairly flat. But the thing that really startled me was when I did an "ink test" on the back page. I tried cheap pens, gel pens, watercolor pens, even fountain pens and dip pens, with both waterproof and non waterproof ink. One pen was old and didn't want to flow, so I wetted the tip; it leaked considerably after that, and left a big wet puddle of a letter. That was the only thing that bled through at all, and even that was far less than the bleeding I get on some books even with a medium application of a gel pen. There was some ghosting visible on the other side, but it was light. I am including photos of the front and back side of the ink test page.

My conclusion is that this inexpensive little set of books is of a quality comparable to a number of mid-range to expensive lines of books and papers.

title: Tiny, tiny grid. Top notch quality paper.
text:
I just got this because I needed graph paper. I didn't look closely enough (not the fault of the manufacturer... completely my own fault) and I didn't realize how small the grid would be. 8 per inch is miniscule!

However, I was pleasantly surprised when I started using it. I really wasn't keen on using it for its intended purpose, because the grid was so small, so I decided to practice brush writing on it. This paper is amazing quality. It takes the ink beautifully (though the grid lines resist slightly); yet there is no bleeding at all, and no feathering... And I put on a pretty heavy application. The ghosting is minimal. I didn't expect this lovely benefit, so I am very pleasantly surprised. Who would have thought such value paper would be such high quality?

title: Creamy and smooth
text: Oh my gosh, this paint marker is so pleasant to use! It's not like any other pen I've ever used. It's a bit like oil pastels, but much creamier. And it really is permanent. I tried it out on plastic as soon as I got it. Once it dried, I couldn't even scrape it off with my nails. I only bought one to try it before investing in a set. I will definitely be buying more. If you like a tactile experience with art, you will love the smoothness and creaminess of this marker.

title: Not waterproof, but works beautifully.
text:
I've read artists who say this is the only white gel pen for them. After trying it, I understand why. It is more opaque than an other brand I've used, even the good brands. It goes on with no hesitation, smoothly. So far it has worked on every journal surface I've tried it on, including over acrylic paint, texture mediums, and rough collages.

My only difficulty is that it is not waterproof. That is not necessarily a criticism, as for some purposes you want a pen that isn't waterproof. But for most of my purposes, I would prefer waterproof. When dry it does not smudge at all, but with even a tiny bit of moisture it completely reactivates.

If you use it for mixed media and want to waterproof it, my advice is this: First, spray it with a fixative. (Fixative should be used outdoors because of the fumes.) If you don't have a fixative or don't want to go outdoors, you can get slight protection with hairspray, though it's not as effective. Then take a [[ASIN:B003DNWYZ0 Plaid 34106 10-Piece Spouncer Set]] or makeup sponge and dab it straight up and down with a waterproof medium such as [[ASIN:B0027AAOSO Art Advantage 8-Ounce Acrylic Matte Gel, Medium]]. Your other option would be to get a different brand that is more water resistant, but this really is a pleasure to use.

title: Accurate and simple
text: This is an easy to use, accurate cutter. Not all trimmers are, and especially at this price. My last trimmer was off by just enough to prevent a 90 degree angle; this one isn't. The swing out arm means it can measure far more than you could otherwise, and the markings on the surface are very helpful for measuring common sizes. They, too, are straight and accurate.  The only two criticisms I have are fairly minor: 1, I wish that the numbers were marked at both top and bottom, because it can be hard to see the top markings when the paper is covering them up. 2, the blade (which is replaceable, and it comes with a spare!) is a tiny bit too easy to come out, and has fallen out without my realizing, so that I had to search for it. If you are more careful than I was, this shouldn't be an issue; and the flip side is that it is very, very easy to replace. The bottom line is that I suspect this is the best trimmer you will find for the price.

title: Compares to Sharpies, but with some differences.
text:
First, you need to know that these are permanent, alcohol based markers like the regular, non-metallic Sharpies. They have most of the same features: they will mark almost anything, are not opaque, and will bleed on ordinary paper. They are not identical to Sharpies, though, and have some advantages and disadvantages.

Pros:
* The case is fantastic. They come assorted into three different "families" of colors, arranged by hue, if that sort of thing matters to you. The case is also pretty sturdy. I didn't expect that.
* The color selection is better than Sharpies. More choices in one place.
* The tips are much more precisely shaped than the equivalent sized sharpies. The tip is pointy instead of round, giving a lot more precision.

Cons:
* I found them to be more dry and less smooth than sharpies. They weren't exactly dry, but not as "juicy" as Sharpies. Still, if you lay it on more slowly that will compensate.
* The ink barrel is smaller, so they will run out faster.

Neutral:
* This is either a positive or a negative depending on what you are looking for. The ink goes on less boldly, so you don't get a smooth, even layer of color. It's negative if you want it to look bright and smooth. On the other hand, this gives you more control over the strength of color, if you want to do any shading.
* Most of the colors blend a little better than Sharpies, but a few blend worse.

For those who are interested in shading, it takes a bit of practice, and you have to go dark to light. First you apply a dark color, and then you apply the lighter color in a similar hue and it will lighten the color that's already there. If you try to go light to dark, you will not be able to blend at all.

Overall, while I won't claim that these are amazing markers they are a pretty good deal, and they are enjoyable to use.

title: Pleasantly surprised
text: I thought this was going to be a cute/fun piece of junk but it turned out I really like using this pen. It works better than some of my far more expensive paint pens, and it flows very nicely. The only two things to be aware of are 1: the one that says it is red really is, even though the cap and pen look pink. 2: You do need to shake it and push in the nib before using, or you will get a nice flow of non-opaque ink. title: Respect the ink
text:
I loved this ink! I couldn't believe how full the bottle was when I opened it up. I thought it was one of those air bubbles that makes it look like it's all the way to the top, but no, the ink was that full! I carefully filled two pens with this, and secured the lid back on the bottle. I like the shade of blue it's personal preference for me, and Mr. Noodler makes awesome products.

Side note. As full as the bottle was, I left it on the counter and was going to bring it to work with me as thats where I use my pens the most. Well, as luck (bad luck) would have it, my wife was cleaning and decided to move the bottle. I don't quite know how this happened, but I suspect my curious 10 yr old was hoping she could figure out how to load up a pen I got for her, and didn't quite secure the light properly. Now, imagine if you will, someone reaching of a small 3oz bottle what could possibly go wrong, right! The cap let go of the bottle, the bottle hit the counter, the ink splashed on the wall, then the wife, then down the cabinets, on to the floor and into the dogs water bowl. This all occurred in just a second of two. I wasn't home at the time but I imagine there was some @#$%^@ and @^%@#$, and )#(#@ flying around while she fully took in what just happened and exactly what was in that little bottle.

Gents, learn from my mistake, when she calls you and yells at you because you don't know how to put the lid on properly, do NOT... I repeat do NOT say, "Well, if you weren't touching my things, that probably wouldn't have happened now would it..." or anything close to that. Have you ever seen National Lampoon's Vegas Vacation? Remember the beginning when they try to join the mile high club, and end Clark gets his foot and hand in the blue toilet water... well, coincidently this ink was also blue, and the wife's hand looked A LOT like Clark's hand in the movie. (She was less than thrilled when I pointed that out) Somehow she was able to clean it up, although she threw my ink away, now I'm waiting to get a new bottle in the very near future. I'm so glad I didn't buy the bulletproof ink I can't imagine her having a blue hand the rest of her life.

Buy this ink, respect your significant other's things and be careful with them.

Thanks for reading this.

title: meh
text:
I think the rotating mechanism kind of works, but not as well as just rotating the pencil myself. Using this pencil has taught me that I have actually been unconsciously rotating regular mechanical (or non-mechanical) pencils as an unconscious practice anyway. I think I do that better than this pencil does, so while it often seems to work okay, it never feels quite as sharp as I'd like, so if I don't concentrate on *not* manually rotating it as I write I just go back to old habits.

So basically, take a look at how use pencils. Maybe even take a little video while you are writing with one. I bet I'm not the only person who just unconsciously rotates their pencil whenever it feels less than sharp. If you do that, you don't need this pencil. In fact, this pencil will only be annoying.

This pencil also has a glaring design flaw. Using the eraser wears it down, obviously. But if you do that, and lose the extremely losable little plastic cap that goes over the eraser, you will no longer be able to click to advance the lead. Trust me, you will lose that little cap. They should just make this without an eraser, because it's lose-lose.

title: perfect
text:
I really love these notebooks. I find the size to be just right -- big enough to use for monthly and weekly calendar layouts, or for making hefty to-do lists, but small enough to fit in my bag without taking up too much space. I love that it has two bookmarks and the elastic to hold it closed. I love that it comes in hardcover, so it's harder for me to destroy it. And this might be my favorite paper for fountain pens. It feels nice with any pen, but I tend to use fountain pens. I have found that some paper meant specifically for fountain pens is too slick for my taste. This paper is very smooth, but a touch more porous than some fountain pen specific papers, and I really prefer it that way. I've been using a Micron Graphic 1 for my calendar outlines -- it does show through quite a bit, but that is not a problem because I line up my calendars so that they overlap with what is on the opposite side of the page, if that makes sense. Regular fountain pens don't show through to distraction.

I actually replaced my Hobonichi Techo planner with one of these. But went for the notebook instead of the planner so I can do a planner/BuJo hybrid with layouts the way I like them.

title: you get what you pay for...
text: For some reason I thought I would be one of those lucky people who didn't have problems with Prismas chronically breaking.  Nope.  Lack of quality control is strongly evident. Pencils arrived with clearly broken leads that just fall out every time you sharpen them, no matter how careful you are.  Pencils arrived with cracked casings.  Several leads clearly very out of center.  I have been able to draw some with these, and if you get a pencil that sharpens without the lead falling out it is a nice drawing experience.  What I have learned is that it's fun to draw with really soft pencils, and I will be saving my money to buy soft pencils that have excellent quality control, that can take more than a couple of layers, and that are light fast.  Still deciding between Derwent and Caran D'Ache.  I am confident that over time neither of those more expensive brands will prove to be much more expensive than Prismas that come damaged or unusable.

title: Compact and functional
text:

It easily fits all the colored pencils and accessories I need right now, with room in the back for things like my compact folding task light, 5x7 paper, a small tin of graphite pencils, and sharpeners. The little pockets in the front have plenty of room for other accessories like a 6" ruler and erasers. Two of the three pencil/pen/marker holder sections are held in with velcro and come out, and I can fit as much as I can in the back because I didn't need one of the sections and was able to remove it. I think my only minor complaints is that it seems like the elastic loops aren't all precisely the same size (not a big issue), and that there isn't a layer of protection for when you have two sections of pencils that lay against each other when the case is closed. I might find a small cloth I can put in there to provide a little cushioning. These are pretty minor things so I'm giving it 5 stars anyway.

This is a really convenient and cute case, and will travel well. I am very happy with my purchase.

It isn't that great for heavy-really heavy handed writers because you will feel the indentation on the pages.
Overall, I would purchase the journal again and recommend it to anyone who is looking for a good journal with minor flaws.

title: One of those rare products that is worth every penny.
text:
This is one of those few products where you take a chance, buy it, and feel like you got more than your money's worth.
I did a lot of looking for the desk that would be the right dimensions (not a full size office desk), was aesthetically pleasing, and would be comfortable/easy to use. Did a lot of comparing and narrowed it down to this model and one that cost around $560. The reviews for this desk were shining, while the more expensive desk complained of wobbliness and a few other issues.
Happy to report that the shining reviews on this desk were dead-on accurate. It's sturdy. It may be because I use it on carpet, but it came with four locking castors and I have no trouble moving it on my California shag carpet. The desk is a comfortable height and I'm 5'8. Adjusts easily, beautiful finish--looks like reddish oak to me. I'm an author, so I use this desk for long hours, all day long, raising it up and down as I feel fatigue either sitting or standing. Those actions take me five seconds to complete, and I'm back to work.
I love the size of the desk top and keyboard tray too. I wanted something that I could have in my living room without overwhelming the room and making it feel like an office. While not enormous, there is room on the top shelf for everything I need: my laptop, coffee, and phone. Or the phone can sit on the keyboard shelf. It really is the perfect size for me. I even 'modded' it by adding a drink holder for my water that attaches to the side and has a garbage bag that I turned into a holder for my pens/highlighers/remote control/etc. I also added a key ring loop (I had this laying around) beneath the desk top (Gorilla Glue'd it on) to help keep my computer cord from getting caught under the castors.
It's not perfect to use while sitting in my rocking/glider chair since the keyboard feels a little awkward, but it is useable and comfortable to do my social media work. Since my glider isn't an office chair, I don't fault the product one bit for not functioning at top capacity in this situation. In fact, I'm impressed that I can use it while sitting in my glider at all. Absolutely love this desk and would recommend to anyone who hates sitting all day and wants to give their back a break.

title: good for tints
text:
I have mixed feelings about this ink... 3.5 stars probably.

At first I was really hopeful, but I've had some time with it and it falls short in a couple areas. I would recommend it primarily to artists who want to mix it with other inks to produce tints/tones of other inks.

Using it as a pure white works OK with brushes or dip pens, it does work in fountain pens, but it's very subtle and will need multiple applications to be particularly visible. When brushed on, or using a dip pen it is more opaque... but for white highlights it doesn't come close to a Pentel Presto!

It looks white when you first put it down but it's quite translucent once dried (unless layered), and all but vanishes if put on too light, or used on lighter paper. It can be used similarly to a white gel pen over darker ink for highlights or on toned paper for lights marks, but again, if you're using it in a fountain pen be prepared to dab on that highlight several times before it starts to look opaque.

Given the claims on the label, and the De Atramentis site, this is probably more suitable to finished works of art than the ol' Gelly Roll, given it's waterproof and light-fast qualities, but it will take a little more effort in its application. I do like that, unlike gel pens, you aren't constantly going through disposable pens.

But if It goes on best with a dip pen or brush, then why not just use gauche?

The site claims that their artist inks are all mixable. I haven't bothered with other colors in this line, but the white ink seems to mix well enough with other brands' fountain pen inks.

What I got it for, as I like drawing in ink and sketching with fountain pens in particular, is to mix with other inks to produce specific shades. You can mix it with colored inks to produce tints, or with black for a nice gray. I mixed it 12:1 with De Atramentis Document Ink Black for a neutral gray that is lighter than other gray inks that I have, with a nice matte, opaque look when dry. I'll probably mix the next batch even lighter... I get asked all the time about it when showing my sketchbook, so it makes and impression.

Given that watering down fountain pen inks has limitations this ink has job security in my kit for making those lighter grays and tints, even if I don't expect it to become my primary white.

The biggest downer is that these grey tints transfer as easily as graphite, so probably you'll want a fixative.

title: Good ruler for graphic design work, very square

it is very strait, and very square, and the center line is spot on. I compared it to my Starrett combination square to see how accurate it really is and there is no appreciable deviation.

This ruler would be my recommendation for sketching page layouts (apps, web, or print) or any other graphic design work, any pen and paper designing (i.e. interiors, product design), bullet journaling, etc. or really any scenario where one wants a clear, flexible ruler. I would not recommend it for cutting, a knife will tear up the edge in no time.

title: Three-and-a-half-star nib holder
text:
This is a good nib holder. Three-and-a-half-stars.

You may find that you have to tweak your crow quill nibs to fit perfectly (they're too loose to start out with from my experience) but I've encountered that same problem on other nib holders, so I was prepared to cope with it.

It holds a crow quill (hunt 102, 107, 108), which is what I wanted it for. It also has 2 rings, similar to the Tachikawa nib holders, which I did not expect, so it holds larger nibs (such as hunt 99 drawing nibs, or G pen nibs).

I prefer this over the Speedball crow quill nib holder, the feel of the wood is better that the plastic (it's grippier without any sharp edges--although this holder comes with NO finish), the diameter is wider than the Speedball holder by about double the thickness at between 3/8 to 1/2 inch at the grip section, it's longer at about 6-1/2 inches without a nib in and is a little heavier than the Speedball holder, but not too heavy.

If you're reading this and the nib holder is out of stock, as it is at the time of my writing this, then you've got a good alternate in the Tachikawa Comic pens line. The nibs fit seems to be identical, the Tachikawa holders are around and inch-and-a-half shorter, but they have the advantage of being lacquered, and you can get them with rubbery grips if you'd prefer that.

title: Favorite for sketching
text:
This is my favorite eraser. You can use it much like a pencil and "draw" in white, adding in highlights, etc. and when erasing unwanted pencil marks you can easily leave in the lines you want, or avoid smudging pen lines which haven't fully dried.

It works well with graphite, less well with charcoal or colored pencils. Works on anything normally erasable.

PRO TIP: if you generally use the side for erasing, where possible, you can achieve and maintain a finer tip, much narrower than the 2.3mm width of the eraser; else cut the tip at an angle with a razor blade (as I would suggest doing with any eraser).

The eraser is soft enough to not damage the paper and the barrel fits closely, to help the tip remain fairly rigidly in place, allowing for great control. The body feels sturdy and it's refillable, and I expect it to last quite some time; I've been using the same one for almost two years now.

title: Cool pen for loose sketching and spotting blacks
text:
Cool pen, and well worth the cost if you're even slightly interested. It's better made than you might expect for a $10 pen and opens up a lot of possibilities for line variation, happy accidents, and a free and energetic quality to your mark making.

I personally love to use it for loose sketching, and for spotting blacks when sketching with an extra fine point fountain pen; you can cover a large are with ink very rapidly with this pen.

It could also be interesting for lettering, maybe even regular handwriting, but I haven't done much writing at all with in and that's not really what I picked it up for.

The advantages of this pen are fairly obvious, you can get a very thick line at a low angle and a thinner line at a high angle. It doesn't behave exactly like a brush or flexible nib, i.e. it's not pressure that affects the line width but pen angle, but it can be used for a similar result. You can also flip it over a write with the back side of the nib, essentially just utilizing the very tip, and get fairly clean and even fine lines.

For me this pen in not very useful when doing clean drawing or writing, although it could be carefully used to do so, my experience and practice with this pen has not yet developed the dexterity for me to be confident to use it in anything tighter than sketchbook work.

title: Plays nice with fountain pens
text:
I like these notebooks for daily notes, to do lists, and the like, as they work better than most others that I've tried for use with fountain pens. They compare reasonably with Rhodia, and when you can pick them up for less than $5 they're a much better deal.

There is no appreciable feathering, no bleed through with even the wettest inks and nibs that I have. Permanent markers will bleed, but I only know that because I sought to find out, I normally don't write notes in marker.

The poly cover and the rings are study, they'll certainly outlive the notebook... actually I would rather they were cheaper and biodegradable... since they're going to be trash in a couple of months.... Maybe I'll come up with a clever way to repurpose them before it's time for the trash.

A better option for me is [[ASIN:B00015YORO Black n' Red Twin Wire Hardcover Notebook, 8-1/4 x 5-7/8, Black/Red, 70 Ruled Sheets (L67000)]] as I prefer the hard cover over the poly cover. I'm grabbing another one of those if I see the price drop below $8 or $9 per book.

title: Perfect for Pen and Ink with Wash
text:
This has become my favorite ink [see the update at the end for an suitable and less expensive alternate]. It has the most admirable properties: it flows well, is a deep, opaque dark gray (black when put down heavily enough), it dries relatively quickly to a fairly matte finish, doesn't smear, feather or bleed badly and, most impressively, is the most waterproof fountain pen ink which I have used.

It's neither excessively wet nor dry, although if it goes down too thin it will be conspicuously gray, when using it for sketching I do sometimes find it desirable to restate the more important lines. This could be seen as a fault, I prefer to use it to advantage and allow some lines to be weaker and subordinated, and other to be bolder and more pronounced.

I do use it sometimes for writing and signing, it works excellently for that purpose, although I do have less expensive inks which work adequately well for that. What I really love it for, and where it shines above other fountain pen inks, is as a drawing ink. I have used others but none are so permanent (Noodlers Lexington Gray is also excellent in this regard, although is truly gray, not black).

Now I use De Atramentis Document Ink-Black almost exclusively when sketching, as I can go in with light washes of value or color after the ink is dry and not worry about the ink smearing or contaminating the colors. There is also less concern with smearing the ink as you draw, which has been a problem with other fountain pen inks I have tried using for sketches.

It's gained a reputation with the urban sketching community and other artists for a good reason.

UPDATE: An excellent alternate ink to De Atramentis Document Ink, and one which is rather less expensive, is Rohrer & Klingner sketchINK--I've reviewed the color 'Lotte' here on amazon. The cost comparison is a significant one, 35ml for $25 compared to 50ml for $14. I still love this ink, but since I can get one that suits me just as well for less than half the price I'll probably use it a whole lot less frequently.

title: Color Wheel Green
text:
On the whole this is a fantastic product. It is a very strict green, exactly the green you would find on a color wheel, it's very rich and bright, and highly saturated. A very attractive color.

The green appears to be a mixture of yellow (or yellow-green) and blue dyes. It offers up some shading and you can pull the blue and yellow apart somewhat by wetting it after putting the marks down. You can also completely disintegrate any marks you make by wetting them.

I've mostly been using permanent blues and black, and probably would have gone with a permanent green but I really like this hue and the bottle puts it over the top; it's a work of art, quality glass, great shape, really substantial lid, I'm happy to put it on display. I will keep the bottle and continue using it for other inks.
