title: Surprisingly good paper, suitable for use with fountain pens
text:
I like these notebooks for daily notes, to do lists, and the like, as they work better than most others that I've tried for use with fountain pens. They compare reasonably with Rhodia, and they're often a little less expensive.

There is no appreciable feathering, no bleed through with even the wettest inks and nibs that I have. Permanent markers will bleed, but I only know that because I sought to find out, I normally don't write notes in marker.

title: More fade/water-resistant than G2
text:
I was recommended these, and the Pilot Juice Up refills as an alternate to the G2, as I was looking for a water/fade-resistant option, and am very happy with them. These are a great, they use pigmented inks and meet my needs, and the Juice Up (which I get through Jet Pens at this time) are even better.

They make for suitable sketching ink when wetter inks won't work (on cheap or thin papers for instance, where fountain pens will bleed and feather badly), or when filling out or signing forms which have been printed on cheap office paper.

This refill (and the Juice Up) Fit the regular G2 body, or any of the many pens designed around the G2, such as the inexpensive, high-quality, and fun Pilot MR Retro Pop Gel Rollers.

title: Useful, some quality issues; suggest clear version
text:
Summary: The Ink Miser is useful and I would recommended it to fountain pen users who use converters, or piston fill pens, and bottled ink, not cartridges or eye dropper pens, but I would suggest getting the clear version to more easily see the ink within.

There is a little quality issue. The casting process can leave bubbles in the piece. Of the two which I received they both have little bubbles open to the inside of the cone, which trap ink and make it harder to clean out between uses.

I never found the clear version of the Ink Miser on Amazon, so I bought it through Goulet Pens. I am very happy with it as a simple and functional tool. I think that clear is a better option than black, as one is then able to see the ink within it more easily, but either will be effective in helping fill a fountain pen with converter.

It comes with a bulb syringe, that is cheap and will likely have to be replaced at some point, but which is otherwise perfect to get the ink out any bottle and makes the Ink Miser ready to use right out of the box.

The Ink Miser is particularly useful when filling from a 4.5 oz. Noodler's bottle, not just to get ink from the bottom, but to use them conveniently at all, as the larger Noodler's bottles have very narrow necks and come with glass eye droppers. It is as useful with the 3 oz. Noodlers bottles, when they're not topped off.

It's also been suggested that you can soak pens in the Ink Miser, using it with cleaning solution in the reservoir, which should work as it doesn't seem to tip over when pens are left in it.

I have also found it useful with dip pens, although it would be nice if it were a tad more stable (heavier or wider base) for this use.

title: I wish they were waterproof
text:
These are an almost-great compromise when it comes to everyday office use. I prefer fountain pens, but most cheap papers don't play well with them, so printed forms end up messy looking with bleed-through, feathering, etc. that wet inks produce on such papers. These gel pens write well, they're smooth, rich and cover well, and they don't bleed or feather, but unfortunately they do smear when using highlighters over them. I wish they had a waterproof gel, then they would be a great compromise to fountain pens.

I am going to be testing [[ASIN:B019WF17J6 Pilot 0.38mm Black Ink Refill (LP2RF-8UF-B), for Juice Gel Ink Ballpoint Pen, (LJU-10UF-B), ×5 Pack/total 5 pcs (Japan Import) [Komainu-Dou Original Package]]] as a waterproof alternative and will add a review there once I've formed an opinion of them.

title: "Rose Red"; almost magenta, but mixable
text:
Pro Tip below for those who, like me, feel this ink is too pink.

I hesitated on getting this ink, now I sort of wish that I had gone with something else. I won't return it, but I want to try and help other potential purchasers know what they're going to be getting if they purchase this ink.

The color is listed as "Red", and the ink in the jar looks VERY red (I did worry about the pink box and label). Now that I own a jar (although you can just barely read it in the photo now that I check) the label on the box, and the jar, is "Rose Red", which is a better descriptor, as this is not a pure red hue. It's too cool for my taste, almost a magenta; I would rather a too orange, than too blue red.

It does seem fairly water resistant, writes smoothly and lays down well. It's a good partially-opaque pigmented ink... I just don't care for the particular shade of red.

PRO TIP: I do own a Sepia toned ink ([[ASIN:B003IMP0R0 Platinum fountain pen Ultra pigment ink particles Blanc sepia INKG-1500 # 65 (japan import)]]) which I have mixed with this ink. I am happy to result they mix well and produce a nice earthy warm red, which is totally usable.

One other thing that I want to say is that the jar is pretty great (as with all Platinum Carbon Pigment inks which I've purchased). It's very functional and unpretentious and it comes with a conical insert that assists with filling pens, but also makes it an excellent choice for using with dip pens. This insert is so incredibly useful that I wish all ink manufacturers made similar devices standard issue with each of their bottles.

title: Great ink; the beautiful bottle closed the deal
text:
Talk about getting what you pay for!

In need of blue fountain pen ink I deliberated for a bit, and considered this and two other permanent blue inks. Montblanc Permanent Blue does cost about twice what the other inks I was considering do, but I have had my eye on it for some time, and really the unique bottle shape sold me on getting it (I will never throw away that bottle, no matter what I have in it down the road).

Suffice it to say that I am glad I did get this ink, it is excellent. It writes very smoothly, dries reasonably quickly, is subtly shading on the right papers, and shades very slightly on even cheap paper. The hue is just a touch warmer than what I would consider a "pure blue," but it is very close. It doesn't bleed or feather much at all. I compared it to a Platinum Pigment Ink, sepia tone, and to a Noodler's Bulletproof Black. Both of these other two inks appeared to feather and bleed through the page more so than the Montblanc Permanent Blue; albeit none to any considerable degree, and to be fair the Montblanc is also the lightest in value of the three, but in the end it did out perform the others.

I almost exclusively use permanent inks and therefore was curious to see just how permanent this one was. Writing and sketching a little, and then leaving it to dry about half an hour I then saturated the page and let it sit in stagnant water. The ink remained entirely legible and there was no appreciable degree of additional bleeding. There was only a slight amount of run when agitated while wet, less so than I have seen in the Noodler's waterproof inks... So this is definitely permanent under wet conditions (I have not tried solvents on this ink).

The one place that it does under-perform compared to the Noodler's and Platinum inks is that it can be easily and significantly faded using an eraser, the others are much more permanent in this.

This ranks among the best inks that I have used and is worth the price if you want a premium quality ink to write with... and a gorgeous bottle.

title: Nice, but does not work perfectly with crow quill nibs
text:
This pen holds the larger diameter drawing/calligraphy nibs well (G pen nibs, hunt 99 drawing nibs, etc.), and is comfortable to use with those.

Crow quills are loose in this holder but if you're willing to stretch or pinch your nibs and work on them until they fit right then it does work. This is a better option in my opinion than using the crappy plastic Speedball nib holders, although the nibs fit really well in those.

Maru nibs fit it well, so maybe I'll switch from crow quills to those.

title: long, lightweight nib holder, better than plasticy ones
text:
I much prefer using a wooden pen over the cheap plastic ones that I began with.

The ferrule is metal and holds the nibs very securely, over it's lightweight and the cork grip is nice, it has a good diameter (around 1/2 an inch) and is also now the longest nib holder that I have at around 6-1/2 inches.

It's best with hunt 99 or similar sized nibs, and will work with a G pen nib.

title: Good strong clip
text: These are great clips. They are strong, large and easy to work with. I use them for holding drawing paper and my reference to drawing boards. I also used the holes in the bottom of the arms to bolt two together end-to-end, this allows me to clip reference to the top of a canvas (or sketchbook), it would also let one clip a transparent grid to a drawing board when doing a still life or live portrait work.

title: My first recommendation for an entry level fountain pen
text:
I'll start off by saying that the combination of quality, beautiful style and low cost, warrant 5 stars. I have a couple of little gripes, and it's only those small points which cost this line of pens one star. If I could rate it 4-1/2 stars then I would.

I got the Gray Barrel with Hound's Tooth Accent, Fine Nib and love the look of it.

And while I personally prefer the Lamy Safari as a better writer, with more nib options, etc. the Metropolitan is a better looking pen and, for mainly for this reason, has become my #1 recommendation to first time fountain pen users. It seems to me that many people find the look of the Safari a little off-putting, but everyone so far has been on board with the Metropolitan pens.

And this is an excellent pen, I literally heap praise on this it and Pilot in general, when introducing new people to fountain pens.

Overall I very much I like the Retro Pop line, the geometric patterns and bright colors are eye-catching, classy and cool. I really like the look and find my self using them all the time, they're just the right size for a front shirt pocket so tend to be the one pen that I nearly always have to hand.

Pros:
Looks nicer than a Safari and is a little more pocket-friendly.
Ink flow is good, certainly adequate to not discourage a beginner.
Quite inexpensive.
Comes with a converter, and a filled cartridge.
The fine nib is finer than the LAMY equivalent

Cons:
Not as comfortable in the hand as a Safari (or AL, or Joy), although still comfortable.
Nor does it write as smoothly given a comparably sized nib.
Fewer nib options than the aforementioned Lamy pens.
The ink in the cartridge would not satisfy a discerning user, but again, fine for an introductory pen.
It's a little leakier than I would like, and more so than other fountain pens I have used.

title: very fine line; one of my most used pencils
text:
I find myself using this pencil more often than almost any other mechanical pencil that I have (At this writing I own 6 that are capital 'N' Nice and only my Staedtler Mars Technico 2mm gets more use).

At 0.3mm the line is very fine, and yet I find that I rarely break a lead (just don't advance it too far, and be prepared to click every couple of minutes to keep the lead exposed). It's great for small sketches (or smaller details in larger sketches) and also handy for taking notes.

The pencil is sturdy and the mechanism works perfectly. It has a nice hexagonal barrel, which helps prevent it rolling, and a round metal grip area, slightly wider than the rest of the barrel, with a gently knurled texture. It's got the typical button on the back for advancing the lead and there is an eraser under the button, and you can also twist the button top to indicate the lead type: B, HB, H, 2H, 3H, and 4H. The low center of mass is comfortable but nothing special, the balance is nearly identical on my Alvin Draft/Matic Zebra DelGuard pencils; the Muji is a hair lighter.

title: Yep, it works in Kuretake No. 8 Brush Pen
text:
The converter works perfectly; exactly what I needed.

I'm using it with [[ASIN:B001C0CT2O Kuretake No. 8 Fountain Brush Pen (DP150-8B)]] so that I can use different inks than come in the Kuretake replacement cartridges (which is not my favorite shade of black--actually I've been inking it up with Noodler's Lexington Gray, which is nice to have in a brush for direct sketching, or augmenting pen sketches)... filling a brush pen with a syringe can be a drag, as they put down so much ink you'll find yourself dismantling the pen, digging out the syringe, etc. so often that it becomes tedious.

title: OK, but a little disappointing
text:
This is a pretty good pencil holder for slightly larger diameter pencils. It can work on standard sized pencils but beware that it will have to be tightened down as far as it will go, at which point it's pretty easy to over-turn the tightening mechanism just slightly and strip the threads on the collar. This is the primary reason for my disappointment with it, that and the fairly limited range of sizes that it works well with.

Pros:
Excellent size and weight
Replaceable eraser

Cons:
Easy to strip the threads on the tightening collar
barrel accepts fairly narrow range of pencil diameters
The pocket clip is movable and quickly scratches up the finish on the barrel

title: The ink isn't quite as smooth as Cross
text: The ink isn't quite as smooth as the Cross branded ink refills but I appreciate the unusual color options, and the purple color is pleasing.

title: These notebooks are nice and thin
text:
These notebooks are nice and thin, with flexible covers. I like that they aren't bulky and they lay flat when you open them. I have one or two of them nearby at all times to take down notes or do sketches in. The pages are strong, but not stiff; the color is off-white or cream.

The page aren't thick and wetter media will show through, so it is inconvenient to use both sided of the page if you're using heavy black ink such as fountain pens or felt tips. Ball-points and pencils are ideal in these books.

I haven't yet decided if I am going to continue buying these, or carry on the search for the perfect notebook. They're useful, simply made and inexpensive, but still... I'm not in love.

title: more chocolate colored than sepia (review includes a hack to fix this)
text:
Overall I like the ink, under the right conditions I love it.

To my eye it is more chocolate (or burnt sienna) than sepia (read to the end if you want to hack it to be sepia). I have not rigorously tested it's permanence, but it has proven to be water resistant under normal circumstances.

I wouldn't actually use it much except that it mixes well with the other pigment-based Platinum inks for some really unique hues. And there is shines.

Here are some suggested mixes*:
Add a little blue into the sepia brown to achieve a truer sepia hue
Mix blue and sepia brown closer to 50/50 for a transparent 'chromatic black'
Add sepia brown to Platinum rose red to achieve a warmer, more pleasing red hue

I still have to see what sort of purple I will get with a rose red and blue mix.

*combine inks at your own risk. I haven't seen any ill effects in my own pens, nor have I tested its permanence when mixed.

title: Good notebook, nothing more
text:
These notebooks are nice and thin, with flexible covers. I like that they aren't bulky and they lay flat when you open them. I have one or two of them nearby at all times to take down notes or do sketches in. The pages are strong, but not stiff. Nor are they thick and wetter media will show through, so it is inconvenient to use both sided of the page if you're using heavy black ink such as fountain pens or felt tips. Ball-points and pencils are ideal in these books.
I haven't yet decided if I am going to continue buying these, or carry on the search for the perfect notebook. They're useful, simply made and inexpensive, but still... I'm not in love.

title: Actually pocket-sized brush pen
text:
This is my second brush pen, the other being a [[ASIN:B001C0CT2O Kuretake No. 8 Fountain Brush Pen (DP150-8B)]]. The Pentel pocket brush has the advantage of being actually pocket sized; the Kuretake is a little long to be very portable. Since I can more easily bring it along, I am getting more use out of the Pentel than the Kuretake.

These brush pens come with very nice and very black ink, and can be refilled with cartridges. I wish they sold the ink in bottles, and that there was a converter available.

As opposed to the Pentel brush, the Kuretake takes a more standard sized cartridge, allowing for the use of a converter and thus a wide variety of inks; I have yet to find a suitable converter for this Pentel pocket brush. Another advantage of the converter is that these pens both can put down a ton of ink, and I feel better reusing a converter than tossing out a spent cartridge every few days (I recommend refilling use cartridges with a syringe, although I have see a few examples of these being eye-droppered). I do prefer the brush on the Kuretake, if allows finer control and retains its shape better, but the Pentel pocket brush is in no way a poor quality.

title: Nice art pen; not practical for everyday writing
text:
I am very happy with it, but there are trade-offs.

Summary: I use this pen (with an extra-fine nib) for ink sketching, it is well suited to that purpose and I would recommend it for that. I keep two Lamy Joy pens inked up at all times for sketching (one the regular black-bodied pen and the other is a white version) , one is always loaded with waterproof black ink, and the other with whatever alternative ink I've decided on, usually either a water-soluble black or brown, or with grey ink.

For more general use I would recommend the Safari over the Joy, it's just a more well-rounded pen, but the Joy does have some advantages and it is my go-to pen for ink sketches. I swapped an EF nib for the 1.1mm stub that came with the pen, I prefer the EF nib for sketching, although I do use the 1.1 nib in a Safari for everyday writing.

Let me first compare it to the more common LAMY Safari, and then I'll talk about a couple of Pros and Cons with this pen specifically.

From the ink window forward to the nib the Joy and Safari are identical and completely interchangeable.

The most obvious difference is that the stem on the Joy tapers, which is nice in the hand, and allows one to pull their hand back further from the nib, which can benefit looser mark-making. This can done with the Safari too, but it is less comfortable as the cap and clip interfere with one's grip. It's mainly this feature which makes the Joy a better drawing pen.

Overall the Joy is longer than the Safari (all in the stem); at first it seems significantly longer, about 40mm but that's bit deceiving because once you post the cap on the Safari that difference drops to a negligible 3mm, and even with the cap posted on the Joy (which sort of works but doesn't really) it's only 10mm longer than the Safari.

The wight is very similar, both are light pens, with the Joy feeling just slightly heavier. Again, the Safari with a posted cap, vs. the Joy without (which is how I would suggest using each) leaves the Safari the slightly heavier.

They balance very similarly uncapped, with the Joy balance a couple mm further to the rear. With the cap posted the Safari however balances about 15mm further back compared to the uncapped, un-posted Joy. So the Joy is more forward heavy than the Safari, and I find that it feels a little more comfortable, but that's probably going to be a matter of preference and in either case the weight and balance of these pens is of negligible importance..

Pros: It is a LAMY Pen. If you're a fan, like me, then this is a good thing. LAMY, in my opinion, invests value in the right places in their pens, meaning that they are an excellent balance of quality and cost in a writing (sketching) tool.

I really like 1.1mm the stub nib. I liked it so much in fact that I switched it to my Safari, so that I could use that for my everyday writing. Both of my Joys are fitted with EF nibs.

Personally I like the balance, length and the taper. It's nicer to hold than a Safari and you don't have have to choke up on it. This is an advantage for making freer strokes and is more often how I use it when drawing.

Cons: The length is also a drawback, as it cannot easily be carried in a pocket. A jacket's breast pocket would be OK, but not a shirt pocket.

The taper makes the posted cap wobbly as it's only snug right at the end, and posting defeats the value of the tapered stem. This leave you with a cap to put somewhere and retrieve when you're done. Not too big a deal, but overall on the negative side of the ledger. (EDIT: to meliorate this, or even move it to the "Pros" category I have found that one can clip the pen to the outside of a sketch book and leave the cap there there when removing the pen to use it for sketching. This means that it isn't a pocket clip, its a book cover clip :) and it works very well as such.)

title: Very fine lines, second favorite sketching pen
text:
I may have never edited a review or changed a rating as much as I have than with this pen. I like this pen, I do, but there are issues. Despite everything it's among a few go-to pens that I prefer when sketching in ink, the other and more frequently used sketch pen is the Lamy Joy with EF nib.

This is the second Platinum Carbon Desk Pen that I've owned, sadly I lost my original. Unfortunately this particular pen does not write quite as its predecessor, or at least as I remember it to. The previous one produced a very, very fine line, worthy of the "Super Fine" moniker. Both produce nice lines, and are uncharacteristically (for a $9 fountain pen) smooth and reliable.

Super fine lines can be created using the backside of the nib. The flow is understandably less reliable in this orientation, but when going for the finest of lines it works well.

This is almost a five-star pen (particularly considering the price) but I cannot give it a perfect rating as it appears that the quality control is flawed, as supposedly identical pens perform very differently.

The ink that it comes with is good, but it performs better with De Atramentis Document ink... and even Noodler Bulletproof black.

Overall I do like the shape and feel of the pen, but the [[ASIN:B0002T3ZKG LAMY Joy Calligraphy Pen 1.1 mm (L15-11)]] is similar and more comfortable to use (and can be fit with an extra fine Lamy nib for similar line quality); the body of the Platinum Carbon pen is very narrow. The Joy also has a pocket clip on the cap and, while neither the Carbon Pen or Joy are good pocket pens, a clip on the cap makes it easy to hang the cap from my sketchbook, which I cannot do with the Carbon Pen as there is no clip on the lid. With each of my other fountain pens (aside from Platinum Carbon Desk Pen and Lamy Joy) I use them with the cap posted; the cap does not post on the Platinum Desk Pen.

I do grab this pen to draw in my sketchbook fairly frequently; it feels quite right in that circumstance and produces very fine lines. I wouldn't recommend this pen for general use, letters, memos or note taking for instance, for that I would suggest a Lamy Safari with extra fine nib, or a Pilot Metropolitan with a fine nib, each of which costs a little more than Platinum Carbon Desk Pen, but are otherwise totally reasonably priced.

Why fine and extra fine nibs? Most paper laying around is junk and will bleed and feather no matter what nib you use, but italic (my preference for handwriting), stub or broad nibs will make the problem worse.

An alternate to this pen would be a Lamy Joy with a Lamy EF nib; that would result in a similar pen (longer, tapering body, hard, fine nib). The Lamy is more expensive, but also more comfortable to hold, a little more reliable, offers several nib options if you want variety, and the EF nib produces very nearly as fine a line... and it's what I use almost every time, in preference to the Pilot Carbon Desk pen.

title: You get what you pay for
text:
I'll summarize in one paragraph, everything beyond that is detail, for those who may be curious.

This is one of very few fountain pens which I have thrown out. The overall impression is that more attention was given to making this pen look nice, than to making it function well... and unfortunately the finish wears quickly, so the look doesn't last. The performance is probably what one would expect from a $6 fountain pen (unless you're buying a Preppy, the Preppy performs much better), i.e. not very well at all, while it tries to appear more valuable than it is. My recommendation would be to ignore this pen and get a $20-$30 fountain pen and be satisfied... Or buy a Preppy, which won't look as nice, but which will write better.

I've been living with this pen for a few weeks now. I don't use it everyday, as it is not a suitable pen for most writing (i.e. that done casually and quickly) but I have found occasion enough to write with it.

It puts down a good amount of ink. The flow is neither good, nor terrible. It writes well with a slow hand, but skips during quick movements. It both has more flex and yet requires more pressure than the Pilot and Lamy nibs that I have used (although to be fair this is a medium nib and I have only tried the fine and extra-fine of the other brands).

The nib is stamped "Jinhao 18K GP"... which it certainly is not. I don't know if it's a mistake, an attempt at deception, or what; in any case it is a point of carelessness.

The style is nice, but the finish started chipping the first day I used it. The chipping ceases with that first spot (about 5mm x 10mm), so it seems that it was just there that the paint had poorly adhered, but nonetheless the aspect of a fairly nice looking pen is ruined. The build quality, while feeling mostly sturdy, is slightly lacking, but for the cost it's not unexpected that a couple of corners were cut. It's heavier than my Lamy and Pilot pens and the cap connects very securely, with quite an audible snap. But the pocket clip is very wiggly and some of the internal components look to have been hastily completed.

It comes with a converter, which is nice. The one I got had debris within the chamber that I fished out before filling it. I assume they were flakes of plastic left over from manufacturing. It works as expected.

Overall an OK pen for the price, but I would have preferred that they had invested the value in the feed and nib, and saved on the body, then at least it would be more useful.

I tried to modify it with a G nib but didn't get good flow, so I cannot recommend the pen for that purpose either, although based on videos on YouTube, others do seem to have had success with it; I was unwilling to noodle with it long enough to get it working right, and have since tossed it out.

title: Excelent nib for thin to thick lines
text:
I have been using this as a finer and more flexible fountain pen nib in a pen from Ackerman Pens (ackermanpens.com), and have been very happy with it; it's become my go-to sketching tool.

These nibs are very flexible and capable of fairly thin to rather thick lines and spring back to their original shape time after time. Overall a very reliable nib.

Using these regularly, several hours a week, and keeping one in an inked-up fountain pen, they seem to last about 3-4 months before the corrosion starts to get bad bad enough that I need to change it (so the two boxes of 10 nibs that I got should last me 5 or 6 years). Using as a dip pen, as long as you rinse and dry after each use, they can go much longer, some say a single nib can last a couple of years.

title: Nicely made, a little short... and I don't really use it.
text:
The construction is very clever. In the retracted position the pen stays pretty well put, won't leak or smudge anything. A firm press on the tip of the barrel can expose the pen tip, so it's not perfect, but it clicks in place and does take a bit of direct pressure to accidentally push the point out. When it's deployed it writes well and does not push back into the body, even under quite a heavy hand. It telescopes from just under 10cm to just over 12 cm, which is a little short for my preference, but very similar to the typical Space Pen length. There is no clip, but you can get one separately.

I don't write with it at all often but I keep it around and I appreciate the quality of the build.

title: Almost made me hate fountain pens
text:
TL;DR Get a Platinum Preppy fountain pen for about the same price as this one, or invest a little more and get a Pilot Metropolitan or Lamy Safari. This is just a terrible pen.

When I decided to try out fountain pens I grabbed one of these from a local drugstore. It was cheap, and available, but I wish I had done a minute of research before getting it, as it almost turned me off of fountain pens altogether.

The ink quality is nicer than a Bic, but there isn't much else I really can say in it's favor.

The flow is terrible; there is a piece of something fibrous in the feed, that I assume is meant to help with wicking, which really shouldn't be necessary if the feed was well designed. The nib is not at all smooth to write with and it has tiny "sweet spot" where it will work at all. The flow quits altogether rather frequently, and while a shake of the pen with the cap on will generally get the ink going again, one shouldn't have to resort to continually capping and shaking ones pen to get it to write.

It does write a little better when using the back of the nib, but not well.

Luckily I decided to give fountain pens in general the benefit of the doubt and tried another brand. I have since come to love fountain pens and use them daily for writing and drawing, actually almost exclusively.

So if you're interested in getting a fountain don't get this one. If you want a starter that isn't expensive, don't get this one. You can get a Platinum Preppy for about the same price and if you're willing to go in $20-30 the market really opens up to some quality pens, such as the Pilot Metropolitan or Lamy Safari.

In short, I would strongly encourage anyone give fountain pens a try, and strongly discourage anyone from purchasing this particular pen.

title: Not unhappy with it but probably a one-time purchase
text:
TL;DR middle of the road paper, adequate for many tasks, ideal for few. Inexpensive, recycled. Would recommend for casual use, students.

For pencils or other solid media a more textured paper would be desirable. For ink work or markers, denser and smoother pages would be ideal. And for paints (watercolor or gouache), thicker and heavier weight pages, and something that is sized and has some cotton content would be best.

That said, I have used graphite (hard and soft), charcoal, drawing ink, gel ink, fountain pen ink, ink washes, water color washes, and gouache in this book, and it is basically OK in all cases. And since it's recycled paper, and the book is inexpensive, I'd have to say it's better than expected.

The best use in my opinion is light ink sketching.

The pages are thick enough to take heavy inking on both sides without trouble. I will say that using a sharp nib isn't great, the recycled paper is pretty soft (not as in an extra fine fountain pen or a super fine roller ball, but a steel nib such as a crow quill or G nib).

Watercolor and ink washes do cause the pages to buckle some but I have used it that way and it's not too bad if the washes aren't to heavy. Multiple washes do not work well at all.

Personally I don't mind a weathered feel in my sketchbooks... in fact I rather think that adds to their aesthetic in a Wabi-Sabi sort of way; I want it to look worked in.

The only other complaint is that it doesn't lay flat at all, you can force it and use spring clips to hold it open.

So it's fine as an economical sketch book but I'll be in the market for a different book when I use this one up. I will however use it until the last page, as it's not a bad sketchbook.

title: Well priced, very dark, smears badly
text:
I am not particularly happy with this ink and will not purchase it again, if I ever run out, since I don't use it for much... and I have 130ml to use up. I plan on using it for my "crappy sketches" and save my pricier inks for more polished work... also I am going to try diluting it for gray washes. I'll report back on how well that works.

As indestructible as this ink is purported to be I was very surprised to so severely smear a week-old ink drawing when brushing wet over it. Granted the lines stayed inked, but the amount of ink that went everywhere else was upsetting, and not at all the desired effect.

I later found that I could smear it with my finger or a dry paper towel, and can significantly fade it with an eraser, even after letting the ink completely dry. This smearing, wet or dry, is why I particularly dislike it; I have nice inks I like to write with, but wanted a dark black fountain pen ink for sketching. I can use this for sketching, but if I do a pencil under drawing then erasing those lines afterwards will smear and lift the ink, and if I try and do washes over the black line work then it smears.

It is nice and dark, and quite economical given the volume to cost ratio (about $0.15 per ml). But even at that price, I doubt I'll be re-purchasing it.

I've taken to using De Atramentis Document Ink, Black; it's not as black as Heart of Darkness, but smears less, feathers less and bleeds less, although it does also cost 5x more, and is a little harder to come by.

Lastly I tried out the pen that came with it, called "Charlie", and tossed it out (there is a short sad list of pens that I've thrown out, they're the ones I couldn't even give away). It wrote well enough, although too wet by my preference, but the smell of the body of the pen was just not something that I could really live with... apparently a thing with Noodler's pens... don't know, I haven't bought any other their other pens because of my experience with Charlie.

title: Not as good as I had hoped
text:

With what appears to be a well established brand name attached to this pencil I was expecting to be impressed with it. Unfortunately I seem to have expected too much.

This pencil isn't too bad, and I do use it. I am not, however, likely to buy (or recommend) another Koh-I-Noor pencil.

The threads on the tip don't hold and I have to re-tighten it every time I use the pencil; the sharpener on the back is OK I guess, but it's wide open, so be prepared to drop graphite dust all over the place; and the pencil is actually too short for the full length leads that I have (which are 5 inches long).

A friend of mine recently got a Koh-I-Noor 5.6mm lead holder and it fell apart fairly instantly. I looked inside at the build before he returned it; I was not impressed.

title: One of the best erasers for art
text:
This is my favorite eraser for drawing and sketching. You can use it much like a pencil in order to "draw" in white (or technically the color of your paper), adding in highlights, etc. and when erasing unwanted pencil marks you can easily leave in the lines you want, or avoid smudging pen lines which haven't fully dried.

It works well with graphite, less well with charcoal. Works on anything normally erasable.

PRO TIP: if you maintain the habit of using the side for erasing, where possible, you can achieve and maintain a finer tip, much narrower than the 2.3mm width of the eraser.

The white eraser is soft enough to not damage the paper and the barrel fits closely, to help the tip remain fairly rigidly in place, allowing for great control. The body feels sturdy and is refillable, and I expect it to last quite some time; I've been using the same one for almost two years now.

title: Never been so happy with a ruler purchase
text:
This is simply a well designed and well crafted ruler. The underside is so flat and well polished that it glides along the paper almost frictionlessly. It's brass, which is lovely and just steals the show next to its plastic, aluminum and stainless steel cousins.

My favorite special feature is the little kick tail along the back edge; it's the sort of thing one probably never would appreciate until they've had it available to them. Gone are the days of clawing with futility to gain purchase on my straight edge. The raised edge also allows for inking along that side (for instance with a technical pen, fine liner, fountain pen or flexible steel nib) without it bleeding under the ruler.

It's short enough to fit in my go-to sketching kit and sturdy enough to not get damaged while traveling about.

The markings are not permanent, but I use it as a straight edge, the measurements are irrelevant to me.

title: Get this pen, you cannot regret it
text:
UPDATE: The more I try other fountain pens, the more I am impressed with the LAMY Safari. It writes better and is more comfortable in the hand than any comparably priced pen. Overall the most well rounded inexpensive fountain pen that I could recommend. I have used various of their nibs (EF, M and 1.1) and they all perform well.

The LAMY Safari with extra fine nib is my new favorite pen. I wish I had skipped less expensive options when getting into fountain pens and gone straight for this one. It cost 4X the price of the entry level pen that I originally purchase but it's worth about 100X. Excellent flow (which I could not have said for the economy pens I started with), lines are very smooth, writing and sketching require virtually no pressure, allowing for relaxed, smooth work. The lines have character and class that you will never ever ever see with a ball point, gel roller, multi-liner, etc. with varying widths, and the loose confidence of a relaxed pen hand.

I'm not using LAMY ink but I will say that another advantage to the fountain pens over gel pens and ball-points is that the fountain pen ink invariably looks better and there is such a variety in color and properties that you can find one that really speaks for your personal aesthetic and character.

The extra fine nib is really great. As with most fountain pens I have tried, a gentler stroke makes thinner lines and a heavier stroke thicker, but with this nib it is only subtly thicker. The back on the nib can be used for truly hairline strokes.

The body is a little fat for a front shirt pocket (although that is where I keep mine at all times except for when it is in my hand) and if you hand it to uninitiated persons be wary of their heavy, monkey fisted writing styles and caution them to the correct methods, less you risk their damaging your nib.

Otherwise I am IN LOVE WITH THIS PEN. One gripe, the "charcoal" color is quite brown, albeit almost black in darkness, but far from a more neutral gray.

For what it's worth I did briefly try many of them myself and they write reasonably well, the ink is thick and they write smoothly. The colors are very rich and opaque, so they work on darkly colored paper too. There were a couple of instances of needing to scribble a little to get the ink flowing, but that's not surprising really as they were standing points up, and the two which didn't flow immediate did after a couple of extra strokes and left smooth lines after that.

title: Overall good looks and good performance at a reasonable price
text:
This is a pretty good stapler for the price. I tried it out head-to-head with a stapler that I already had (a recognizable inexpensive office stapler brand, made in Taiwan), with the same staples in each stapler. This one did work a little better--up to about 20 pages it works perfectly, around about 30 it starts to fail. The stapler that I compared it do began to perform poorly at about 10 sheets and failed at 15-16.

It's pretty. A couple of people I work with commented that they thought it looked nice when I had it out on my desk; I personally think it looks feminine, so I gave it to my wife and she seems to like it.

The internal mechanisms feels solid and the stapler seems well built. It is put together a little differently than others that I have used making it a somewhat more robust than many inexpensive office staplers. One downside is that loading staples requires a relatively decent number of them, say 10 or so at a minimum, or it becomes tricky to get them to lay in the channel correctly. Another minor issue that I had is that you cannot put several smaller rows of staples together in there at the same time, so it you have a few strips that are shorter you cannot combine them all to make the equivalent of one longer strip--they just won't lay flat if you try and combine shorter segments.

All in all it's a good product, a little better than others I tried with a similar price. I wouldn't buy it for myself for aesthetic reasons, but as i said my wife likes it and it is attractive enough to get positive comments from friends and co-workers.

title: This is a very good sharpener with some great features
text:
This is a very good sharpener with some great features. It is quieter than I expected and pretty small but feels very solid; it is also much better looking than many other electric pencil sharpeners, which I think are often pretty sorry to look at and want to be hidden away in a drawer where they're less visible... and less useful if you're trying to work and always keep a sharp pencil on hand.

The points come out very smooth and are perfect, it's also very quick to just to a little touch-up when you're tying to maintain a perfect tip when drawing or writing with pencils; much quicker to use this than manually sharpen and you get a better point too.

I like the feature to be able to adjust the sharpness and it works very simply and the instructions that came with the device are simple and clear so I was able to start using it right away when I opened it.

The best part for me is that you can use a cord or batteries. I prefer using batteries as you can keep your desk free from cords but I would hate to have them run down right when I needed to use the sharpener and having the cable as a back up is very comforting.

I can definitely recommend this device based on my experience with it.

title: You don't want this heap of junk!
text:
I hate this printer.

I hate it so very very much.

I don't recall how or when it happened, but for whatever reason, I was under the impression that Epson was a top of the line brand when it came to printers.

So when my spendthrift husband surprised me with an unexpected brand new printer that we didn't really even need, I held my penny pinching tongue and smiled and thought, "Well, this is going to be good for printing out my digital stamps with anyway"

Except, no.

First, if you really only ever print in black - this is NOT the printer for you. I literally, never print color. I design and sell black and white coloring pages. I use this printer to print them out so I can color them with tangible mediums for example images. That is all I do with this printer. But somehow I always have to replace my color ink just as frequently as my black ink. I have found no way to disable this printer from using the color inks when printing in black or greyscale. So there's my first gripe about this terrible printer.

Second, when that color ink runs out - ANY of it - if it just the magenta or just the yellow, etc... you can no longer print. Now the first time it happened it would let me continue printing with black only, very briefly. (Which is all I ever wanted to do with it in the first place, but I digress). But since that first time this happened, when asked if I want to print with black only, I click proceed and it just sends me back to the Home screen.

Third, Printer Head Alignment function is a joke. It does absolutely nothing. Well, pretty much nothing. Thankfully I am coloring the things I print out so I can hide the jagged lines that pop up here and there, but considering this printer is paid for and not something I found in someone's eviction leftovers on the side of the road - I do expect the printer head alignment to function as expected.

Finally, we've had this printer for a little over a year.. meh maybe a year and a half. Now I am getting Error code 0x97 which seems to mean that my time with this monster of a machine is coming to an end since I have not been able to print anything in days and I'm about ready to go Office Space on it.

title: Neck saving, heavy book stand, good for reading on a desk or table.
text:
I used large texts in my teaching, and textbooks have grown in length and size over the years,. Holding them on a lap or placing them on a desk is not the most convenient for the neck since the head is always leaning forward, placing strain the neck. So, I was taking back and forth from my office to home and back when we purchased this item. I now have a stand in my office and one at home.

This stand is the same brand as my first but is slightly larger. The tray to hold the book can be used to prop a book or can be reversed to hold a laptop. While the surface area will hold a laptop, it doesn't work quite as well for a tablet that has a stand to hold it up. That, however, does not detract from its solid construction, attention to the corners so that it doesn't chip if dropped or bumps a hard surface. I especially like that the tray clicks out to prop a book or can be turned over to used w/ a laptop.

The clamps for holding open a book are especially nice because they hold firmly, and the rubberized tip on the metal is soft to avoid tearing the page. It holds firmly without being too strong or too loose so the pages slip out. Because I need to use my computer to prepare documents, holding a book open is greatly facilitated by this item.

The stand on the back is a plastic "butterfly" so that it's suitable for a children's book prop; however, there are two rubber grommets that keep the book stand from sliding when lying flat. The stand has multiple levels for propping, and it makes it quite handy for different sized text.

title: Invisibly seals cork tiles to glass and other cork
text:
I used strips of this to adhere 3/16" cork tiles to glass to cover up a heat mat on the exterior side of a vivarium, and to insulate the glass. Despite the cork tiles shedding nonstop powdery cork dust/debris, the strips of tape stuck magnificently along the lengths of the cork tiles and onto the glass and plastic of the heat mat. I doubled up the cork tiles layer for extra insulation and this even stuck one cork tile back to back with another. It's still holding strong and is barely visible. Wish I'd used this to secure the heat mat to the glass, too, because the clear tape I used shows very easily through the glass, whereas this tape barely shows at all (see photo).

My only negative remark is that trying to start a corner or edge to peel off the red backing strip is very difficult! I found it easiest to work at peeling a corner/edge while the tape is still on the roll, then folding a tiny flap of the red backing up as a tab. Then I peeled the tape up off the roll and measured, cut and adhered it. It worked much quicker that way.

title: Organization? Product Labeling? Yes.
text:
I can't speak enough good things about this handy little wireless BT thermal printer which my husband bought for me here on Amazon. I've got a bazillion little boxes of items that needed to be organized and found this is exactly the tool to do it. The screen is especially bright and easy to read, the chime sounds are clear, the labels come out looking fantastic (I used the random sample size that came with the machine and then promptly ordered more PUQU brand labels in the same size (30x40mm) to replace them). I've posted a pic that I've intentionally blurred out the QR codes but the text is crisp and clear with good contrast. I was a long-time user of a Dymo dual roll thermal printer at a workplace and the rolls were extremely expensive. I love the price of the PUQU labels! Yes, the rolls are smaller than the Dymo rolls, but that also means you get to buy just what you need.

The printer battery seems to last forever, it hasn't gone down at all even though it connects via Bluetooth. The printer itself has some built-in settings that allow things like speed of printing which is handy. Even the slowest setting is super quick!

The software can be awkward because it was originally written in Chinese. It's a bit difficult to determine what's in the cloud-based public templates directories, but you can choose one of those templates, remove the stuff you don't want and build your own right in the app.

What I like best about it is that you can put together your database in Excel and then point the app at your db and print labels from there! That alone makes it endlessly useful! You can print a range of labels, or just one or two, or multiples of them.

Let me just say that their customer service cannot be beat! I did encounter an issue where the software froze and I ultimately ended up reinstalling it, which fixed the issue, though I did lose my templates. However, it didn't take much to recreate them plus I already had the database in Excel. But even through that, the PUQU customer service was quite quick to respond and excellent at follow-up.

I would ditch any desk-based thermal printers and go with this, given its portability, battery life, quality of thermal print, great availability of different sized labels at a good price. . . . .

title: Like most ink converters, piston mechanism doesn't fill all the way to the top
text:
I use this cover daily in my Sailor Lecoule fountain pen and it doesn't disappoint. Like many converters, though, don't expect the piston filling mechanism to fill the converter all the way to the top. It does leave a slight gap but I was already expecting that from using other brand pens with other brand converters.

I haven't experienced and leaks or difficulty using the converter and I've used it for a few months now with several refills.

Using this converter with my Sailor pen allows me to use a much greater spectrum of beautiful inks with my favorite pen.

title: I admit I thought this would be junky ink.  It's definitely NOT.
text:
I didn't have real high hopes for this ink other than that it was branded by Jinhao. I'd purchased a purple Jinhao FP for a friend who likes the color purple and thought she would get a kick out of purple ink (she's never used a fountain pen before so I thought it was easier for her to start out with cartridges before introducing her to bottled ink), and I wanted her to have plenty of it so I bought her this to go with her pen.

She insisted I keep one of the packs of cartridges even though I use only bottled inks. I objected but caved after she got after me enough. I put this in one of my own Jinhao pens and was instantly impressed with how fluid the ink is, the gorgeous shade of violet, and how it seemed like a much, much more expensive ink.

The cartridge is international sized and will work with almost all of my other fountain pens. It holds a lot of ink. I write with it daily. I didn't use the pen/ink for a two-week period and when I returned to it, it just took a tiny squeeze of the cartridge. The cartridge hadn't dried up in my absence, and it was ready to go after the squeeze to restart the flow. Very impressed.

Needless to say, I'm hooked. I will definitely use Jinhao inks again if they're anything as good as this. Maybe there's Jinhao bottled ink somewhere??

title: Blue-black in color (more blue than black)
text:
This is my first experience with a Noodler's ink. I used it in a Pilot MR Retro fountain pen, using a proprietary Pilot ink converter. The jar was extraordinarily full, and I reckon I received more ink than what the weight measurement indicates. Not complaining about that part, just a warning for when you open the bottle :)

The color is a blue-black hue, maybe a charcoal blue but not a navy blue. It's not as bright of a blue as I had wanted, but I like the color nonetheless.

I've used the ink on 20 lb. copy paper, regular 3M Post-It Notes, and 25% cotton bond paper. The ink dries immediately on each of those surfaces. It feathers a bit on Post-It Notes but not on regular copy paper, nor on bond paper. I purchased the ink to use when I notarize estate planning documents (wills, trusts, deeds, etc.). After having done the research I have on this particular ink, I have full faith that the ink will stand the test of time for these sensitive documents. However, I hope to find one that is equally archival in quality which is a brighter blue in color.

I just wish this one had come with the converter, because I cannot use black ink (the color of the cartridges) for notarizing documents at work, which is why I bought the orange pen (and I have a great bottle of Noodler's Bad Blue Heron ink that I'm dying to use in my orange pen, which I cannot, without the converter that it was supposed to come with).

UPDATE: Pilot's customer service is quite responsive, and they sent me the missing converter -- x2! Along with two complimentary cartridges. They made my purchase whole again so I'm upgrading my review to 5 stars.

title: Looks good, smells gross (initially), feels a bit cheap
text:
I received great customer service, fast shipping, and the item arrived on time as expected, so no complaints there.

EDIT: Turns out the pen just needed a little tuning and it's working a lot better now. For those new to fountain pens like myself, search up some YouTube videos about flex nibs and you'll find some great info about slight adjustments that need to be made to these for optimal results.

The smell is almost completely gone by now. It is apparently caused by some part of the manufacturing process? Glad it went away even though it took several weeks.

Not very satisfied with this pen itself, honestly. Even though it's only my second fountain pen, I can compare it to my Pilot Metropolitan and say it's not quite as nice for about the same price.

The worst part by far is the smell. It's just simply gross. Hoping it will go away with time and I can use it without holding it at the end of my reach so I don't have to smell it.

The color of the pen is great, very stylish. However, the construction seems a bit flimsy as well. Sure, it's plastic instead of metal and the two are fundamentally different, and maybe that's all there is to it, I don't know. It also comes in a cardboard box (not a nice pen holder like the Pilot) and a cheaply printed instruction manual. I think the presentation could be a little bit nicer. It's hard to judge something's build quality immediately so I'll update the review if it suffers from any quality issues in a reasonable amount of time after this is posted.

title: One of my top 3 Noodlers’ Inks
text:
I love this color so much. I use it in numerous fountain pens (Pilot Petit1, TWSBI diamond mini, Pilot Metro, Platinum Preppy) and it always looks great. The color can look like an earthy red iron oxide (which is a red/brown), or a more vivid, almost slightly dried blood red. It truly lives up to its name and the bloody battle of its namesake. I draw with this and write with it. Because it isn’t waterproof or water resistant, it’s nice to use with a water brush to create soft washes of color and shading in my sketches. I really think you’ll like this one.
If you’re like me, and like a waterproof ink for drawing, I’d also recommend Brown #41. It’s a beautiful, rich , medium brown that’s light enough to show the beautiful color, yet plenty dark enough to easily see your writing.. I’m not a fan of the guy it was named after, but it to each their own. I am however a fan of this ink, it’s beautiful to draw with, and the brown color gives my drawings an antique aesthetic. The guy that makes these inks is a true artisan who gives generous amounts in his earth friendly glass bottles. We don’t have to agree on everything beyond that. **Be sure to set this on a counter top, hold firmly steady with one hand, while carefully opening the jar with the other. The ink is truly filled nearly to the brim. As long as it’s on a flat counter top when opened, you should have no problems.** thanks.

title: Green- Great case
text: I’m and artist, so I always like to keep my most used and favorite drawing pens, lead holders and supplies in a medium portable case to carry in my sketching and watercolor bag ( I bought that here on Amazon as well). I use 2mm lead holders, fountain pens,ink cartridges,archival gel pens, Sakura micron pens, kneaded erasers, blending stumps, Kum sharpener,blades for charcoal, a chamois, kukuyo Campus 2b erasers and some charcoal,pastel and oil pencils; all of these snugly fit into this case. title: Great flowing ink and a very pretty green
text: I absolutely love this color. If your a painter, this color is very close to a Phthalo Green (YS). The color is really a nice clear pretty jewel-tone green. This ink is not waterproof, but I love it for writing and for doing quick sketches and color washes for shading.  It flows well in my Pilot Metropolitan fine and medium nib pens, as well as my TWSBI Diamond 580AL fine nib. In a stub, flex or broad nib this ink would definitely shade. The colors are bright and translucent while being very saturated. I would definitely buy this green again.

title: Dry writer with a lot of skipping
text: I wasn't impressed with this pen. I have pens ranging from Jinhao's to Platinum Preppy's and Pilot Metropolitan's all the way to TWSBI Diamond 580Al and Pilot Falcon and Vanishing Points. I actually like Jinhao pens for inexpensive writers and  they make decent quality pens for the price. When I received this pen I inked it up and immediately had issues with ink starvation. I put Sailor Jentle ink in it and was getting a dry writing experience with some feedback. Even after using a brass shim between the tines and smoothing the nib, I was still having no luck with getting a consistent line without extreme dryness or skipping. This was over a 2 week period. The pen looked pretty good, with a transluscent coral orange body, it was clearly a molded plastic body pen, nothing fancy, and I liked that it came with a converter. it looked nice enough for the price. I know some have loved this pen, and I'm willing to assume that I may have gotten a bad run of this pen, but this was my experience with it. I was given a refund by Amazon.

title: Writes smooth I love it
text: I really like these pens, it writes and glides more smoothly than it has any right to. For the price, you are getting a pen that just glides across the paper effortlessly,something I usually have to pay much more for. I would definitely recommend this pen to a fountain pen novice or beginner for its ease of use and low maintenance appeal. It writes a clear line with the nib up on its point,side to side, it even writes cleanly with the pen flipped the wrong way,gliding on the back of the nibs point. I would say this pen leans a little wet or right in the middle, ink-wise. I own a medium and fine nib and I use them for drawing,inking and sketching. The pen itself feels sturdy and substantial in the hand, it's a little weighty but not so much so that it's bothersome in any way and I can easily write with the cap posted. Changing the cartridge is easy and cleaning the pen is a cinch. For a good video on how to disassemble the pen for cleaning check out YouTube for specific Metropolitan cleaning videos, there are several great ones on there. I highly recommend this pen to writers and artists alike, it's really inexpensive and writes like a much more expensive pen. The only draw back is that there aren't currently nib replacements for these. I'm wondering if there are nibs from Pilot or other brands that may fit this pen...

title: Nice detail tool

They have to be pushed down into the tip of the device, which I understand is necessary to hold them securely,but it leaves a lot of the eraser that can't be used. text: First off, I buy my erasers at my local art supply or wal-mart. amazons prices are oddly higher. I got this three pack for $1.88 at Wally World and I love them. It gently clings to itself and rolls up into thin strips  for easy removal from the paper (I use a drafting brush to brush my "crumbs" away) no tearing or pilling of my paper, just a nice clean removal. It also lifts graphite,colored pencil and charcoal pretty well too since it has a soft texture to it. I will be buying more when I either use this 3pk up or I lose them :)

title: Cheap, low Cost and Acts Like It.
text:
I never review products right away as there is too much of a "halo" effect the day you buy something. So it goes with this device. I initially bought it as it was a great value when comparing price to listed features. It linked up well with Wi-Fi; very easy to set up and it is compact - good for apartment type office spaces (or third bedrooms etc.).

However, once I got it into the home and was using it I realized there were some real productivity issues. First, the software "Epson Scan" is really poor software - example: You are limited to name sizes just like you were in DOS. Really bad. It is clunky and sometimes does not work (I use a MACBOOK AIR).

What is really bad however is when you try to scan using the feed tray. Just far too many jams and it is a productivity sump. I like to kick off a scan then not worry about it while I am working on something else. Alas, I have to literally feed pages one at a time to make it work - Just not a good experience.

Overall, if you need something cheap and you will ultimately throw it away this may be OK to use but if you are looking for productivity in your office space I highly suggest you bypass this and go to a more reputable machine.

title: Very smooth writing, but leaks readily.

You're supposed to use a loose hold with fountain pens, but I there is no amount of force I can grip the pen with to avoid my fingers sliding down it. Just holding the pen up vertically, it ever-so-slowly slides through my fingers almost miraculously.

I am upset about it being so slippery, because it is a beautiful pen. The color looks nice and the details are elegant. The grip even looks very nice with a spiraled look as shown in one of my photos. I'll note that the nib shown in the photos is the bent nib replacement I had bought previously after getting my first Hongdian pen--the bent nib creates a thicker line, but writes so ridiculously smooth.

title: The ink I received is not blue-black, but a "deep teal" or dark cyan.
text:
Seeing some of the photos of others, I must have received the wrong product labeled as "19014 BLUE-BLACK". The ink I received is looks much more like "19040 AIRCORP BLUE-BLACK". I know they are both blue-black ink, but one is more blue, and one is more green, and I prefer blue ink.

It looks completely black on 100% cotton, ivory colored paper. On white cellulose paper, it looks like the HEX color #173632, as shown in the attached screenshot. The internet tells me this color is "deep teal". I was under the impression that the ink would be more of a "Black Russian" (#000030) color. This fits with the possibility that I received a mislabeled jar of "19040 AIRCORP BLUE-BLACK" instead of the correct product, "19014 BLUE-BLACK".

When wet, the cyan/green ink runs/spreads readily, but the black seems to not be bothered by tap water. This is shown in the photo attached--note that the other ink in the photo is more blue than purple, so the color isn't completely representative.

I have reached out to the seller. Will updated review following resolution.

While the cartridge works fine oh, the color is more of a purple than a blue, nearly identical to the pens that come in 20 packs for $5. I am most disappointed with the color.

Color aside, the fine tip results in a less smooth writing experience, which is not an issue I've had with a couple other common pens. Additionally it makes writing on softer surfaces more difficult.

Last but not least, the blue ink has inferior color fastness to the black ink. I did a little test to compare some common pens (as well as a fountain pen) to see how they hold up to various things. As you can see in the attached photos, the space pen works as well as other pens, but the blue ink which would typically be recommended for signing documents did not withstand the same punishment as the Black Ink.

I therefore would not recommend the blue ink, nor the fine tip. That being said, it will work for most situations, and the black ink held up well.

title: Take care of your pen and it will take care of you
text: I'm writing to amend my original review of the Pilot Retro Pop fountain pen.  I was new to fountain pens and have since discovered that you have to MAINTAIN those pens if you want them to keep working.  First, you have to use it.  If you leave it without writing with it for a long time, the ink will dry up and the pen won't work.  You must occasionally clean the pen.  Take it apart and run water through the nib (writing tip) until it runs clear.  Let it dry completely before putting a new cartridge in and re-assembling it.  Only takes a few minutes and the pen will work well for a long time.

title: Excellent document scanner, NO PC or Mac required.
text:
Hopefully, this review is not premature. I will update this review in the future if any of the main points I have raised fundamentally change.

I took delivery of the Raven Scanner Pro on August 29th, 2019. I assume you are looking for a scanner of similar feature set which brought you to this review. I, too, was looking at this scanner, and before I wrote this, I found just three reviews on Amazon and one partial review on YouTube, which was more of an unboxing video. I think that video did more damage to my purchase than any review I have read on Amazon.

This scanner is a little more expensive than the Fujitsu iX1500, which I consider being the gold standard of document scanners. I have this scanner and have purchased three other Fujitsu scanners before that scanner. When I want a document scanner, my first choice has been Fujitsu and for good reasons.

This scanner gave me pause. It did so because of a feature I saw which is that the scanner has no required software for a personal computer. That was enough to catch my attention. Each time I buy a document scanner, I have to make sure it will work with my Apple Macintosh. Most times, the manufacturer provides software and drivers but not always. In the earlier days of the Fujitsu, for example, there were specific versions for the Mac and PC. If I switched to the PC, my Mac scanner would not work. Newer scanners, like the iX1500, have drivers for both, and this problem is all gone for me. Gone, but not forgotten.

One reviewer mentioned that he wanted to use this scanner with a Chromebook and a ChromeBox. That is not possible because scanners need drivers and software, which is not how the Chromebook works. The same issue is coming up with the rise of the smartphone and tablet. I have both the iPhone and the iPad Pro, and honestly, those are fast becoming my platform of choice. Sometimes the hardware has an app in the Apple AppStore that allows its use from your iPhone or iPad using a feature such as AirPrint. Printers that use AirPrint are more valuable to me than those who lack AirPrint as a result. I do like to be able to print from the iPhone or iPad.

From what I understand, this scanner uses Android to be both the client and the scanner in a single device. And as such, it can scan your document to itself, and then upload the document to your cloud providers, such as DropBox or others. I am a fan of DropBox, so that's where my scans are now going.

Unlike any other scanner you have used, this scanner has a large display, and on that display, you choose how to scan and where the scan will go. Your personal computer such as a Mac or PC or your smartphone or your tablet has nothing to do with it. The scanner scans documents super fast, and then sends those documents directly to the cloud. If your iPhone, iPad, Mac, or PC have access to the cloud such as DropBox, then you can collect your scanned document there. It is this feature that I wanted. The real question is, what is that feature worth in terms of money or other issues raised by other reviewers.

The unboxing video on YouTube mentioned that the scanner is noisy. Noisy? I wasn't even sure what that meant. Scanners are not loud. According to the unboxing video, the scanner has a noisy fan. I hate the noise. I buy Macs most of the time because they tend to be quiet. I don't think I want a noisy scanner. But I wanted a scanner that takes the pain of drivers and software out of the equation. And since Amazon says this can be returned for a full refund, I decided to try it.

So first I will answer this question. Is this scanner noisy? I do hear the fan as my room is nice and quiet. In an office setting, I doubt you hear it at all. The scanner goes to sleep by itself, and when it does, it is silent. If you are done scanning, press the power button and the blue light behind the power button blinks. I will assume that means the device is sleeping the same as if you stopped using it for some time. Thus it is silent again. I don't think it is excessively loud when on and I am a stickler for these things. The Fujitsu is always quiet. The Raven is the first scanner I ever had with a fan inside it. Of course I wish it were silent, but believe me, it's not at all something to worry about.

Is it true you don't need drivers? Yup. I did nothing at all on my Mac. Keep in mind this means you don't use your computer to scan. You use the scanner to scan. There is no scanner app on the Mac or PC that you use with this scanner. The scanner scans to itself and then sends the output to the cloud. To me, this means I never have to worry about the scanner working on my computer. You do, however, have to have a wifi network or an Ethernet network. In this regard, it differs from every other scanner I have ever used.

Quality and speed. Okay, this is the hallmark of the Fujitsu. If you have never used a ScanSnap the feature everyone loves so much is you put a stack of paper in the feed, and it rips through them, single-sided or double-sided in record time. This scanner wants me to say single-sided or double-sided before I scan. The Fujitsu does it automatically, and that's not always a good thing. If I write on a piece of binder paper, there will be blue lines and a red margin line on both sides. But I typically want one side. Through the software on the Fujitsu, you can change it on the fly to single or double, but leave the preference to whichever you prefer. On the Raven, there are four large squares on the large display. Side, Color, Quality, and Destination. They stay stuck to what you last used. Super simple to change from single to double-sided anytime you want right on the scanner. This is a feature, not a bug unless you have 50 sheets and some are double, and some are single. In that case, it would be better if it had an AUTO choice. It does not. You either scan single, or double. In my specific use-case, I do not mind this, but I can see others seeing this as a problem. Raven should seriously consider an improvement here.

As for speed, it feels like Fujitsu to me. The speed does not disappoint. Single or double, the scan is lighting fast.

There is built-in software that allows you to crop and rotate and make other changes, like naming the scanned document. And then you can email it. Unfortunately, the email function lacks, in my opinion. I expected that if I typed in one email address and sent a document there, and then another email address and sent another document there, that it might remember the two addresses and give me a choice on the third scanned document. Nope. It only retains that last email address. I am not going to memorize email addresses on my own, so this feature is not useful enough to be useful to me. Another area for future improvement, I hope.

So is it perfect? No. It needs an AUTO feature for single or double-sided documents. It could use a quieter fan but believe me. It isn't a problem. The email address feature could be better. It could retain multiple addresses else I think the only time I will use it is to email myself.

All that said, this is a cloud scanner and doesn't require a personal computer to set up, or use. You can take it out of the box, and set it up and start using it to send documents to the cloud or an email address. Once in the cloud, like DropBox, you have access to it and can do all the things you might do from your client. So it doesn't come with free software for your PC or Mac.

Today is what I call the honeymoon period. I use my scanner every single day. I scan handwritten text to a shared folder and my teacher, and I mark it up, and we discuss it. I'm a bit of a language learner, and this is a simple way for me to interface with my teacher as she lives on the other side of the earth. I read and write on an ordinary pad and scan that to a folder. She adds comments, sometimes live via skype and sometimes as homework. I also scan tons of documents which I sent to clients and store in a file system. I have been buying document scanners for years. I believe this is my second one in just a few months and my fifth or sixth one overall. If you need a document scanner, you'll know it. They are not for everyone. As my iPad Pro becomes my machine of choice, a document scanner such as this becomes more of a necessity than a desire. I think this is the first step, and I will bet many more like it will become the norm in the coming years. Unless something dramatic happens in the next few weeks, I'm keeping it.

Update - 2019-09-09 -

It has been more than a week since I started using the Raven Pro and I wanted to post a small update to the original thoughts I posted here.

1. This scanner has grown on me. I still have a recently purchased Fujitsu iX1500 scanner on my desk at my office. And I have the Raven Pro at home. I use document scanners daily, as I previously mentioned. Only now I find myself wishing that I have a Raven at work as well as at home. While the Fujitsu is an excellent scanner, the Raven which does not require a computer to be on or even present at all has won me over. There is a convenience that the Raven has that I feel the Fujitsu cannot match. I scan the document on the scanner. I rotate it if needed. I can name the document directly in the scanner, and then send it to the cloud destination of my choice, all from the scanner itself.

2. There has been a recent update, and I am not sure if I didn't notice this feature previously or if it is new. In either can set multiple destinations for a single scan. That is to say; I can have the scan go to both DropBox and GoogleDrive, at the same time.

3. I placed a document with text printed on one side and nothing on the other. I selected a 2-sided scan, front side up, and then scanned it. I then hoped it would auto-detect and result in a single-sided scanned page. Yup, worked like a charm.

4. In the GoogleDrive, I can traverse the Google Drive hierarchy directly from the scanner and have the scan go to a specific folder.

5. Email is the same as far as I can tell, but the folks at Raven reached out to me and let me know that a feature that remembers previous email addresses should come in the form of an update in the future.
I have used the scanner to do minor things like rotate pages, and name the document before sending it to its final destination. I like this feature quite a lot.

I found I can write for much longer with a fountain pen without my arm at the elbow getting all weird and feeling like I have to shake it to undo the fatigue I feel from regular pens.

I have been on something of a quest for the perfect pen for years now. But I never tried a fountain pen. I was watching a movie where everyone was writing with a feather and got the idea to try a fountain pen. I serious wrote with it for almost an entire day and my arm felt fine. I could never dream of such things with a ball point pen. I end up applying too much force and my arm gets that feeling like I got to shake it and do something else with it else risk injury of some kind. Not with the fountain pen. My hand and arm remain quite relaxed using this. Never going use anything other than a fountain pen from now on.

If you still have doubts about laying down your hard-earned cash then check out the YT clips by searching there under "Law of Attraction Planner".

title: Playful Looking Sweet Writer

The pen takes standard Pilot fountain pen refills, like the ones used in their Metropolitan line. The medium nib writes just as smoothly as the Metropolitan's. It's a different nib though; it has little smiley : ) on it! I'm using Pilot Momiji red ink in it.

title: They Are What They Are
text:
You're buying two toner cartridges for less than $20, not a brand new $75 HP product. By the way, the printer, and HP1109w - cost me less than a brand new toner cartridge.

I installed the first one and printed right off the bat. A full page of gray had some banding but it's not horrible. The blacks are black, although if you look closely you may notice a little bit of uneven toner laid down. It's fine, and is only noticeable on larger bold black type or fat black strokes.

To turn off the "Not a Genuine HP Supply" warning: In WIndows got to Devices and Printers, right click the printer, got to the Ports tab, and uncheck Bidirectional Support. Note that the printer won't tell you when it's running out of toner, but you should be able to figure that out yourself when it starts printing faded-looking pages.
