title: One of my favorite colored pencil in my collection
text:
I got into colored pencils a while ago, and I've learned a lot in that time. I started with watercolor colored pencils to do faceups on dolls, learned that my first set wasn't too good, branched out into various brands for drawing, not just faceups, and have a collection of pencils in brands ranging including Prismacolor Premiers, Holbein Artists, Primsmacolor Verythins, Schpirerr Farben, Derwent Chromaflow, Derwent Inktense, several pencils in other lines from Caran D'ache, some lower cost craft brands, and Sergeant (my first colored pencil set).

I started off by buying one or two open stock pencils, and this Caran D'ache Luminance in Prussian Blue (one of my favorite blues( has become a favorite - in fact, I have some more Luminance colors on the way from Dick Blick.

I appreciate that Luminance colored pencils are lightfast - not all are. When I first used this pencil, I had been using ultra-smooth pencils, so at first I wasn't crazy about it. Then I saw the amount of color it laid down, realized that the sort of graphite feel to it was giving me more control, and everything I did with it was gorgeous. I did some mountain range silhouettes that I put a lot less pressure or strokes into because of the amount of pigment I was getting on the page, so this pencil made for less effort and less work, not less than with my Premiers, but for what I was drawing, I thought the results are best. Btw, it sharpens well, although be aware the Luminance pencils are just a little thicker than normal pencils, so it didn't work perfectly in my electric sharpener, but it was flawless with my inexpensive little Faber-Castell sharpener.

I love this pencil, and I can't wait till the next ones I ordered arrived. I can't say these are the only pencils I'll ever use because I use different colored pencil lines for different styles of art and sketching. And then there's the personal preference thing - what I love may not work for you. But I really, really like my Prussian Blue Luminance pencil, and I'm sure I'll be using these for many years to come.

title: A step up to sharpen my colored pencils
text:
When I started drawing and sketching with colored pencils, I quickly discovered that the sharpener we used for regular pencils didn't work well for most of the colored pencils. I tried a number of sharpeners that didn't work too well. When I saw this sharpener, the EX-20 Colored Pencil Sharpener, I hoped it would do a better job than any of the others I tried.

Good news - it does. All my thin and standard colored pencils from the cheapest to the most expensive sharpen beautifully. I prefer sharp points, and it did a great job - no wasted wood or core, good points. When I tried it with thicker pencils - Luminance, Hobein, Inktense - they barely fit in the hole. The job it did on the thicker pencils varied; all were decent, but the thickest didn't get the perfect point the thinner and standard pencils got My Luminance pencils have better points than the did with the previous sharpeners.

Note: I pull my pencils early to check on progress. I'm so used to sharpeners that shortened my pencils by a quarter inch or more that a small extra step makes me feel better.

One thing to be aware of is that my sharpener took longer to do the stubby points than the sharp points. My only issue with the sharpener is the smell of the adapter. Wow, it's strong! It made the sharpener smell, but that smell dissipated fairly quickly, and even the adapter smell is much fainter.

Please consider this a 4 1/2 star review. If the sharpener fit thicker colored pencils, of which there are many, better, I'd consider this a 5 start sharpener. I love that you can use batteries or plug it into a wall plug or computer to power it. So it's not great but it is good. I'm happy to have it, but will also continue looking for a sharpener to fit my thicker pencils better.

title: The perfect pencil for sketching after all these years!
text:
I've been sketching and drawing for years, but I never found a pencil I liked, so eventually I stopped. A few months ago, I got back to drawing and sketching, and realized I wanted a thicker lead than I was using. Since I was tired of sharpening, I decided to try a mechanical pencil, and when I came across the MyLifeUNIT 2.0mm Mechanical Pencil, I decided to try it.

For me, it turned out that 2mm is the perfect lead thickness, and the leads that come with this pencil are the perfect softer hardness. The pencil feels great in my hand - I realize this is a very personal thing, but I found it comfortable in every way. And it's soft enough to sketch with - I mean, really sketch, not just draw.

I waited several months to review this pencil, and in that time, I've turned out more drawings with more joy than at any time in my life. For thinner lines, I got a set of pencils with various lead sizes (.3, .5, .9 ad .7), but most of the time, I use my trusty MyLifeUNIT 2.0mm Mechanical Pencil. I admit, the brand name is sort of goofy (MyLifeUNIT? really?), but for me the pencil has made me happier than I realized a pencil could.

title: Too much like work
text:
I love my Prismacolor Premier pencils, so when I wanted a pencil with a harder, thinner lead, it made sense to try out the Prismacolor Verythin set of 12. I see a lot of people who reviewed them here really liked them, but alas, I am not among them. Keep in mind that this review only reflects my own opinion and experiences. Your mileage may vary.

I found these moved very smoothly across the paper, which is the one thing I liked about them. The core is hard, which I expected, but either it's very hard or it's not very pigmented, but I can't quite tell which I've never worked so hard to get so little color on a page - not even with my Sargent Art watercolor pencils. I've used other harder pencils, but these Verythins actually hurt my right hand to use, and I've never had pain from using any colored pencils before. I found I had to really layer on the color to get good saturation, and then I also got bloom. That doesn't bother me particularly, but it's worth noting.

This next one could be me or my sharpener, but these are the only pencils where the points broke off while sharpening and getting the point to the shape I wanted was quite the event - even my new Derwent Chromaflows, with their super thin and light bodies, weren't a problem to sharpen at all, so I suspect the problem isn't me. in any event, the cores weren't always centered.

And speaking of sharpening, these don't come sharpened - not a huge deal, but a pain in the butt. My Prisma Premiers came sharpened, but since the Verythins come in a flimsy cardboard box, perhaps sharpening them would have simply caused a lot of breakage during shipping.

Everyone is different, so if you love hard pencils that require some work to get the most color from, you will probably like these better than I do. I've gotten budget pencils, student pencils and art grade pencils, not to mention cheap pencils from little-known Amazon brands, but I disliked these pencils the most of all of them, and they're the only ones that have ever made my hand sore. No big deal, as they're also less than $9, and I do love to try new art supplies, so it wasn't a total loss.

title: Nice chair for most
text:
I ordered a chair from this page that isn't listed any longer, but the chairs on this page seems to be the same exact chair with different upholstery all from the same seller.

First off, the one I bought was white faux leather. I bought it based on the flip up arms and a couple things I noticed in the pics - the seat faced down in the front a little, second, the seat back was naturally tilted back a bit and third. The lumbar support didn't seem intrusive - at 5' 3", lumbar supports on every chair below a smaller Herman Miller hit me above the lumbar area, and this can be painful.

First off, I emailed Myka's a question and they got back to me quickly with a clear response. Always a plus to buy from a responsive seller.

The chair arrived in a virtually perfect box - most chairs arrive here in boxes that look like they've been drop-kicked off a plane into a war zone. Not only was the box undamaged, but the chair parts were packaged carefully and thoughtfully with an eye to keeping it clean and undamaged, which it was. I've bought much more expensive chairs that weren't half as well packaged.

Assembly could have been easier, but some issues are par for the course at this price range. One screw came, as my husband put it, pre-stripped. While assembly was a bit frustrating, it didn't actually take long. The tool it came with wasn't quite right, and there was a piece of welding rod in one of the wheel receptacles. Again, not unexpected at this price range, and neither turned out to be a real issue.

When the chair was fully assembled, it was very attractive, although that's not my main concern with a chair. But it doesn't hurt, either.

I'm 5' 3", and my current seat is set at 17 1/2 inches, so I thought 18 1/2 inches would be fine, but the lowest the seat went to was almost 21 1/2 inches, and my feet didn't quite reach the floor. I thought I could use a foot rest, so this didn't worry me particularly.

The wheels are a step above chairs in this price range and 2 to 3 steps above the average cheap desk chair. The arms are nicely padded and flip up easily. The seat padding is, as others have said, on the thin side, but we have some really nice memory foam cushions, so that wasn't a major thing.

For me, the problem was that the seat didn't angle slightly downward as it clearly did in the pic; it angled slightly upward as do most desk chair. This is quickly painful for the backs of my thighs, perhaps due to my height, and it was painful with this chair, as well. I was going to arrange to send it back when my 6' 7" husband sat on it. It's perfect for him, and he's been working from home using a dining table chair. So we're keeping the chair, and he's very happy with it.

Since not every shorter person may have my particular issues, I'd like to point out that if you're comfortable on a regular desk chair, the fact that the seat doesn't point down won't be an issue for you as it is for me. if you want a seat back that's always in touch with your back and you're shorter, be aware that the seat is generously deep, so you may need a cushion. Since I prefer more front to back seatroom, I found it ideal. Taller people will find the extra chair depth a good thing. My 6' 7" husband fits with no discomfort.

For the price, it's a very nice chair - better than others I've tried out or owned at up to twice the price. If you're not rough with upholstery and don't have cats who love scratching leather and leatherlike stuff, and you need flip up arms, these chairs are definitely worth considering.

title: Shreds 1 to 2 sheets at a time
text:
After owning this for more than a year, I want to update. I'm currently shredding a bunch of papers - no cardboard or heavy papers - and at this point, it struggles with 2 or 3 sheets and chokes on more. It also causes it to overheat quickly, although it generally heats up fast and takes around 15 minutes or longer to cool down.

If you're looking for a light duty shredder, this could still be a solution. If you want to shred single folded sheets in envelopes or 6 sheets at a time, you might want to spend a little more.

Here's my original review:
It was time for us to get a new shredder; our old one served us well, but it's pretty much shot, so we got this one - the Fellowes Powershred P-30C Cross-Cut Shredder. So far, so good - let me tell you what I like and what I'm less impressed with.

This is shorter than our old shredder, and I find it more convenient to move about. It has a clear window in the front so you can see how full the container is of your shredding. Like most shredders, you can run it forward or can reverse the direction to empty the teeth. It's not a super powerful shredder, so the name Powershred isn't a great fit, but it does shred staples as promised, and it did a great job shredding my old credit cards - far better than the old one.

Now the negatives. It does slow down significantly when shredding 5 or 6 sheets of paper, but it does shred them. When I went to register the product with the manufacturer, their form wouldn't accept the number at the bottom of the box even though I was clearly typing it right, but maybe that's because this is a new model. You're only supposed to shred for 3 minutes at a time; the manual says if you shred for longer, it will go into a 40 minute cool down period.

I wanted to mention a couple odd things. I suspect they actually tested this shredder, because there were a couple shreds of paper in the teeth when I first took it out of the box. It didn't look used and still had all its packaging from Fellowes. And the manual doesn't mention anything about maintenance - not whether you should use shredder sheets to keep it lubricated or anything else. I'll probably contact them about this and find out how to care for the machine.

I've been shredding like crazy since we got this new shredder. So far, I'm happy with the size of the cuts, which are the size the company claims, and I'm thrilled at how well it shreds cards. You can do a fair amount of shredding in 3 minutes, and I've been letting it cool for a few minutes between each cycle. It's a little quieter than our old one and much more effective. So far, so good - I'll edit this review with any changes or new information, but at this point we're pretty happy with it.

title: Very nice, but...don't expect to necessarily receive ones that match
text:
I work at a smallish law firm and, after coming into our lobby everyday and being greeted by a display we have of attorney business cards sitting in numerous completely mismatched business card holders, the OCD in me took over and I decided it was time to do something about it.

So I purchased several sets of these, assuming they'd all be uniform and finally give a more professional look to our business card display area.

Well, unfortunately, they don't match each other. Not only did I get sets that had two holders that looked like they were made of different types of wood, but the appearance and finishes also differed from set to set. Not so much that they necessarily look bad when put together, but it definitely detracts from the intended effect, which was complete uniformity in appearance.

As for the quality, these are really a good deal for the money. They are sturdy, well-crafted, very smooth (both inside and out) and very uniform in size and, for the most part, also in shape.

I think the fact that they are not sealed with a urethane isn't at all a negative, either. Instead, it gives them a classy, understated look. And, despite the lack of a sealant, they do NOT look either amateurish or unfinished. But I also wonder if the finish will be durable over time. I guess we'll see. The fact that the finishes are so smooth makes me inclined to say they'll be fine.

Anyhow...long story short: unless you are really focused on uniformity between the appearance of these, these are a no-brainer, excellent buy!

title: Nope! Messy & the least effective eraser I own. Also smudges horribly + leaves permanent residue.
text:
I do a lot of sketching, so I own numerous erasers for all of the many, many mistakes I will inevitably make. Of all the artist's erasers I own, this one is by far the worst. A total waste of time, money, and effort.

Firstly, it is SO messy. It leaves so many large strings of rubber cement on your work that it requires vey careful manual removal (I usually use a very light makeup brush to remove eraser residue. Can't do that with this! The tighter cement residue gets stuck in the brush hairs!).

It also doesn't erase well AT ALL. I was so disappointed in how little it actually removes from the page that I actually thought it might be a problem with the new paper I was using.
So i took all the erasers in my desk out and did a comparitive review. Guess what? You know those pink erasers you used to use in the second grade when you were practicing how to write? Even THOSE erase about 1000 times better than THIS eraser.

Lastly, it also smudges. Like BADLY. And if you rub too vigorously or quickly, the rubber cement heats up and actually becomes sticky and adheres to your work. In fact, it COMPLETELY RUINED a beautiful portrait I had been working on for DAYS when it left a large sticky, discolored smudge where I erased, and NOTHING could remove it. Not even solvents.

title: Pretty good, but the locking mechanism is a joke
text:
I like the function of this staple gun, but I'm not even sure why they have a locking mechanism, because when the handle gets pressed down on slightly, the locking mechanism disengages VERY easily. It's really poorly designed. The metal staple guns have that little loop that goes over the end of the handle, and they COULD have done that here, but instead they put a little tab-lock just underneath the handle. All it takes is a modicum of pressure to cause that tab to disengage. If you carry it in your toolbox, just moving your tool box around could result in something pushing against the handle and disengaging the safety lock.

That said, ergonomically, it's a nice staple gun. It's design is more use-friendly than the basic metal staple guns with which we are all so familiar. Using this extensively is less likely to cause hand cramping, soreness, or fatigue than some of those other ones.

In fact, I was worried it would all glop out finally, because that's what would happen if I "fed" any other paint pen the way I had to with these.

title: Don't hesitate.  Here's why:
text:
Although I tend to buy legitimately brand named fountain pens at this point from official manufacturers, I too had a lot of misgivings about buying a Kaweco Fire blue Lilliput for the asking price.

I'm an experienced fountain pen user and I own LOTS of name brand pens From TWSBI ECO's to Pelikan, to Falcon, Sailor, and a number of chinese knock-offs as well.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS:

This pen comes in a sturdy cardboard box. It's not super nice, and the box arrived damaged in a bubble mailer, BUT, the PEN was in a firm foam insert and was totally UNDAMAGED because of that.

This pen had a coupon and cost me UNDER $25 with free shipping to Alaska. it did take about 10-12 days to arrive, I hold the seller absolutely harmless for that as it shipped reasonably fast and many items I order take longer than expected, especially THESE DAYS, and to ALASKA. So to my mind that's a good score.

It came with a good quality converter, and the pen body loosely assembled with the converter inside. No ink cartridge, fine, good, I like to pick my own ink and usually chuck the mystery cartridges manufacturers include.

Inked it up with Birmingham Pen Co Freshwater Bog, an ink I'm new to. it immediately wrote nicely and the cartridge functioned well.

This pen is sold metal. the inside appears to be treated with the 'fireblue' coating. I'm not a metallurgist, I can't tell if it's really Titanium, but also, I don't really care! I bought it because I liked the looks and it is completely satisfying in tat regard, lived right up to the expectation I would have had of the actual Kaweco item.

I have several authentic KAWECO pens, a couple o AL sport special editions, a couple Sport plastic pens. Ive used the KAWECO 'mini' converter which holds basically less ink than a cartridge and I'm pleased this has a good capacity converter included.

another reviewer noted the threads... I'd agree the machining is crisp but I would not say they are sharp. Over time they will mesh together and wear, and I expect this pen to both last, endure, and wear with use, cosmetically and otherwise. My impression is: this is a well made, durable pen.

YOU ABSOLUTELY WON'T GO WRONG FOR THE ASKING PRICE.

I have NOT ever used an authentic Kaweco Liliput. but in comparison to the AL sport I'd say it compares very closely in manufacture quality.

It is a generic Nib. Looks like what you'd get on a Chinese moonman or other knock-off pen. but it's decent for a steel nib and writes fine.

the grip is a little short for me and has no molding or shaping... it's a straight cylinder. it is a tiny bit small for me, but i am 5'9" and have good sized hands for a female. I like TWSBY ECO-T and most 'western' type grips. the metal isn't slippery on this pen, and I think it would be comfortable to use to write notes or letters with. My hand tends to cramp because I grip pens tightly and press more than I need to. this pen is a wee bit small for ME to avoid my own tendency to do that, but, it's not enough that I would avoid the pen.

I would recommend this pen over a number of others, and If i find major faults will report back. the fact it's all-metal and comes with a converter are major points in the pen's favor. no huge drawbacks at this price point and I'm super happy with my purchase.

I'd love to put that Bronze Kaweco fancy clip on this pen. If it fits, I'll let you know about that too, since nobody seems to have that answer in the listing yet.

enjoy!

-A.

title: Pleasantly surprised, but not a Vac 700r
text:
First things first: I own numerous twsbi pens, including the Vac 700R, and although these particular pens are much higher quality than other models of wing sung pens, they are NOT of the same quality as the twsbi VAC 700R. The Vac 700R has much higher quality standards- everything fits snugly with no wiggling, and when you use the Piston mechanism, the rubber stopper at the end doesn't 'wiggle', the shaft doesn't move out of alignment, and all the machining tolerances of all the components on the vac 700R fits snugly, and when you handle the pen, nothing feels loose or out of alignment.

This particular set of three pens you can tell quality differences from one pen to another within the set. You're basically paying about $6.50 per pen with this set. And that's about the right price for the quality of this pen. Each pen has kind of wiggly parts but functions properly. I wouldn't try to disassemble the piston mechanism on these pens though, I suspect I wouldn't be able to get it back together In a working fashion.

The nib is sort of tight and stingy with ink. I took the italic nibs out of a pilot plumix, and did swap the nib in one of the pens. If you're looking for a high-capacity italic/stub pen, and for some reason you don't want to eyedropper a Plumix, you can do that with this particular pen since the nibs absolutely swap and are identical in size and fit. I can only remove the nib and feed from one of the three pens though, and I didn't want to potentially break one of the pens with the amount of force it would have required to attempt to get out the nibs in two of the three pens. Again this testifies to the inconsistency in manufacturing quality, but you're getting three pens for a third of the cost of a vac 700, so if you feel like rolling the dice, it's a pretty good gamble with these particular pens.

If you want a fine or extra fine nib, that's what you're going to get with these pens. And although they're very stiff and somewhat dry nibs, they're adequate.

I would say even if you receive one pen cracked, these pens are worth $10 a piece. Even though they have blemishes in the finishing and wiggly parts, and I would not expect them to last as long as a Vac 700, I would say that the asking price is appropriate for these particular pens. If you've never used a vacuum filling pen, watch a few YouTube videos on how to fill a vacuum filling pen, and try with water first. These pens would be a good introduction.

I've only had them about a week but I do have a lot of experience with piston and vacuum filling pens, I don't think the quality is so poor that with proper use they would be leaking. If you experience leaking there's several things you can check:
Be sure you've completely screwed down the knob on the end when you're ready to write. This particular pen is designed with a gap between the plunger and where the ink needs to flow, and you should not leave the knob unlocked to write with it. Be sure that all of the parts of the pen are screwed together snugly. If you separated the body of the pen from the grip section at any point, the threads are not greased and since they aren't the best quality, it's possible it could come loose and contribute to leaking. The mechanism that holds the housing for the nib and feed into the grip snaps in and out of the grip. So if you messed around with the nib at all, it's very likely that you've gotten something loose or slightly out of place which will lead to air bubbles and a lack of properly flowing ink, or, a situation where ink is allowed to pool inside the mechanism and then burps out of the pen during use. Carefully remove the nib and feed housing, and make sure that everything is aligned properly and fully seated as far down as you can push the nib into the housing, and then put the housing into the grip, make sure that it snaps beyond the little clips that you can see through the plastic that are supposed to hold it in place, and then make sure the grip is entirely screwed into the body of the pen properly. Always make sure you screwed on the cap snugly but not too tight. If you screw anything too tightly on a pen like this, especially in a place where there's no metal band to prevent the plastic from expanding, little cracks will develop, and that will cause leaks.

These pens are worth the $6 to $10 asking price, but remember if you want a pen worth $70 with the quality that you'd expect and a warranty and packaging and maintenance instructions and tools, then buy the real pen that this pen is a copy of! There's a reason people rave about twsbi pens! They're completely amazing and the quality is vastly better! But these pens are okay too. Just don't expect Lamborghini performance out of a Ford fiesta. 😜

The plastic used for these pens is prone to cracking. I don't trust them a lot. I'm spoiled by good quality pens, perhaps, but still if you have less than ideal expectations and can coddle these pens you won't be too disappointed.

title: bad for wet media
text:
This book comes with watercolor pencils, but the paper in the book absolutely cannot handle even light washes. if you sketch with ink, it cannot be layered without being to wet for the paper. the paper pills with small amounts of moisture, and is NOT sized. if you draw with the watercolor pencils and then try to activate the pigment with water, the paper really can't take it. it buckles and breaks down and changes the texture of the reverse side.

That said, the paper is good for pencil. it will handle graphite and colored pencil. it can also handle fast drying inks like in fineliners, so long as there is not a lot of lines crossing and layering while still wet from the previous lines.

it was a weird idea for moleskine to include water media with this type of dry media sketchbook. their watercolor sketchbooks are great, but that is NOT the paper in this set. these watercolor pencils are Meh. you'd be better off buying like faber castel albrecht durer or derwent watercolor pencil sets of 12 with the proper 5x8 moleskine watercolor art book instad of this set. the cost would be very comparable and of much better quality to be used together.

title: Total copy of Monteverde Monza-  a comparison
text:
This pen is basically a complete replica of the Montaverde Monza. In this review- the Jinhao 992 pictured is transparent orange, with a black feed, and has a carriage and horse imprinted on the transparent feed casing. I purchased these pens in 2018, and it is now late 2021. Jinhao 992 pictured in this review was used over those three years with pigmented ink, and was just cleaned.

The Clear pen is a brand new, never inked Montaverde Monza 3, which is completely clear, even the feed. It has a flex nib installed.

If you'll look closely, you can see that both pens include the appropriate o-rings to use these pens as eyedroppers. I used one briefly in that way, but found I did not use the ink fast enough to justify it before the ink dried up. They come with converters and I used those mostly.

Look again and you can see even the threading is identical on the parts for these two pens. Note that the orange and clear sections and the orange and clear nib units have been swapped in a few of the photos.

The included nibs are Jinhao nibs. Any nibs that will fit a Jinhao 992 may be interchanged with these pen bodies.

In addition, The nibs designed for the Monteverde Monza can be screwed into the Jinhao 992. SOOOOO if you need a spare part for either of these pens, you can consider that parts for one to be used in the other.

The Monza 3 costs about $24 at this time and comes with three different converters and nib units in a plastic case. I believe I bought five or six of these Jinhao 992 pens for about $18.

There is of course the possible ethical issue of intentionally buying "knock-off" products here on Amazon, and I personally find that the usual name brand products that I want to purchase are becoming dramatically MORE difficult to shop for here on Amazon with the glut of knockoff generic cheap Chinese manufactured products and fake review-farm type reviews. I got my badge by reviewing stuff, and I say what I mean about products.

HOWEVER,
There is something to be said that a company which claims to be a US company, yet employs very few Americans in the production of its goods. The pens Montaverde sells might be completely manufactured in China. given the evidence in comparing these pens, I would say if they told me it was manufactured in the US, I would really NOT believe them, and would instead think they were manufactured to their specs BY Jinhao. Jinhao makes a LOAD of pens, and they sell LOTS of knockoffs. They sell these in a No-Frills set, but the pens are just EVERY BIT good as the Monza, and it costs less per pen. The price difference may in fact employ a few Americans who administer and design the products, but I can't say one way or another which choice the ethical implications for purchasing THIS specific item should lead me to make. I bought these pens before the Monza, and now I know they are the same durned pen. I might use parts from one on another. I like the color offerings on the Monza WAY better than these colors. But in my opinion, it seems like Monteverde makes their choices about manufacturing, and the package for that pen says it was in fact made in China. I'm American, and I don't like some of the laws and politics which make the differences between American and Chinese manufacturing and importing and human rights etc... but to be completely honest, ultimately it is for Americans, the _American_ laws which make companies find those choices to take their jobs overseas compelling enough to do so. SO it hardly seems fair to blame Chinese manufacturers for using the equipment they have for their own purposes. I vote with that in mind. I buy things with that in mind. Although an employed American in a factory located here does help my country more than the employed Chinese factory person, but it's better to vote for legislators who help companies make choices to keep their manufacturing here, or who create job training programs for higher value jobs, since basically all of our manufacturing has already been a victim of the laws which created the global capitalism supply chains we currently face. But I digress. My solution is to shop less on Amazon and more with smaller retailers when I can, and vote for candidates who support educational and social supports for impoverished Americans currently facing the issues these changes to manufacturing face. Tax breaks for capitalists won't help individual Americans as much as stronger day care, head start, or educational investment programs will. so my choice of pen purchases has a smaller impact on the future of Americans going forward, than complaining about the decisions already codified into law and how they got us where we are today. whether I buy the Monza or the 992, that money is going to China either way. If I don't like it, Voting is my recourse.

That said,

I cannot tell a quality difference between the resin used in ANY parts of the pen bodies. I personally have not broken or cracked any threaded part of the pen bodies. To my satisfaction, the o-ring which seals the body to the section does help prevent screwing the body on so tightly that you will crack the pen body by overtightening, however, I HAVE broken the tip above the metal clip off one of the pens I bought in 2018. I think I dropped the capped pen on a hard floor and it broke the tip of the cap, the part above the metal clip. off, and the metal clip also came off. the functional part of the pen still works the same though, and the cap still remains properly sealed by the transparent insert inside the lid.

All threading appears FULLY and functionally compatible. honestly... it's as if they were built on identical or the same equipment.

Now that I know these pens are essentially and materially interchangable, it opens up the possibility to use specialty pens that the Monteverde MONZA 3 nibs and sections and will be accepted on the Jinhao 992 and vice versa. (FYI the '3' in the name Monza 3 *MAY* refer to a set which includes one pen body but three nib and converter sections- I bought the clear Monza used in this review from Goulet pens as a part of the Monza 3 set).

I have a JOWO Conklin/Montaverde nib unit from Goulet that fits a Duragraph- THAT nib unit will NOT fit in the Monza or the 992. The grip where that Conk/Monte nib unit screws into needs to be larger. On the 992/Monza, the opening is SMALLER than that JOWO nib unit (which fits most Conklin/Montaverde pens.) SO if you have a Monteverde Regatta or a Montaverde "mountains of the world" pen, or a Conklin Duragraph, be aware that those nibs are NOT interchangeable with This Jinhao 992 or Monteverde Monza. FYI

...and thanks for listen to me try to work out the global implications of the current state of capitalism in my pen review. I wonder if Amazon will print it? -A.

These pens are maybe worth one or $2 a piece and if you want to harvest the converters and parts out of them to use in other pens that take standard international converters, they might be good for that. The nibs are stingy and the ink flow skips. The nib is not comparable to a brand name Lamy.

One of the caps busted in my bag inside of a pen case. All the other pens I had were fine but this one was completely cracked and shattered. I've had the same problem with other plastic Jinhao pens-- where the plastic is just an inappropriate material for pens that are used as writing instruments. The plastic they use is very brittle and it just doesn't have enough flexibility in the polymer to stand up to repeated usage of opening and closing the pen cap, etc. If you've ever used a platinum preppy you know that the plastic in those pens can crack if you over tighten the body to the grip area, but the plastic in these Jinhao pens is even more brittle than that and not as good of a quality as the $4 Platinum preppy. The nib on the preppy is better, the plastic on the preppy is better, and I would any day buy a preppy over one of these pens because the preppy very inexpensive but at least they're reliable and you know what you're going to get and you know what to expect about its durability as a product.

title: Nibs are poor, pistons don't seal properly
text: These nibs are pretty substandard. The piston mechanism doesn't seal properly, and ink easily gets behind the piston up into the turning mechanism knob.  It's extremely  difficult to disassemble the turning mechanism at the end of the pen body in order to clean it, and one of the four had to break in order to get it cleaned out so it's not intended to be disassembled in the first place.  These pens are extremely cheap and if you just want them as pants that will last you a short period of time the price is okay but they're not very pleasant to use compared to a higher quality nib.  They are lightweight, and they are inexpensive. So if you just want a pen to throw an ink sample in and try it out for a little while these pens would work well for that but there's certainly not pens that you would want to display or have or use for any extended time period as your everyday pen, or a similar intentional use besides sampling inks.

title: Waterproof
text: You really can't go wrong with Mitsubishi uni writing products.  These fine liners lived up to my high expectations.  Really good black lines at all sizes.  Lightweight comfortable to hold, etc.  If you want these to do watercolor line and wash I haven't had one smudge ever, I've never had one bleed when wet, and I've never had to worry about  waiting any particular time for the ink to dry before I go right in with my watercolor.

title: Pretty enough
text: I like the well enough to hold my notebook pages open. They are not as strong as the solid binder clips but I like that I can see the page underneath them. It would be great if they were one size larger, they don't really fit on a hardcover sketchbook very well.  If you're part way through a SketchBook they'd be fine. They're just not big enough to go over a standard moleskein width art or watercolor sketchbook. But they're just the right size to very snugly fit over a mead composition notebook, which is maybe 1/8 to 3/16 thinner than the moleskine.  They're strong enough to hold your pages but they are a little bit more rickety because there's more sideways motion with all the parts attached to other wire parts instead of being attached to the big flat metal springs that you find on your normal black binder clips of this style that are solid metal.

title: Just regular masking tape
text: There is nothing special about this.  It's totally just plain old making tape.  It's not even white.

title: Includes shaperner and eraser
text:
These are shorter than the magic pencils that have the hexagonal marbled cases. Those are standard length. Theese are about 12 cm or 4-3/4" long. A standard pencil is 7.5" long. these are about 2/3 normal pencil length.

The package is all paperboard and will hold the set together pretty well for a while. The eraser is an abrasive type with grit. Not reccommended for handmade paper because it will pull up the soft surface of the fibers on such papers. But it did erase the colored pencil completely, unlike a plastic eraser without grit or a kneaded eraser- those are not able to completely erase colored pencils. The included shaperner is plastic but made specifically for this set of pencils and works well.

The swatches have some curly shapes to show changing colors. The right side of the swatch has been blended with the included blender pencil which works well.

I'm new to regular colored pencil art. I've used pencils for coloring and watercolor pencils for mixed media work. I'm hoping to use these for sketching. For the cost I think this is a quality set and think that they grouped the colors well in each pencil to create textured masstones but not alarmingly jarring color variations in a stroke.

title: Great lightweight ruler, precise manufacturing.
text: This is a high-quality, very well manufactured products. The edges are square, and noticeably so, but not Sharp. The joint in the middle is well machined and flawless.  The ruler does not bend as it is thick aluminum and it doesn't flop around loosely or fold back in on itself unless you're giving it a bit of pressure while you use it. I have kind of a firm grip and unless I intentionally want to move it it won't flop around on me at the hinge.  I really like that I can fold it down into half of its length to fit in my pochade box.  I also like that it's much lighter than a steel ruler would be. I have the black one and it's also quite snazzy looking and attractive.

title: Waterproof once dry. Outstanding pens.
text:
I bought these for urban sketching. I do a pencil sketch, then I finalize my line art with these markers, and then I watercolor over them. They have excellent use for this purpose and work fantastically. The ink is very solid and opaque, the lines are reliable, and these are awesome pens. They don't feather they don't bleed they don't go through paper unless it's extremely thin, and I'm very happy with this purchase. I would highly recommend any of the super ink pens by uni. I have some uni ball pens that I bought at the end of the 90s and in the early 2000s, and they still write like champs if I haven't used them for a while. There's lots of ink in them and they work a long time.

I have to say I've never had a product from this company that I was disappointed in. They're white gel markers are the best on the market. If you like gelly rolls, you were going to love their white gel pens. They're even more noticeably opaque and the ink goes on excellently..

title: H. U. G. E.  SKETCHBOOK.  Almost pizza box sized.
text: For reals...this sucker is ginormous!  Same as other moleskine watercolor sketchbooks.  25% cotton, slightly off white paper, hard cover,etc. If you like watercolor moleskine sketchbooks, and want a large format, this is it!!

title: Convenient pigment ink.  Not a bad price, good way to carry extra ink without a bottle.
text:
Here is the famous carbon black ink! it's easy to take a few cartridges in my sketch kit with me and be able to refill if my pen runs out. the price of these is not too bad and I could reuse the empty cartridges from a bottle with a blunt syringe, more cheaply then buying the official converters. I'm going to experiment with plugging the refilled cartridges with a little bit of tombow putty or Blu tack to see if a little plug of it can just be removed in the field and used as a regular refill without leaking or leaving blue tack in my pen. Since it does fit into my preppy pens, and those are fairly cheap, I'll experiment that way so that I don't have to worried about a better pen getting wrecked with BlueTaC.

if you are someone who is looking for it spelled out.... Yes! This ink is great for urban sketching with watercolors, it's WTAERPROOF once you let it dry, and you can wash right over it once it is dry without smudging or fading or bleeding. It's good stuff.

different papers do have different sizing and drying times. I would keep a page set aside in your notebook to do some sample marks and make sure your materials play well together, and that you know how long it takes to dry on that specific paper before you can wet it. I do have a Strathmore 400 watercolor journal that has very picky sizing... noodler's never really tended to be very waterproof on it and it took a very long time to dry. This one did dry more quickly than noodlers on that particular paper, but it did take longer than I initially expected before the ink set up dry and waterproof. I also use De Atramentis archival ink-- it dried about the same length of time as this Carbon Black one does, and is about the same amount of blackness and as waterproof. Personally I like this ink better than noodlers, and I also really like the De Atramentis archival ink. but again, different papers are going to respond to materials differently and you'd be well off to make a sample test page to make sure you know how your materials handle in specific combinations before you get down to doing work that you spend a lot of time on.

title: Good value
text: These are light weight and decent quality.  It's definitely a student grade set, but for $3 it's just what is expect.  It's not gonna last for years, but it will get you through a few classes.

title: They are ok. Quality control not fantastic.
text:
They have strong springs and grip well. The metal is a teeny bit thinner than I expected. The powder coat along the group saves is not well finished.

Another reviewer mentioned they or repackaging. Mine arrived clipped together also, not really scratched or anything, but definitely the gripping surfaces have cold or something and could potentially be abrasive toward whatever surface they are affixed to. I'm using them for sketchbook paper so I'm not super worried, but the other surface is going to be a sketch board. (Binder clips are much smoother).

I mean, for the price, they are decent enough. But they do come off like factory seconds perhaps. Functionally, they will hold things tightly, but if you're wanting to hold photos or something with a scratch able surface (like enameled metal) I would have some concern about those surfaces that come into xontach. It's also a very small edge with contacts, with focused gripping on that edge, so hence the concern. If they'd even bent the metal a touch flatter just where that contact is applied, or rolled the edge a bit, it would be better.

title: I bought for watercolor pencils
text:
I have the Faber castell Magnus watercolor pencils. They are big pencils. I wanted this larger sharpener to use with them because my Kum sharpener is too small. It's not the best sharpener. I think mine has a blade screwed in slightly akimbo. It's kind of choppy as it sharpens instead of a totally smooth motion. It does the job though without breaking the softer watercolor leads in the dürer Magnus pencils.

The pencils included are good. Also the eraser. Worth the money as a set.

title: Staedtler Mars is a teeny bit better, but...
text: I wanted something that had a different barell color that I could tell apart because I load them with different leads.  The lead pointer is meh.  There eraser is nice, the leads are good, and it's lightweight and functioning.  But it just feels a notch down on quality from the staedtler one, which mine is admittedly pretty old and I can't speak to comparing new ones side by side.  But I find both Faber castell and staedler to be on par both good quality and comparable products, but this one was ever so slightly less well finished than the staedtler lead holder.  When compared in this set for the extra items, it's totally a decent deal, and that's the other reason I liked this set and am happy to use it.  Really, it's a nitpicky thing, and not a significant enough difference to deter you from purchasing if you're a fan of FC products.  Go for it.  You'll be happy, and if this seteets your needs it's a better deal than a standalone Mars lead holder.

title: It was nice but...
text:
I returned it. It was made very well, was hefty, etc. But I have good sized hands and I just didn't like the feel of it enough to keep for the price. I also bought the cretacolor wooden ergonomically one. I really liked that one. Felt nice in my hand, light, study, well shaped. I loved the look of this one but found it too short, and for the diameter, the anti roll hexagonal shape just didn't feel as nice to work with. YMMV. It's a good quality device, and attractive. I just personally liked using the cretacolor one better.

I kinda liked the Art Alternates one better too. It wasn't as heavy.

title: Amazon can't handle fragile items.
text: I ordered 2 packs.  all arrived busted into little unusable lengths. Maybe this has something to do with the warehouse packing it with a 2 foot length of crumpled Kraft paper in a large carton also containing a case of paper plates and an xl jug of shampoo.  Gee.  Charcoal that small is gonna get nailed.  Duh.

title: Watercolor masking fluid removal
text:
I've been using this for watercolor masking fluid removal. They do a great job. they haven't smudged the final coat of paint on me yet. I find that my fingers are not very good for removing masking fluid because it's too easy for my hands to put pressure on the pigments and smudge them. these rubber cement pickups do a great job at just grabbing The intended target: Rubber cement, or watercolor masking fluid. they're weird little cubey things--- but they do such a great job at the one thing that they do.

I'm also glad that it was a two pack because I can put one in my sketch travel kit and one in a different kit that I use for art upstairs. I was looking for more than one at the time I purchased it so that just sweetens the deal.

title: Works and worth buying
text:
I like this desk. I was worried that it would not be any better that holding the laptop in my legs directly, but it actually is better, very much. It makes me tense my legs less and hold the computer less with my forearms. So I can type more easily for longer and door in a more comfortable seat than at at table or desk. Helpful because I have lots of back pain. I put my feet up on an ottoman and I can work for hours like that.

It's attractive. I would have liked maybe less of a bold pattern, but it's actually fine. Would also have liked the slot to be wide enough for a tablet and not just a smartphone. But I don't really use that feature anyhow. I would if it were for my pad though, with a keyboard. Works very well with my 13" MacBook air.

I have used it in lots of different circumstances too. A little annoying to carry around to waiting rooms but does make it so so much easier to work actually on ones lap than with just a laptop.

title: love them!
text:
Good quality paint. Iridescently pigmented and lots of mica flake. The flake is fairly fine and spreads evenly in washes. I can tell there is a lot of flake because it absorbs a bit oddly compared to other watercolors, it kind of puffs up and separates when a droplet of water is added to the pan. I usually use an eyedropper to dampen paints a moment while I Sketch my design,then paint once the water takes up the pigment and softens it. With these, I do need to take a little extra care mixing on my pallette, and also smooth out the cake of paint in the pan if using it on the brush directly. It handles a bit like a thicker type of paint because of the flake.

I like using them in skies or on water surfaces to add a little extra gleam and luminosity, so I tend to thin them out a good deal and.mix with other colors. They hold up well and blend well without losing their sparkly quality combined with other paints.

I also have the box of various blacks,and experimented mixing these with those on the page and ended up with profoundly 'velvety' luminousity. Like a photo of a velvet dress or curtain. Lovely. I will be buying more of these when they run out, which probably won't be anytime soon... They are large 2cm x 3 xm pans, about half full, for a total of 4-5 mm depthof driet paint. They do not stay sticky like sugar based or gumarabic based binders. The pans are firm and tackless when dry. Would highly recommend.

title: As expected except the smell.
text: I like the pen...  except...  for some reason it smells HORRIBLE.  It smells like someone soaked it in vomit.  I haven't been able to get the smell out of it, It makes using the pen very distracting.  I know this sounds kind of squeamish, but seriously.  It smells like barf.  No clue why.

title: Unimpressed paper snob
text: I was pretty unimpressed with this paper. I bought it for writing letters with fountain pen, and it really wasn't what I wanted and had hoped for.

title: Pretty good value for the price
text: These are really good envelopes considering what's available on the market. I would say their finish is similar to cranes kid finish, but they are a little bit lighter weight.

title: Pretty good.
text:
It's not the best paper I've used, and I'm pretty much a paper snob. Yes, seriously, there is such a thing, and I'm it. It's a little heavier than I would like for letterwriting, but it's definitely good for a resume. It also prints well in my printer.

If anyone out there has found a good substitute for Crane's thesis paper (no longer made), please let me know. Do not answer if you haven't personally USED Crane's thesis paper. It's my favorite and I want to find a paper which compares to it.

title: Highly unimpressed paper snob.
text:
I'll admit it. I'm absolutely 100% a paper snob. I used to work in a stationary and art supply store, and I've gotten completely directed to cranes 100% cotton papers. I write letters very frequently with fountain pen and custom inks, and I like the way other papers take the ink far far better than this paper. I'm not a huge fan of Southworth but it seems to be the only thing on the market anymore.

Honestly it's kind of like comparing gumballs to truffles.
I guess gumballs are fun, but truffles cost more for a reason.
This paper is truffle cost for gumball quality.

I guess I'm spoiled, but this is definitely not what I would ever use for a thesis. Cranes used to make an outstanding thesis paper which was smooth and watermarked and it takes pen and ink from fountain pens like you would not believe! This stuff sure ain't that! The texture of the surface is far rougher than even an average quality copy paper. When using a fountain pen on the top corner to write and actually smacks the nab and folds the corner over. I have not used this in a printer. It would probably work fine. I'll probably use it to print a manuscript because it is archival an acid free, But I would not consider this good enough quality paper for just about anything. It beats the heck out of a five dollar ream of copy paper, sure. But it's almost 30 bucks for half as much paper. I could buy 100% cotton cranes crest for 60 bucks and get 500 sheets. It's what I should've done.

title: They don't have very stiff covers, they're just not what they used to be. But they're better than most other ones on the market
text: The covers aren't very stiff, but none of the brands I've seen are anymore. I was hoping to find some five star  with plastic covers, but I haven't been able to locate any locally.  These will probably hold up for a three month writing class that I'm teaching middle schooler's.  i'm not sure I would expect them to last an entire year, though. The stitching is good and the paper is quality. They're basically what I expected, but they're just not as good as they were made 15 or 20 years ago with a real cover made of actual cardboard that was stiff.  I have some that are over 30 years old that are in great shape from when I was in middle school, and these would never hold up the way those have. Same brand.

title: Terrible
text: These are terrible. It's hard to find a good pocket notebook with a hard cardboard cover. They are not sewn, they are glued, and as soon as I opened the book the binding cracked and pages started to peel out.  The cover is about as thick as a shiny heavyweight index card. It might be great for index cards, but it's terrible for a cover of a pocket notebook.

title: be wary of purchasing used.
text: I bought used from Warehouse sales.  Whoever used it prior had changed the combo and it is non functional.  I wasn't able to return it within the time frame.

title: one of my favorites.
text: Lovely flexibility and responsiveness in the nib.  A bit small for a medium nib.  But the ink flow is great.  It has a rubber bladder fill system, which I find a bit weird, and hard to judge remaining ink levels.  I have three of these pilot fountain pens, and they are great to travel,  Haven't had any issues with leaking or drying up.  These are inexpensive pens, but very reliable.  I use with Diamine shimmer inks, they are not quite wet enough or wide enough a line to REALLY dramatize the metallic nature of those inks, but, on the right paper (cotton wove works great) they still have a subtle and noticeable sheen to the glimmer inks.  With Iroshizuku inks, the flow is beautiful and gives a uniform color in the strokes.  I find with a wetter nib, the Iroshizuku has more color variation in the pen strokes-  if you're wanting that or a very dramatic pen stroke with a glimmer ink, I'd recommend a Jinhao medium over this one.  it's a nice nib and gives lots of ink flow, but, those are more variable in their quality too, and slower to write with, and might need more adjustments, they also can go dry pretty quickly.  I'd say the pilots tend to need ZERO adjustments, and overall are more reliable.  But this pen is a faster writer, a good hand size, and great feel to write with.  I would also recommend it over a Cross pen for ease of writing, nib responsiveness, and metallic inks.  I've had every Cross go dry and require lots of cleaning from J. Herbin inks, Diamine Glimmer inks, and even the Iroshizuku inks.  Cross also has a stiffer nib and less ergonomic shape, IMO.  I've seen the shimmer and anniversary J. Herbin inks go completely flat with a Cross pen- they seem to completely lose dimensional qualities, as with making the Iroshizuku flatter as well. I love the looks of some pens, but the Pilot pen is always one of my go to pens for actually WRITING with.

title: Secret messages!  Fun fun fun!!!
text: My boyfriend and I send naughty letters back and forth with the UV inks. It's tremendous fun. The blue ghost is actually completely invisible on most papers. Works best on light papers, though. I tried it on black paper, and once the ink was dry, it wasn't visible on UV light anymore. I thought that it would stand out more against a dark background when it was given UV, but in fact it was totally invisible.

title: 5x8 cards fit!
text:
5x8 cards fit, beneath the tabs. I have another expanding file that the half page or cards stick out above the divider tabs, and the corners get abused a nit in that one.

Amazon packed my first one in a box with heavy stuff in my S&S order -that one got smooshed. But the next one that arrived was very good. I'm happy with it.

title: Diamine is beautiful
text: I have 9 shimmer inks and one 'regular' ink from Diamine. They are my favotite multi- dimensional ink. I love Iroshizuku inks for their unique colors and depth. At heart, I love the little metallic sheen and variations. It's why to use fountain inks IMO. I've not been disappointed by Diamine. It's lovely stuff.  My favorite is Orange inferno, and this- blue flame- my second favorite.

title: Underwhelming sparkle, FOR ME. I love these inks for the shimmer.
text: I have five or six other diamine shimmering inks. I particularly like the brightly colored ones because they have a lot more dimension in terms of the pigment transparency and glimmer combination during a pen stroke and how they vary.  This one is truly essentially a black ink with some silver. It's the same quality of other diamine inks, which in my opinion is some of the best ink that I've tried so far of its kind. I'm also a huge fan of Iroshizuku colors and flow. But, when it comes down to it, I do like a bit of color, and this is not flashy enough to make it stand out from my other "black "inks. I also have J. herbin storm gray and find that this is slightly blacker but otherwise similarly a little too subtle for my particular taste. If you were looking for a dark ink with a neutral tone, and very little shimmer, but just a hint, then this is probably the ink for you, it is more shimmery than the J. herbin Storm Grey 1670.

title: I have three of these. Recommend.
text:
I have about 20 different fountain pens with refillable ink cartridge converters in each of them. Five of them are Cross pens. I got them on sale after the holidays, and invested and additional seven dollars in each one to buy refillable converters like this and use my own bottled selection of ink. They work quite well and are of comparable quality to all of the converters that came in my other pens.

If you have a cross fountain pen, there are two different kinds of converters, some that screw in, like for the Bailey model, and some that pushing like for the Townsend and aventura models. The Corss website has the listing for which one your pen needs. It's a worthwhile investment for the pen considering cross ink cartridges are quite limited. You may need to soak the nib section of your pen overnight if you were switching from the cross cartridges to another Inc. which is lighter or colored because the feed assembly really retains a lot of the deep pigment.

title: Not celluloid
text:
if you're hoping this pen is celluloid, it's not. It's a pretty wanting facsimile of the old vintage pen colors and textures which were. It's an olive green and black sort of airbrushy pattern.

That said, I am finding that the Jinhao X-450's are really great pens and they're very consistently good performers with all kinds of inks. I'd buy more colors if they had a broader rainbow.

title: can't beat it.
text:
Nice writier.

I can't believe these pens go for around five to $10. They're nice heavy pens, this glittery one has holographic specks which are really fun in different light. The gullor ink cartridges which come with pens have terrible ink in them, but I intended to use the refillable cartridge converter that came with the pen with my own selection of bottle inks.

title: Lovely jam free paper
text: my printer loves this paper. All the positive reviews say it already. I use it in my small duplex printer. It was cheaper to buy nice paper and extra toner cartridges to print multiple copies of my manuscript then it was to go to an office store and make copies on their cheap crappy paper. The manuscripts look really nice in the paper is wonderful to work with.

title: Lovely inks for grumpy pens and wet pens alike.
text:
nice flow.

Lovely vibrant colors with unique hues.

Ink dries with shading per your pen strokes, this gives a character I like.

I have 9 of these inks. The more intense colors do not shade as much, but some. The lighter, brighter colors are brilliant and show more shading, which intensifies the color if more ink saturates an area or is gone over again.

I will be buying larger bottles of my favorites and dedicating certain pens in my collection to them. I have some pens, especially ones with fine stingy nibs, which are picky about inks despite fiddling with adjustments. This ink works well in pens with grumpy nibs.

title: High hopes, disappointed.
text:
These leads are just Ok.
They are pinkish red.
They DO erase better than other red pencils I've used.
They break FAR more easily than pentel black graphite leads. I'll go with the pentel red leads next time and see if those break less.
I write firmly. I need stronger lead. I'd buy these again in a pinch, like if it's the only brand in a store, and I need it immediately. But given the option, I'll try another type next time.

title: It's a nice pen.
text:
Look, you could get a plastic high end pen for this price which isn't refillable, and for which one can't choose one's own ink.

I have used Pilot Iroshizuku fuyu-gaki, and Diamine orange inferno in this pen. It lays down a nice line that will be wet enough to show the shimmer of the ink and also gradation of flowing color on both. For my writing, the top is a bit lighter shade and the bottom is a bit more saturated and deep.

I have the orange pen. If I am feeling it a bit heavy, I use it with the cap off. Otherwise it's a comfortable pen overall.

title: Decent item
text:
this is not a 5 star item, but I was not expecting one for this price.

For what I paid, it does what I need well. The stitching is good, the zip installed properly. The lining is velvety and the elastic holds good sized pens. I'll update with photos some time soon.

title: not for HP460C- but did not claim to be either
text: nice case but did not fit my HP460C portable.  I measured the printer carefully and figured it would fit, but it wasn't quite right.  too bad, it's a nice little case.

title: You get what you pay for!
text: Super cheapo shaperners. But they are about what I expected for the price. And kids, they love a bright colored new plastic thing in their goodie bags. These fit that bill.

title: It’s ok..
text: It’s ok. Does the job. Not very comfortable texture on my neck, rubs my skin and the material is annoying. It’s just a lanyard made of some cheap feeling synthetic material that is fairly OK but for near $10 I would like something softer or with a better texture and more flexible. The clip is nice though.

title: Great paper, highly recommended
text: Fantastic paper. I was trying to print 110# cardstock on my printer that I had done before, but it just wasn't working. This works beautifully, and is the perfect thickness for my paper crafts.

title: Perfect weight for junk journals
text: For some reason my printer has stopped printing on cardstock. I was at my wits end, and then saw a YouTube video where someone mentioned 65# paper,so I thought I'd give it a try. It worked flawlessly! A+

title: Great scale for the money
text: Great little scale. I had to send the first one back because it didn’t work, but that wasn’t a problem at all. I’ve used it a lot now.

title: Stackable, cuts tape neatly, looks nice.
text: I ordered these for my larger rolls of sparkle washi tape that I bought for some unknown reason. I barely used the washi tape and figured if I had an easier way to cut them and store them, I would find more uses for them. This did the trick. It looks cute on my desk, but also stores nicely in a drawer. I have been using them more often, and I finally don’t feel like I wasted my money on sparkly washi tape. Oh, and these were a very good price and great quality.

title: You get what you pay for… not the worst, but not great.
text: These were not horrible by any means. But they also weren’t blowing me away. They were very inexpensive, and you get what you pay for. The color and tone is great. They aren’t sheer at all. The gripe I have is that they don’t last at all. They run out so quickly, that is the long run, it’s cheaper to invest in more expensive pens. I was only able to complete one little project, and with a typical generic paint pen, I can do 10. I won’t repurchase, but if you are looking for something cheap to give to kids, or something in a pinch for one time use only, these will work. The tip is nice, though. Extra fine and sturdy. And the colors in the pack are nice. I just wish there was more paint in them.

title: Great deal!!!
text: Exactly what I needed. I compared the price to another seller that was advertising 4 per little case, for about $5 more. I get these and turns out there are 4 in each thing, not 3 as advertised. Bonus!!!!

title: I love these pens
text: I love these pens! I use them with my adult coloring. The metallic is smooth and doesn't clump. The colors are different than any other metallic gel pen out there. They dry quickly which is also a huge plus. This style Pentel has always been my go to regular pen because of the comfort and way they write. I am so happy they have metallic gel pens now! title: Enjoying the Realo's bigger ink capacity!
text: I love Sailor fountain pens because their nibs, weight, and size are perfect for me and have many that use converters. A downside is that Sailor converters have a small ink capacity, which means that I have to fill up frequently and constantly unscrew the barrel to check ink levels. I purchased the Realo model because it holds more ink than the converters (though certainly not as much as other fountain pen brands, such as Pelikan, for example) and am happy to report that it is everything that I love about Sailor pens with the added ink capacity. The piston fill mechanism works well and smoothly and I can go a little longer between refills. The ink window is a big plus since it lets me see just how much ink is remaining in the pen even without having to uncap the pen. The pen writes well with that characteristic Sailor feedback that feels a lot smoother with the broad nib as compared to finer nib widths. Super happy with this pen and just ordered another!

And not only have I tested them thoroughly, I use them almost daily for work.

As the title states, the ink itself is transparent. It turns out almost pastel, especially for the lighter colors. You can see this from the photos attached. It is buildable so if you go over it a few times it can darken up. That makes it fun for drawing or doodling.

They actually erase quite well which is kind of mind-blowing. I don't know the science behind it and at this point, I don't question it. Just go with it!

The eraser itself is at the top of the pen and doesn't shrink or leave behind little pieces like a pencil.

Overall, I really do like these markers. They are different and I haven't seen anything else like it!

The caps fit snugly so you won't have to worry about them falling off, as long as you make sure you push them all the way on. They move smooth and look great.
These are brilliant glitter highlighters. They are all bright enough to see, including the yellow which can sometimes be too light, and the sparkle is clear in each and every one of them. It's quite a nice sparkle too but not so much that it gets in the way of what is being highlighted underneath.
These will jazz up anything needing a little extra something and they will make it look beautiful. I definitely recommend these.

title: Excellent Gel Pens
text:
These are great gel pens. There are eight in total with four being black colored and the others being one red, one blue, one purple, and one green. They have a gripper that makes them incredibly easy to hold on to comfortably and they glide nicely across the paper but you have complete control of the pen so there isn't any slipping like you can find with some gel pens. They don't smudge either. The weight of these is excellent as well. That is, there isn't a whole lot of it. They are nice and light so you can hold on to them longer without your hand getting tired too quickly.
I definitely recommend these if you are looking for a decent gel pen like these. They work great and the ink looks terrific.

title: Stunning pen
text:
This pen was a bit too heavy for me to hold comfortably for long periods of time which was 100% perfect for my husband because he stole it almost immediately anyway. Since this was the case, I asked him to give me some feedback for my review. Here is what he had to say:

"This pen comes in a beautiful red wooden box. It really is so nicely crafted and maybe you won't write with it. Maybe you will just sit there and stare at it.
As to the pen itself it's just as pretty to look at with the wooden design and gold trimming. There is a section between the tip and the outer of the pen which is laid out in a striking black between the wood and the gold which you can use to grip.
The writing quality is pretty good. The ink is thick when it comes out so it's more of a pen for a careful writer. If you have messy hand writing you might do better with a thinner tip. The ink doesn't smear or stay wet and it generally does write very well."

That's what he had to say. I will add that this pen is something that is highly giftable. It looks terrific and writes nice enough. Mainly it just looks so nice.

title: Great refill!
text:
This is a tape refill for AmazonBasics hyper repositionable and refillable adhesive. You can get one of these for about the same price as this refill for it. I'm not sure if there is a difference in the amount of tape you get with it and this refill or if you are just paying the same price for the refill that you would pay for the holder (that comes filled). That said (in a way that I hope wasn't too confusing), this is a good refill. It's so very easy to put it inside the holder and it only takes a matter of seconds.
This can last quite a long time as long as you aren't doing something like wrapping a ton of gifts or anything like that. I love the dispenser so I, in turn, love this refill to go in it. I do recommend the whole thing. It's a time saver for so many things!

title: Great compact size
text:
This is a little expensive for what you get if you buy just one so don't do that. If you purchase this item purchase the pack of three. It's much more cost efficient that way. Just thought I would get that out there. At the cost for three, I really like this tiny compact tape adhesive.
This little thing is just that, little. It fits nicely in a pocket, backpack, purse, etc. If you are in school or have a job where you may need a little tape on the fly this is a great little gadget to keep with you. Of course there are so many other reasons to carry this with you. I carry it just in case and I don't fit into any of those categories. This is a good double sided dispenser. It's tape that has a glue like feel/stick to it so it works great on paper of almost any kind (perfect for envelopes).
It's easy to dispense as well. You just remove the white protective cap,press down a bit on what you want to tape/glue, and drag across. When you pick it up it stops. It works similar to a white corrective tape for ink.
I really like the compact size, the ease of use, and the perfect amount of stickiness.

title: Excellent!
text:
These are great! They work incredibly well. They are so easy to use. Once you get them situated in your hand the right way, which may take a little second or two just to figure it out the first time. You may have to flip it around a time or two to get it right but once you do you'll feel how it seems to be made for you hand and your hand alone. Then when you go to use it to correct that dastardly mistake, you'll feel and see how it simply glides over them and they disappear under a perfect whiteness. It's a nice smooth surface to write on top of as well and there is no wait for drying.
I really like these and since you get 6 in this pack you won't have to worry about them running out for a very long time, even if you are prone to make a lot of mistakes. I do recommend these, at least giving them a try, because I think you will find that they are worth every penny.

title: Works great and is convenient
text:
This is one of the very best things to happen to tape in a very long time. This particular dispenser is excellent. I have had to stop myself from running around taping everything that needs/could possibly need if I stretch my imagination far enough double sided tape. It's actually really fun to use. You just open up the cover that is covering where the tape sits waiting to be used, hold it flat to whatever you are taping, swipe it until you are where you need to be, and then push the cutting button and it leaves you a nice piece of tape that is stuck to whatever you are sticking it to and a sticky side up waiting for you to stick something to it.
The dispenser itself is well designed. It's comfortable to hold and so easy to work. It's also refillable which is a great big plus. The fact it's refillable helps explain the cost a bit as well (even though the refill is the same price as just buying this again I believe, but I could be wrong).
I really like the ease of use of this. Double sided tape is so useful sometimes but you do have the cost to consider if you are going to use a lot of it.

title: Excellent coverage
text:
This correction tape is excellent. It takes just one swipe with it and all the writing is covered up completely. There is no need to go back over repeatedly or at all. It's so easy to hold as well. Though I do admit when I first picked it up I was turning it all over the place trying to get it to feel comfortable. Once you get it though and give it a try you quickly see how terrific it is. This has a duel action applicator as well that makes it so you can easily correct an entire line or just one letter.
These run a bit high price wise for just two of them but I would definitely recommend them for those that have to have very neat work. College papers, business papers, anything at all to do with numbers, etc. These are great for covering what is underneath completely and neatly, able to cover whole lines/words or just one character perfectly, and can be written over smoothly and perfectly.
These are exceptional.

title: Easy to use and long lasting
text:
These are different from other pen style correction tapes I've used in that these have a cover on them. I love that unique little feature. It's just one little thing that really makes them stand out that much more. They are pretty simple to use, just make sure you are holding them exactly right before you start sliding them across to correct what you are correcting. I tend to hold them off just a bit and either have nothing work at all or get a sketchy blotch of white lines. It's all just about getting the knack of holding them right. It's not hard, it's just something that you have to get in the swing of doing when you get them for the first time.
These are nice too because they come in a pack of four. One lasts a very long time, and I like to make a lot of errors so that's saying a lot. I've been using the same one for about three weeks so far. It looks like there is a good bit left as of right now as well.
I would recommend giving these a try if you are in need of correction tape. They are a decent price and work quite well.

title: Nice!
text:
Since this was something I wanted but since we got it my husband has more often used I asked him to jot down a few words about it. Here's what he thought:

"I suggested this intending for the wifey to use it. She is one of those tiny creatures (I'm cutting in on his words here because I'm not that "tiny" of a creature. I'm 5'8". He just happens to be 6'1" and we have a tall house with tall closets that I happen to be about half an inch too short for! Okay, I'm stepping back out now) who can't get into higher places.
For a step stool you want to know it's solid. It is. There are two steps, all metal, with a handle bar going across the top. I tried jumping and putting weight on one of the steps and there was hardly any noticeable flex at all. This is good. It might be the most solidly constructed item in our home. I also tried putting a lot of weight on the handle and it held up fine too. If you wiggle around a bit you can shake it from side to side. I don't think that would happen with a solid plastic step stool but that's not a problem.
There is no assembly, thankfully. Just push the step inward to open it up. It does have rubber feet to keep it secure on the ground and I see there is no locking mechanism for it. But once you are on it the step stool will be secure enough. I don't think you would need it and you aren't that high off the ground anyway.
There is a simple hook type latch to keep the top step in place once it is unfolded so to unfold it you will need to lift the step up while pushing the back legs in. Simple and effective.
4 stars. Very happy with it."

There you have it. Those are all the thoughts he had on this step stool. He's used it way more than I have even though I'm the "short" one.

title: Practical and convenient
text:
This is a very good portfolio case. It has so many practical things in it that can be necessary for every day ventures. It comes with a pen and three bands for pens to clip to, a calculator, a little built in pocket for papers or whatever you'd like with a spot in front for cards (business or otherwise), and another little pocket, plus the whole left side is a big lift up pocket. In the middle there is a four ring binder with document bags. On the right is a paper holder clip and a writing pad.
This portfolio has so many things in a small easy to carry case. I don't know how I managed to get stuff done without mine. I love it!

title: These work great
text:
These BIC brite liner highlighters are excellent. They are chisel tipped and have an soft easy grip so you can hold on to them with ease. They work so good. I've had no ink smears at all. The brightness of the yellow is perfect. It's easy to quickly find the highlighted text when looking at a page and with the chisel tip you can have thick or thin lines with a simple finger movement.
