There are circles cut out with measurements that are nice for bullet journals, art journals, that sort of thing and can double as knitting needle/crochet hook gauges in a pinch. There is a nice collection of triangles there as well.

There is a ruler running along one side, which is useful to too many purposes to list. There are also ruler marks going back into the case, similar to what you’d expect of a quilting ruler and appropriate for making seam marks for sewing a block. This is great for getting an even measure for scrapbooking or the like. No risk of the line going at an angle. There is even a little hole for a dot at the bottom of each measure mark, ideal for book binding.

Overall, I see this as a tool that will see a lot of heavy use. The quality is excellent and they really thought of everything.

title: Nice notebook but needs a bigger pencil case
text:
This is pretty decent. The only thing I don’t like, and what I’ll ding it a star for, is the pencil case is way too small. I can’t fit a phone in there, for example, and a student might need a scientific calculator, or full set of colored pencils, or something along those lines size-wise depending on their classes. If you just need a few pens and pencils, this will suffice. If you like the notebook, but need more space, an internal pencil case designed for loose-leaf ring binders will do the job, and the rings are spacious enough, this should not be a problem. The thing is, this looks like it’s trying to push itself off as a notebook that can do the job of a school backpack, given it’s also holding your textbooks, and if it wants to do that, it needs to offer space for the loose supplies.

In the photo, I have the D&D Player’s Handbook, which is a fairly large hardcover, in the bands. There is ample room left for more books, and it holds well, particularly with the band on the bottom adding support. I have two of my larger pens (the blue is a fountain pen) in two of the pen loops. There is a third on the bottom, but I think putting a pen there looks weird. I have a standard container of floss in the pencil case. That’s about as thick an item as it can handle, and it is a tight fit.

I found some issues with the stitching, but nothing noteworthy. Expect you might have to cut off an errant string and that’s the worst of it.

With the addition of an internal pencil case, this is a great notebook for work projects now, and would have been perfect for high school.

title: Too large for a binder
text:
The first main selling point about this is that it fits in a looseleaf binder. Well, it’s hole punched for one, but that’s as far as it goes. It’s far too large to actually fit. And there is no reason for that. An 8 ½ x 11 piece of paper sits in the folder with a lot of space above it. Shorter, this would fulfill that part of it’s purpose.

The second main selling point is the useful information printed along the side. The way the side is set up, it sits under the paper when the folder is full, so you can’t read all that great information. I mean you could if you rip the perforation, but the first time I tried that it ripped the folder.

For what it’s worth, on the left side you get conversion tables (metric, which makes no sense – who need to look up how many kilograms are in a gram?) and the conversion between metric and imperial. You also get a 15 cm ruler. On the right side you get a 6-inch ruler, a 12 x 12 multiplication table, and then a handful of tables: Dry measure conversions (ever wonder how many quarts are in a peck? According to this, 8), Dry measure conversions (expanded? It’s called the same thing but has slightly different information. There are apparently 4 gills in a pint). Avoirdupois weight conversions (this is the 16 ounces in a pound type information), Linear measure table (inches in a foot), circular measure table (minutes in a degree), and surface measure table (square inches in a square foot).

To be fair, I never knew there was a unit of measure called a hogshead before, so it is educational.

I needed these to fit in a notebook, and I simply can’t use these.

title: Adorable but don’t pop into the notebook
text: [[VIDEOID:7bd1a2d20152bb65c9459cd4a384b343]] I can’t easily store them in the notebook, but I can cut out sections if I need to do that, so easy workaround. They’re cute and strong  I like them.

title: Everything is perfect except the box they came in
text:
It shipped in the box it’s sold in. Literally, Amazon threw a shipping label on it and sent it. Not a problem, except it doesn’t seem like it was meant for that, because it looks kind of flimsy for that purpose and the box arrived damaged. Luckily, the contents were fine.

Both sides have a slightly different texture. If you fold it so that you bury the bump, which is the way I was taught, you get the smoother side on the outside and the rougher texture on the inside.

The card is a modest card stock. It can handle a reasonable application of paint and ink without a problem. The envelope is much thinner, but while I wouldn’t try as much with it, it’s not bad in its own right. It’s certainly thicker than typing paper. I used it as the internal envelope making the Junk Journal Booklet designed by Dawn Meadows over at The Book Vandal Shop, and it was so perfect for that, I’m going to use it again for the next one.

These are great for any kind of crafting, junk journal, scrapbook, cardmaking, anything. When I need more I’ll forgive the bad packaging and buy again. I love them.

title: Ghosting, poor QC, unsuable margins
text:
For the most part these are good. The main selling point is the page protector strip. It’s great, and it’s convenient not to have to deal with those silly little round protectors, but looking beyond that, it’s not the best paper on the market. Good, not great.

I’m not sure what’s up with the arrows pointing to each line, or the things that look like QR codes on the top and the bottom. They’re not in the product picture, but they are on every page, front and back. The branding is on the front of every page right under the protector strip, and the strip can’t be written on. All of this is intrusive if you’re using the Cornell note taking system. I would have preferred to see a cleaner page, and the ability to write on the strip. Who doesn’t take notes in the margins?

The quality control is lacking. For three of the 100 pages, the holes weren’t punches right. Usually that’s not a problem, but removing the excess bit made the page protector on the side come loose, and as soon as it is the least bit loose, it just peals right off. Just turning the pages lifts it. The photo with my finger under it is what happens as soon as the rest of the hole punched bit comes of and the damage progresses rapidly. The protective strip is only on one side of the page. For some, as you see in this one, the protector strip is warped on arrival.

The paper doesn’t bleed per se, but it does show substantial ghosting (you can see this in the fourth photo). I don’t normally see this in paper at this price point. For weight and thickness, this is akin to much cheaper paper.

I was hoping to love this, given the hole protectors and the clever use of the triangular punches, but sadly, the quality here starts and ends at the hole in page. I will not be buying these again.

title: One binder roomy enough for the entire project
text:
What I don’t like

There are too few color selections. I like a different color binder for each project, and these are so perfect I’d happily pick up a dozen.

What I do like

This thing is sturdy. The zippers are in secure. The rings are solid and show no signs of going loose or out of alignment. The stitching is perfect, and the material is strong. In short, this is a quality notebook that looks like it should last a very long time.

It’s extremely roomy. You not only get the two-inch binder rings you get a built-in pencil case that runs the entire length and is closed with a zipper. You also get a Velcro closed pouch in front of the pencil case that can hold a pack of Post-Its at least. Behind the pencil case, you get a generous folder area. It has six large sections with five dividers and little paper inserts to label the tags. These are ample for oversized envelopes.

I have a full set of six boxes of Hunt-A-Killer still in the envelope (for those who don’t play, the contents of each box about 1.5 times the size of a one-subject notebook, only about 9 x 12 rather than 8 ½ x 11) in just the back area. The front area has 50 page protectors, 100 pieces of loose-leaf paper and 8 dividers, and it isn’t close to full. There is enough room for 6 more boxes, same as in the back. I also stuffed a 4x4 pack of Post-Its in the smaller pocket.

Everything is closed with either zippers or Velcro. It’s very secure, and I don’t worry about anything falling out. Since I am using it for that kind of game, I have to deal with a lot of small, loose pieces of paper, and even though I store them in the page protector, it’s still good to know once I close it all up everything will stay in there and nothing will get lost.

It has a convenient carry handle that is comfortably padded and well secured into the body of the binder.

In short, this is the best binder I’ve ever encountered. I took a chance and bought two out of the gate, and I think I’ll buy another two, more if they release more colors. I wish they had these when I was in school. They’re perfect.

title: Strikes a good balance between sturdy and thin
text:
This strikes a nice balance between sturdy and thin.

If you need it to be sturdy to stand up to really hard wear, there are stronger brands on the market. A restaurant near me hangs a sheet protector stuffed with take-out menus outside the restaurant, and people come by and pull them out all day long. These aren’t suited for that kind of hard use. They would probably tear.

If you need it to hold a few pieces of paper together or hold some non-punched paper in a binder (what I bought it for) then it’s strong enough. I would feel confident putting a few pieces of paper in a single sheet protector to keep them together. Or using them to hang evidence from a Hunt-A-Killer box on a murder board or store samples of knitting or crochet swatches.

The upside of the thinner material is it reduces bulk, which is especially helpful if you’re using this to store material in a binder. I will be able to store many more of these in my notebook than I would if I had picked a protector suited for that restaurant’s use.

They come neatly packaged in a lift top box that reseals for easy storage. It was extremely well sealed to prevent damage in transit.

These are great. If I ever run out of this abundant supply, I’ll pick up more of the same.

title: Sturdy but hard to write on the tabs
text:
I’m old. I remember when you could write on a little tab of paper and slide it into the divider tab. These don’t do that. These you can write directly on the tab, and if you do so with paper it will (a) smear easily and (b) be erasable (at least what’s left of it) at the end of the school term or project. I tried ballpoint pen, and it didn’t take the mark well. What little mark I was able to make was easy to erase. I ended up testing to see if the pen was out of ink. It writes perfectly on paper and barely at all on these tabs. I hate to sound like the “get off my lawn” type, but I prefer the ones you slide the little bit of paper into. I do like the size of these tabs, though. They are just big enough for my needs.

They are sturdy. Heavy plastic all the way down, not going to tear, not going to give you trouble. I can see these taking a lot of abuse (my cat chewed on one and did minimal damage).

title: Flimsy box; blue ones are way too dark
text:
The box these came in (the product box, not the shipping box) came open and slightly damaged. It seems kind of flimsy. If you need it to be sturdy for any reason, look elsewhere. The note blocks inside were not damaged at all.

I’m not a fan of very dark Post-It notes because I like to write on them. The yellow is fine, the classic color. The cyan is pale and perfect. The pink runs slightly darker, but still serviceable. I wouldn’t complain about it. The blue is way too dark, something like ultramarine or navy blue. Dark ink on that will be hard to read. I’m almost tempted to use a white gel pen instead.

I have a feeling I’ll run out of these soon – not because it isn’t an ample supply, there are a lot of them in this box, but because the project I’m doing calls for a lot of them -- and I’ll look for a better color combination when I need more. It feels like 25% of them aren’t going to be that useful.

title: It isn't really letter size and the top isn't compatible with the bottom
text:
One half of the case isn’t entirely compatible with the other half of the case. The bottom is substantially larger than the top when it is fully open. I had something like this back in the 80s and the top and bottom would both accordion to the same size. With this one the bottom expands and the top doesn’t. You can either have full size, or you can have a top cover, but you can’t have both. Who thought that was a good idea?

This isn’t well-suited for letter size paper. It can squeeze in there, but it can’t lay flat. The edges are forced to curl in a little because this is just a smidge too narrow. I get the feeling it was meant for A4 paper, which it looks like it will suit just fine, and then someone found out that these sell better in the US if you put “letter” in the description. They didn’t bother to find out what that meant, or if they did, they didn’t bother to test and just put the word there.

I’m using this for a short-term project, and I plan to try to make do, but I don’t like it and if this goes to long term I’m replacing it.

title: Branding is too intrusive
text:
I’m going to start with saying I use folders for two purposes – filing papers around the house, and as a craft supply. This review will focus a little on the former, but mainly on the later. The first picture is a sample project (a file folder folio awaiting decoration) just to show what I mean. All three photos are the same folder. I don't know why the color looks so different. The first is true to life.

The main thing I like is the colors. They’re great for crafting. Most are so dark that for filing they will require using a heavy black marker for labeling, or just a peelable label, but that’s not a big deal.

These are a medium quality folder, which is what I was expecting. They’re reasonably sturdy. I tried folding back and creasing then closing and re-creasing the front cover a few times to check for stress on the score line, and it was fine. I scored one myself for a project using a score-pal and a bone folder and then tried to adjust that score line. It tore slightly from the stress. That was disappointing, because I do that to folders all the time and usually they don’t tear. I’m hoping it was a one-off, but even if it wasn’t, it’s not a stopping point, just something to be aware of.

They are roomy enough, I can store the package from Hunt-A-Killer, or about 100 pages, in one with no issue, and sturdy enough I can pull that out without tearing the folder.

My main concern is the branding logo (second picture). It’s way too large and way too far into the folder, so much so I’m dinging it a star. For one thing, it makes these far too unprofessional to use in an externally facing business situation. I wouldn’t use one of these folders to bring resumes to a job interview or to hold papers I was presenting to a client. For internal-only or household files, they’re fine.

For another thing, it interferes with craft projects. It sticks out of the angle pocket (third picture), something I have never had happen before. You can also see it in the final project photo. The plus is it comes in so far from the score line it will be easy to cover it with a decorative element. The minus is it diminishes the benefit of those beautiful colors. I was hoping to leave it orange.

Overall, I'm a little disappointed. I think I can rework some of my plans with them to add concealing decorations, but I don't think I'll be buying them again.

title: One of the best
text:
These are some of the best out there. Moleskein has a long-standing reputation for quality, and it is well earned. These are smaller notebooks, not so much soft cover as card stock cover. I have found a few traveler’s notebook covers that can support these. Carpe Diem has a few that work with this.

This is the best I’ve ever seen. No feathering. No ghosting. No bleeding. No issues at all. The paper is a pleasure to work with. The binding, while simple stitch binding, is secure and sturdy. There is a small pocket on the back cover (they folded it such that the back cover was longer, than folded it in and glued the bottom – not amazing, but functional). It can’t hold much, but I can fit a few pages or business cards in it, and for the size of the notebook, that’s plenty.

They do not seem to be acid free. Two years in and they’re starting to yellow a little. This isn’t necessarily an issue, but if you need this to last a very long time, look elsewhere.

The perforations shown in the product image don’t seem to be on all the pages, just the last few.

The lined are closer to college rule than medium.

I love these and I use them all the time.

title: Great pins; clips too small
text:
The pins are perfectly fine. They even go into the clips to hang something from the board you don’t want to put a hole in.

The clips are a little on the small side for my taste. I like clip that can hold a big stack of paper and this is comparable to a large paper clip. I can’t use them to hold a sketchbook or the like open, and I use clips like this all the time for my bullet journal.

They are all really cute. I like them. I don’t love them.

title: Nice for line work; doesn’t blend well
text:
These don’t blend well or smudge easily. If you want to use them for line work or for finishing details, that’s a plus. If you want to use them in place of colored pencils altogether for urban sketching or something, that’s a minus.

The 0.7 size seems to be the most common for colored leads. I have found 0.5 but there are fewer offerings there. So you’ll be able to find refills easily at this size. I haven’t found refills for the erasers yet, but they’re so large I haven’t needed them either.

The pencils have a good grip. They dispense the lead easily. I hate the ones where you need to sit there clicking and nothing comes out. These don’t do that. They’re comfortable to use. The color selection is nice. I use that in my bullet journal all the time.

title: Hard to smudge for better or worse
text:
They’re great for detail work. They don’t smudge much, even when you try to smudge them. Naturally they have and keep a much finer point than standard colored pencils. I use them ina drawing as the last step to establish details

I also use them a lot in a bullet journal for decorative elements. I get the best of both worlds. I can erase, especially if I start lightly. I don’t have to worry about smearing the pigment when I go back later to use the spread.

They’re also good for urban sketching when you want the most convenient way to add color to your drawings. No need to bring a pencil sharpener or deal with shavings. Just keep in mind you’re better off using them as a linear tool, closer to a pen but easily erasable.

They’re versatile and fun.

title: Good coverage. Easy to use easy to write on
text:
These are convenient. They don’t tend to peel or split after they’ve been laid down. They are thick and capable of fully covering even a dark line. They lay down cleanly and easily. They are easy to write on once laid down.

This set is good quality and a good value if you generally go through covering quickly. I use them almost every day. Each one lasts a good while and there are plenty here so I don’t need more often at all.

The dispenser is comfortable to hold and easy to use. I gave one to an elderly lady who struggled with liquid corrector because her hands are no longer steady and she found this very easy to use.

These are great.

title: Works with Boox, Supernote, and Remarkable 2
text:
I got this for the Remarkable 2 after losing the stylus that came with it. I have since used it with the Supernote and the Boox Lumi Max and it works for all three without an issue, both the writing and the eraser part. The eraser is why I went with the jumbo. I would have preferred the slimmer pencil offer that option. I can’t see why it wouldn’t.

It’s on the big side, and oddly shaped, which probably makes it easier for kids. For me it took a bit of getting used to, and I use large pens like the Lamy Safari all the time. I’ve used it for taking notes in 8-hour meetings, and it’s not bad for that.

It comes with six nibs if you include the one in the pencil, and a tool to remove them, though honestly, I don’t bother with the tool and I find a pair of tweezers to be much easier to work with. The nibs last a good long time – I used one over about ten of those 8-hour meeting sessions and it kept going – and whenever I go looking for replacements, they are widely available.

This isn’t a bad option, and I’m torn between it and the Lamy EMR as my favorite. The eraser is why this one might win (you need to hold down a button for the Lamy to erase). The style and comfort is why the Lamy might win.

title: My go to when I turn to my best tools
text:
This is pretty good at holding a lot of notebooks. I did the trick of getting extra bands and running them behind a notebook so one internal band can hold three notebooks and I was able to add four extra that way without it becoming excessively bulky. Out of the box, there is room for four notebooks, and it is big enough to comfortably house a Moleskine Cahier.

I like the size and adaptability here. When I need a larger notebook, or too many notebooks, or too many loose bits of paper, it can handle it. When things get crazy and I need a notebook system I can depend on to adapt to my day on the fly, this is up to the task. It’s my go to when I need to pull out my best tools.

It holds closed nicely, whether or not it is overfilled.

The elastic pen loop is very adaptable, so I can keep a thinner or thicker pen in there without a problem. I’ve gone as thick as a Lamy Safari, which has given me problems with smaller pen loops.

The front cover has a large pocket area bound on top and bottom, a somewhat smaller flap in front of that, and three business card pouches, the last of which has a transparent window. I inadvertently got paint on that window and it was easy to clean it off.

The back cover has the same large pocket area bound on top and bottom and a somewhat smaller area bound to that on three sides (the top is open). I have yet to find a use for that last pouch, as it is too long and narrow for much. The rest are very useful.

It’s well-made, sturdy, and easy to clean. I love it.

title: Love them
text:
I love these so much. They are recommended in art class after art class, and having been using them for a long time, I can see why. They’re the perfect blend of affordability, convenience, and quality.

These are long lasting I can use them every day for months and not run out of ink. The tip doesn’t wear down. They’re work horses and you can get a lot of use out of them.

They are reliable. They don’t skip, they stable explode, they don’t glop. They just produce a nice, stable line (well, except the brush pen, which makes a variable line depending on the pressure). You can use these with confidence.

They don’t smear, even when wet. You can do a watercolor wash over them when dry and they handle that perfectly.

I’ve used this and higher end technical pens that you fill by cartridge or converter, and I have to be honest, for the increased convenience, lack of skipping, and convenient line, I keep coming back to these.

These produce a dark black line that is archival safe and lightfast. They’re great for lettering, setting up a spread in a bullet journal, art (these are a must for Inktober), and writing.

title: Much better than filling directly with the converter
text:
Advantages

The traditional way of filling fountain pen converters comes with a handful of issues.

1. Filling a converter in the traditional fashion makes it hard to get them to fill all the way, be they bladder, or piston. You end up with a lot of air in them. Filling a converter with this means you’ll get a full converter every time. Just go a little slow at first so you don’t overfill. I like this brand in particular because it’s a little “sticky” and if you go with it, it fills more slowly with less risk of a problem.

2. Filling a converter in the traditional fashion can muddy your ink. It’s hard to get it perfectly cleaned, and when you’re trying to pull in the ink, especially with a bladder fill system, it means squirting ink back into the bottle. These are easy to clean perfectly, meaning your ink stays pristine. I like the length this particular one offers, for both the needle tip and the body.

3. Filling a converter in the traditional fashion means dealing with the converter after it’s been in the bottle and while you’re putting it back in the pen. This can lead to inky hands. With this, you aren’t touching the needle tip that goes into the ink at any point, so you won’t get ink on your hands. The needle goes into the ink and then into the converter, and if you don’t overfill, it never touches the outside of the converter so no mess. The longer needle tip here is a big help. You don’t want one of the brands with a short tip if this is an issue.

4. There is no good way I’ve ever found to use the traditional converter method to fill a brush pen, such as the ones from Kuretake. This works perfectly. It’s the only thing I’d even consider.

Safety

This one is especially safe. The needle tip is not sharp. It can’t cut or scratch you. It will bend if you push it to hard, but it won’t break skin.

Ease of cleaning

These are so much easier to clean than a converter. Just pull the plunger all the way out (I so love how this brand allows that) run it under water, run water through the body and you’re done.

Issues

I have once or twice had some issues reassembling them after cleaning them. I won’t ding it a star for that, since I can get them together again. It’s just that these are particularly fiddly.

title: Well made, beautiful book
text:
This is a very comfortable to write in journal. The back offers excellent support if you want to write with the book on your lap instead of on a table.

The pages are well bound. The paper, a little off white, is of a good quality, with no issues of bleeding or feathering. I've used black ink in a broad nib fountain pen and not seen the least bit of ghosting. The lines are somewhere between college ruled and wide spacing. Closer to college ruled, but just a smidge more space between them. The lines are fairly light and unintrusive.

The ribbon is a nice satin ribbon, cut at a diagonal at the bottom, and it hasn't frayed on me yet, even after a cat managed to take a swipe at it. It's well-secured and extends only about an inch past the bottom of the book.

I like this one. I might get another.

title: Great value; great quality
text: These are my go to. I use them all the time for scrapbooking, and when that means a few hundred photos going in all at once, the excellent value of this pack comes into heavy consideration. Despite the low cost per sheet, the quality is excellent. I don't want problems when I'm scrapping. I introduce enough on my own, thanks. These don't give me any issues. The prints always come out clean. They aren't prone to jamming or smearing or generally do anything some other papers like to do to give me a hard time. These are awesome.

title: Comfortable, stays clean, mediocre sharpener
text:
It has a very comfortable grip and sits easily in the hand.

It’s easy to load and feed the lead, and it didn’t seem stiff at all.

The graphite doesn’t stain it easily. After a long drawing session my hands were filthy. The holder was perfectly clean.

It comes with one lead entirely in the barrel to keep it from breaking. Unusual not to have it stick out a bit, but smart.

The sharpener was mediocre. I couldn’t get a good point with it. I tried the opposite end of the lead they sent and couldn’t get it close to as good as the side that came sharpened. I did get a lot of good graphite dust for a reductive drawing and it was even and the sharpener doesn’t leak.

title: They last a good while
text:
I like these because they don’t dry out quickly. They can last several months of light use, no problem, where other brands I’ve tried dry out just sitting there.

They are pretty easy to clean. I use a white board spray and a paper towel at the end of a project to get everything cleaned off, and even writing that has been sitting untouched for months comes right off. The eraser will leave a little ghosting, but that’s normal.

The colors are pretty good, none of them too light to be read easily. There is one that is particularly pale, but it’s not too bad.

They are supposed to be low odor, but I don’t smell a thing with these. I don’t go sniffing markers, but I don’t notice a small when I’m using them.

They make a nice, thin line. This might be too think if you’re using a whiteboard for a conference room or a classroom, but for personal use, such as Kamban or family notes or something like that, where everyone who needs to see it can walk up to it, it’s fine.

title: Restickable
text: These are good if you need to reposition them a lot. They can peel and restick and they hold for about twenty or so repetitons of this, which is above average to my experience. They're really good.

title: Great for wrapping gifts for the holidays
text: These are so convenient, especially around the holiday times when there is so much wrapping to be done. It comes with a lot of tape. It is, of course, refillable. It's small, out of the way, works well, and makes the job faster and easier so you can get back to celebrating. I like them a lot.

title: Perfect for podcasters or touch typists
text: I'm an old school touch typist, and this lets me keep the document to the side angled exactly as I was taught while typing. If you're from that era and want something like what we used in school, this is it. If you want something comfortable to hold your script or notes while podcasting, this is also great for that.

title: eye catching
text: These are good when you for want a flag to stand out above the rest. It can be taken off and reused many times. It's really bright and really eye catching. I use these sparingly for the most important points.

title: Good quality; easy to blend colors.
text:
There is one holder for each color, which is nice. Everything came in perfect condition. The holders are great. None of the leads were broken No defects or issues that I could find.

I like how nicely these spread across the page. At I guess I would liken them to the hardenss of a 2B, just to give a sense of how soft and smooth they are, and I am able to blend them easily enough, either to mix colors or to fade one out. I do the trick of drawing lightly, going in multiple directions in turn to cover an area, then doing the same with the color I want to blend in. Then back with two passes of the first color. Using that technique, these are fine. I tried the trick of doing one heavier pass of each and I wasn’t as satisfied, and while it could have been my experience, or lack thereof, causing this, it felt more like the binding in the pigment wasn’t suited to that. They need at least a little tooth in the paper for this. Crush it down and they stop blending.

Fading or blending with a cotton swab works well for these as well.

title: Erases cleanly and gently
text:
This is a very gentle eraser. You can use it on watercolor paper without distorting the surface, which for me is important since I erase a lot. I've also used them for subtractive drawing with charcoal, and they're good for that. They pick up well. I can sometimes clean them by rubbing them against a bit of sandpaper, but a few times I did need to resort to shaving them with a craft knife. To be fair, that was after heavy use with charcoal, so I can hardly hold that against it.

If you need to use a knife to shape them to get into a small place, they handle that just fine as well.

I would consider them best of breed and as soon as I have only one left in the box, I reorder. These are supplies I always want to have at hand.

title: None of them came broken
text:
None of these came broken, which was unexpected and delightful and uncommon. I've gotten other brands and usually at least one is snapped in half if not more.

I use these for loose, impressionistic drawing or shading large areas, and they are great for that. They lay a nice, thick line, very smooth, easy to blend. I'm able to get a nice fuzzy line extending the point pretty far past the end of the holder and then turning the whole on it's side and going softly. Good for random shading in the grass, or bits of clouds. Or secure it properly and use the point for a somewhat crisper line. I can sand the tip with no problem, both to get dust to rub into the page as a foundation for a reductive drawing and to sharpen back the point to its original state.

I may try their 4B next. I went with the 2B because, as I said, I'm used to them coming broken and 2B is a good compromise between a dark line and a sturdy lead, but given how well these showed up, I might risk going for something softer.

These exceeded my expectations. Five stars.

Update: While I still love the 2B, the 4B came mostly broken. About half were in one piece. I would advise sticking with the 2B.

title: When you need a quick and elegent monthly spread, these are nice
text:
These can tollarate being pulled off the page and repositioned VERY gently, once. It can take any kind of ink on top, felt tip pens, fountain pens, gel pens, anything I've tried works. They do not peeel off on their own. They are seriously adhesive and I love it.

They're beautiful and understated. They are undated, so work any year. They are nicely laid out for ease of use, with ample room for the crazy times in our lives, which is when these are the most useful.

I know the bujo crowd loves the artistry of making pages and spreads, but there are times we're all just too busy and want a pre-build monthly. For that, this is a good choice, and remember, there is no rule saying you need to use all of them in the same year. Some folk just want a functional but beautiful bujo and don't want the hassel of designing it and doing all that work. For those journallers, this is great.

title: Extremely useful and reliable
text:
This has an ample supply of a wide variety of sizes.

I found the dark blue a little too dark for my liking, given I write on these, but that's the only color I took issue with.

I use them for kanban in a bujo, and they can handle that much peeling and re-sticking back and foth throughout the day. I use the flags for key highlights in a book until I can take notes, then I gather them up as I take notes and reuse them in the next book. They can go through a lot of that before they don't stick anymore.

The case they come in was a lot nicer than I'd expected. It looks professional and elegant and I plan to keep stocking up on these as long as they keep selling them. This rapidly turned into a must-have item when I'm working.

title: Good quality ink
text:
This has a good variety of colors and a good number of cartridges for the price.

I like Lamy ink. It flows well, dries fast, and is nicely pigmented.

I like these cartridges because they snap in tightly, but easily. They have a little well in the bottom that doesn't flow out easily. That stores the last bit of ink until you flick it out, so you won't run out unexpectedly. It's the saving grace for the Lamy pens not using standard cartrideges, and at least these work in all Lamy pens. Keep in mind they only work in Lamy pens.

I used to keep a set of these at my desk at work, in the days when I went into the office, and found them extremely convenient.

title: Beautiful ink
text:
This is one of my favorite colors. This was the special edition for 2020, but I keep seeing it, so maybe the added it to their lineup. I hope so, because it is a beautiful ink.

The thing I like about these cartridges is the little bottom well. If you see that shape of the cartridge, there is a small, thinner section on the bottom. That doesnt let the ink flow easily. Instead it holds a small amount of emergency backup ink so when the main body runs dry you can flick your finger against that backup to drop it. It's very clever.

title: Reliable, but some of the pigments are too light to be useful
text:
These produce an even, thin line that is perfect for writing, particularly editing or annotating documents where I need to get a lot of text into a small space.

They are reliable. I've never had any of them leak or give me any trouble. They don't skip or smudge. The ink lasts a long time.

The only thing I don't like is that some of these, such as they yellow, are way too pale to use. I've tried them on dark paper, but they are no better. I wonder if someone using a lot of hatching could incorporate them into a drawing, but for me, those are useless.

title: They don't smudge easily, for better or worse
text:
The thing to keep in mind is this is meant for line work, not blending. The colored leads don't blend that well or smudge easily. You might have an easier time cross hatching for shading. Blending then out will be a pain, even with a tool like a stomp or tort. If you want a blended effect, you're better off getting a regular colored pencil that needs a sharpener.

They don't smudge that easily, so if you want to use them for small detail, the line will stay crisp. You can run lines over each other without them blending or losing the precision of the mark. For that, these are much easier to use than a regular colored pencil.

So depending on what you're trying to do, these are brilliant or horrible. I want them for the detail work, so I'm giving them five stars.

title: Nice pen; doesn't take standard cartridges or converters
text:
This is a good pen if you can get it. The limited editions can be hard to find after a while. Sometimes they enter the permanant lineup, and I'm really hoping this one does. It's a beautiful color.

These are a go to pen for artists, especially urban sketchers, who like to work in ink, and it's easy to see why. They lay down a smooth, even line reliably. The nibs perform as well as a gold nib at a fraction of the price. If you want to learn to draw in pen, this isn't a bad choice to start with.

As a writing pen, they're fantastic. They're comfortable to hold for a long time. They give no issues. They're just a good, reliable pen.

The only thing that comes close to being an issue is that they don't come with a converter and they're not compatibile with standard converters or cartridges. That said, Lamy converters and cartridges are universal across the Lamy line and they're availabe pretty much everywhere -- I got a three pack of converters from Amazon pretty cheep.

These are great, fun pens. I can't wait to see what limited edition is offered next.

title: Ample supply
text:
There is an ample supply of these in a sturdy box. The colors aren’t dark at all. I never understood the point of notes you can’t write on. They adjust about as poorly as you’d hope — that is the point of the thing after all — but well enough to stay put in a book or file folder, or to stick to the side of a monitor.

I use them for Kanban in a Bullet Journal and they’re great for that.

title: Can’t handle delicate pencils
text: [[VIDEOID:918196702d8d00b24bfa9a10e7b4f79e]] It’s not as loud or high pitched as my other sharpener. It isn’t great with hard to sharpen pencils (think soft charcoal or chalk pencils). It has a smaller than expected bin for shavings and a five foot power cord.

title: Good for writing or drawing
text:
For any use:

The pages are secured such that you can lay the book perfectly flat without breaking the spine.

The bookmark is well secured and not prone to fraying.

The pocket is sturdy and provides ample space. I use is during the day but empty at night, one because I do the Getting Things Done in to empty thing and two because this lays flat so well I hate messing that up with extra bulk.

The elastic closure is pretty sturdy. My cat grabbed it in his claws with no real damage.

For sketchbook use:

I’ll start off with saying if you just use pencil or dry media, you’ve come to right place. This sketchbook is perfect for that. If you want something that can handle wet media, you might want to look elsewhere. The paper here will buckle pretty badly.

The pages can stand heavy reworking. Substantial ink application (think sumi painting) will bleed but normal ink drawing has no issues and no bleeding. Spray fixative causes no buckling.

For writing use:

Bleeding isn’t a problem, no matter what pen I used. It’s good with fountain pens, causing no noticeable feathering.

Overall I like this and plan to buy more of them.

title: Best bullet journal bar none
text:
This is possibly the best bulled journal available.

The good:

1- The pages are very thick. I have the 160gsm, which is heavy enough to handle a light application of watercolor without buckling. I've gessoed a page and done some light acrylic work on it. I have used thick black markers, such as the Higgens India Ink Brush Pen with no ghosting (let that pen dry a few moments or it will smear however). It won't hold up to an alcohol marker like a Copic without ghosting, nothing will, but shy of that you should be fine.

2- The pages are a perfect size. I picked up the big one because I have a lot going on at work and a homa and a lot to track. This lets me make my spreads big enough for my needs, yet not too bit to tote around. It's a good balance.

3- The pocket is sturdy. I keep loose bits of paper in there all day until I can process in to empty (I do Getting Things Done in a BuJo) and it can handle quite a lot.

4- No more dot counting. It comes with a ruler designed to count the dots for you. Just line up the proportion you want and you're good to go.

5- Numbered pages. This saves me the trouble of numbering them and helps make sure I don't skip a page by turning two at once.

6- Pre-built index. A little added convenience is always nice.

7- Two pen test pages, also good for starting an acrylic pen.

8- Plain cover in a great color. I like covering mine with stickers. I do recognize some people prefer the fancier covers, which sadly are not available on the pro.

9- The pen loop is very secure.

10- The two ribbon markers are secure and do not fray.

11- The elastic closure is deep enough into the cover it doesn't slip loose.

12- It can lay flat for a two-page spread or to keep open on your desk while you're woking.

The bad:

1-There are only 148 pages. This is a necessity caused by the thickness of the pages, but it's still a negative.

2- Most of the bujo-stickers on the market aren't designed for this size. Not a failure of the product, but something you need to be aware of if you want to use those in your BuJo.

Overall, I'm glad I took the plunge and tried this. I'm going to be staying with these for a long time.

title: Tricky to start, nice brush pen
text: [[VIDEOID:4042604b1d7bcf6a9312f8b8705ebd55]] Nice refills. They work thick to thin, fit in any Cocoiro barrel and last a good long time.

title: Good for Kuretake brush pens
text:
I use these in the Kuretake brush pens. I find using a pen-filling syringe (not included, but Amazon carries many kinds of those) is much easier when trying to fill a brush pen. I also find it's best to let the brush pen sit for about 5 minutes after you fill with a converter, to let the ink seep into the brush. It will give you a better performance that way.

I have not tried it with a normal fountain pen, so I can't talk to that. Just brush pens.

title: Best for watercolor paper
text: These are extremely gentle. While they do erase well, they do so without damaging the paper. This is ideal for watercolor paper when you want to lay down a light drawing then paint over. Any damage or rough texture in the paper will impact how it takes up the paint and how the final painting looks. These can let you rework an area quite a bit without any problems.

title: Stays exactly where you put it
text: These are the same as the Levenger's ones except for two points, they don't have the name embossed on them and they're a lot cheaper. They hold the page well, and I have used them to track a specific line such that I can put this one the page, put the book in my backpack, walk around with it in there for days, pull it out and it's still pointing to the same line. They're thin so you can have many in a book at once if you need, and there certainly are enough of them for that.

title: Fun
text: They don’t blend well, but they’re good for line work or details. They work in a standard 0.7 mm refillable pencil. They don’t break any more easily than a normal hb lead. The pigmentation isn’t bad. They’re just fun.

title: High quality
text: It’s great. It comes with a lot of lead. I haven’t figured out a refill eraser yet, but I suspect I will. The pencils load well, descend the leads cleanly, and feel comfortable to use.

title: Wonderful starter pen
text: Waterman is the gold standard for fountain pens. This is a good introductory pen. It takes standard cartridges and a converter for bottled ink. Converter is not included. It has a good nib. It has a good weight. You can snap the cap in the back and it is a snap on cap. It performs brilliantly, exactly as one would expect for Waterman.

title: Large and expensive
text: I expected more than one. These are a little larger than I was hoping. I use them for holding a sketchbook open. I was expecting more than one at that price. That was me not reading carefully enough. For what it claims to be it’s fine. Just not what I expected.

title: Beautiful, precise line
text: These are great for writing or line drawing. They lay a clean line, very smooth, very thin. This set hosts a variety of similar colors, which is nice if you want to do something in a unified pallet but still primarily linear (changing the color for hatching for example). These are popular for bullet journaling and urban sketching and I love using them for both.

title: Good writing notebook, horrible sketchbook
text:
I like this as a writing notebook. I would normally go for a lined writing notebook, but that would ruin the experience with this one. The pages don't bleed and the ink, even from a bold-tip fountain pen with a long drying time ink doesn't feather.

I don't like this as a sketchbook. It doesn't tollerate even the gentlest of erasers and any kind of reworking ruins the page.

title: Good quality for scrapbooking
text: I normally use the Canon paper, but decided to give these a try for scrapbooking, and I like them. They don't jam. They print on well. They are stiff enough to cut down to size in a guillotine-style trimmer. I've had some in scrapbooks for almost a year now, no yellowing, no curling, no problems. They're perfect if you want to scrap with them, and honsetly, I can't think of a use where they would get harder wear. They're a bit too big to runa round in a wallet after all. I'll buy more once I run out.

title: The nibs are mediocre, the rest is great
text:
The nibs are a little splitty. The tines open too easily, which causes splatter. I'm dinging it a star for that. The pen itself is great, and honestly, I just swapped in a different set of nibs. The wax seal is nice, especially since there are three wax sticks and they are each fairly large, and the spoon is a nice touch. I ususally just let the wax drip onto the paper, but using the spoon makes the flow more even. The ink is better than expected, given this looks kind of kitchy. It's actually a really good quality. Ultimately, you will want a seal of your own design if you get too far into this, but as a starter kit, this is perfect.

Great for D&D fans, casual scadians, and stationary fans.

title: Sturdy, stays open well
text: I've been using this in my attempts to learn to play piano. The bad -- I still stink at piano. The good-- this holds the music nicely, stays open in the stand, makes it easy to grip and turn pages and keeps everything neat and tidy. I can put two sheets in back to back at need.

title: Perfect for lettering
text: I mostly use this in my BuJo. It's a delicate difference between the thick and thin lines, but the pressure does change the line width and it is sufficient to be visually interesting. I like how smooth these pens are, how easy it is to lay down a clean line, how they don't skip, and how nice the ink looks. They are among my favorites and I pick them up all the time.

title: Convenient
text: It's good for your bujo sidekick or a small notebook to carry around. It's just large enough for the smallest Moleskeins. I tend to keep it in my purse for when I need paper and pen handy, and I pull it out more than I thought I would. It's very convenient.

title: Very sweet
text: I used it as a journal. The pages don't feather. They don't bleed too much. I mean, I used a Copic on the cover page, knowing full well there isn't a paper made that won't bleed that, and I put a divider to protect the next page, and yes, that bled, but for normal markers and brush pensg, I've had no issue, and no issue, certainly not with a regular fountain pen. It's good quality. The binding is sturdy. It's a comfortable size, lays open well, and has a nice closure.

title: Good for scrapbookers
text: I use this for scrapbooking. If you follow Club Scrap, these are similar to the ones she uses. She cuts them in half, and I have tried with these and they're fine that way, so you can get twice as much use out of them. I haven't had any issues of anything falling off, yellowing, or being any trouble at all. I have found that if I leave them somewhere they can be pushed around some, like in a scraps box, they will occassionally peal off on their own. My only concern.

title: Good for journalling, not for urban sketching
text: It works well enough for journalling, but I was hoping to use it for urban sketching. To be fair, it was not advertised for that purpose. It doesn't handle heavy erasing, and it feathers a bit more than I like for drawing, when I use a bold tip pen, but is fine for writing with a medium tip or smaller. I'll say it does what it says it does perfectly. The pages are roomy, feel nice, and don't bleed. It's a great journal.

title: Excellent quality
text: This is nice for a softer sub-header in a BuJo. It doesn't make a very thick line, but it does do thick and thin. It's a medium grey. It handles brilliantly well, no skipping, no smearing, no issues. If you haven't tried one of these before, they're simply a must. They're perfect.

title: Pleantiful
text: I'm not running out of these any time soon. This thing is huge and it's loaded. I use the flags all the time and I feel confident I'm going to have ample. I might buy another when we return to office to keep one at my desk, but that's for convenience, not for refill. Quality case. Quality paper. There's nothing here not to like.

title: Roomy, just mind the layout of the ring binder
text:
What you need to know is that the center ring binder is for page protectors and you have to be a bit fussy which ones you get. I'm dinging one star for that, because the goal of all of the rest of this seems to be to fit anything and everythng and going with a simple 3-ring design would have played better into that.

This padfolio is roomy as all get-up. You have room for a second pad in the sleeve. I think the design goal here was make something that can fit any semi-reasonable amount and size of stuff. They did not skimp on space.

Personally, I don't like the the way the handles sort of lock into grooves on the front and back cover. I don't think handles were needed in the first place. That I won't ding a star for. It's clearly a design choice. It could be thought to feed into the "does evrerything this kind of thing can possible do" mindset, and there might be a use case for that even if I haven't encountered it yet.

I intend to use the heck out of this, then buy another. I love it.

title: Not that good
text: It's not terrible. It feels a little scratchy in shorts or a skirt, and it doesn't so much recline as let the cushion slide forward for easier slouching, but that's the worst I can say of it. The back rest is ok. I wouldn't say it's the best at this price point, but it isn't quite the worst either. It looks and feels cheap given the price point. I would peg this as discount store funature, selling no higher than $60.

title: An Inktober or BuJo neccesity
text:
This has a great selection of Pentel products. You get a set of the Sign pens in multiple colors, which are popular for lettering. If you are going to BuJu, and you are new to lettering, and if you are going to do Inktober, and you are new to inking thin and thick lines, these are by far the easiest to learn on. It comes with the brush sign, but I would stick that particular one in the intermediate category.

Then you have the dual tip, which is a little trickier to use, and more suited to an intermediate letterer or inker. It's harder to use than the sign, but gives you more control, and you can do more with it.

You get their refillable brush pen, which is widely regarded as the best. The one and only thing I don't like about this is I've not found a good converter for it, so am stuck with cartridge refills. Everything else about this is perfect. And you get the huge brush pen with the ink filling the entire barrel. Both are better for more advanced inkers and letterers, so this set will grow with you and be good for a really long time.

You also get a full set of fineliner, a high end mechanical pencil and a soft white eraser. There is a lot, so you will want a pencil case to store it all in. The box is meh. Really, I'm having such a hard time trying to find things I don't like, I'll complain about the box it came in.

I love this kit.

title: A little thick but the magnet is strong
text: They're cute and tiny. They"re a little thick if you're worried about denying the book, but the magnet is too strong for it them to fall out easily, so they do their job well.  There are 10 in the pack, so it should be enough for most users. I can see using two or three in my bullet journal. They're well suited to that.

title: Good if you have skills in beading
text:
First, it's beautiful. I love it.

Second, the jump ring that connects the dangle to the body is fragile and came damaged. I needed to replace it. If you know how to do that, as any beader should, and if you have the basic tools and a spare jump ring, you'll love this. I'm plannig to look for more.

If you want a book mark that isn't "some assembly required" then look elsewhere.

title: Way too small to stay in a book
text:
These are far too small to be useful. They don't stay in a book in say a purse or a backpack, which defeats their only functional purpose. If you always keep the book on a nightstand or something and never take it with you, then I guess it's okay, but that's not the most common use pattern for books.

They're okay looking. I wouldn't rave about them.

Overall, I'm underimpressed.

title: Beautiful, but too thick
text:
It's a good 1/8th of an inch thick, which is fine for a book on a night stand I guess, and would have been great in the stay home and read pandemic era, but for those who want to stick a book in a bag and go, read in a waiting room, read on a bus or train, read in the park, it's a bit thick. For mass market paperbacks, it dents the pages and the cover if the book is in a book strap or under pressure, like if something ends up on top of the book in a bag. I prerer my bookmarks to be about as thick as a ribbon or a piece of cardstock. This is overmuch.

That said, for a hardcover, for a book you don't mind damaging a little, or for a stay at home book, this is quite beautiful. I found one ding on the bottom corner that looks more like a manufacture error than damage in storage or transit, but that's not a showstopper.

title: Beautiful and well made
text:
The amount of love I have for this is all out of proportion to it being a pencil case. It holds a nice supply of pencils (or pencils and mostly Rotring pens in my case). There is a small pouch closed by Velcro to hold erasers or a sharpener or stuff like that. When it unfolds to stand it is held together by a magnet (I checked -- it attacts my scissors) which makes it stable and secure. I have it standing on my desk when I use it and no issues at all.

By way of sizing this, the largest pen you can put in the highest part is the Lamy Joy. It comfortably holds around 20 Pigma Microns or the equivilent.

The anime element is subtle, but definitely reognizable. My roommate saw it and said, "That's... Demon Slayer, right?" And images of Tanjiro and assorted iconography fills the lining.

For style, I love it. For functionality, I love this. For workmanship, for materials, for sheer quality, I love this.

title: Nice, not perfect but nice
text:
I like most of this. The binding is good. The workmanship is excellent, and I've come to expect excellence from this brand. The paper quality is good. I've had a few of these that can't handle heavy erasing, but this one can, which is awesome. It even has a nice internal pencil loop.

There are a few issues. The front cover was bent in when the book was packaged, and now it curls, I think permanently. Some of the pages, by design, are misshapen. When all the pages in a book do that, it has an antique, magical look. When one signature in five does that, it just looks wrong. It makes using that section in the same way as the other sections a little awkward.

As to what it can be used for, it's not a great journal or writing notebook unless you want to use white pencil or pen on the black pages. That's less commonly done with text than with art. It would make a great sketchbook if you want to work around the black pages. The largest one would be a spectacular scrapbook. I could definitely see using one that way (I can also see picking up more of these). My plan is to use it as an art journal. I see a lot of promise there, maybe gesso some pages for acrylic paint. Maybe collage some. The pages seem sturdy enough to hold up.

title: They're good at what they do
text: I use these as a clip for my art journal and they keep the pages open without denting them, which is all one can ask from a paper clamp. The colors are pretty. They do what they should well. I like them.

title: Decent pen, weird gimmick
text:
These are a weird gimmick. They are pens that protect themselves from bacteria. They don't protect the user in any way, just the pen itself. I know we're in this strange new world, but I did not get the memo about a mass infestation of pen-eating bacteria.

As to the normal things pens do, like write, these are about average for a disposable ball point. Nothing to complain about. Nothing to write home about. They're good.

title: Lovely, well-balanced, fun
text: I swapped out the nib for a G style for calligraphy per my teacher's instructions and a medium writing nib for writing (two different brands) so I can't speak to the nibs, but the pen itself is wonderful. It takes standard nibs without any problem, so it's not going to be an issue if you want to swap out. It's a beautiful pen. It feels great in my hand, it balaces well, and it's a lovely accent when not in use. I'm having a lot of fun with this.

title: Even good for larger pens
text: I use these for Pilot Parallels, fairly long calligraphy pens, and they work very well. I can store pens, ink, even a few small practice pads in them, no problem. They are large, sturdy, and quite convenient. They're a good value, and I will be buying more.

title: Excellent, fun to learn, fun to play
text:
These are adorable, and they have a good sound given they are supposed to just be toys. If you search online for 6 hole ocarina tutorials, there is one that starts with just C and D and builds from there. I can't link to it, but the url is 6 hole ocarina dot com, no spaces. It's a great way to learn this little instrument. And these are great 6-hole ocarina's to learn on. The craftsmanship is excellent.

They come with cords, and the hardest to string (thus the first to try, so to find the easiest to fit in there cord) is the eggplant. It should have been a potato, since another name for an ocarina is a potato flute, but the eggplant is definitely cuter. The bird is just sweet-looking. So clever. I love it.

They are ceramic, so quite fragile. That's not a negative, just something to know if you want to give these to small children.

I'm having way too much fun with these.

title: Glides over the page
text:
The pen absolutely glides over the page. It's amazing. I used the nib in it first, and that acts like a common writing nib. The others go broader for calligraphy, and I like them, but I like the initial nib best. I've had better for calligraphy, but none smoother for normal writing.

It stores about as much ink as I'm used to in a quill. Okay, nerd confession here, I used nothing but a bottle of ink and a dip pen for all my undergraduate classes. I know. Weird. But after hundreds of hours of writing with quills and dip dips, I've become quite fussy about them. This one is remarkably smooth. Here I'll also point out, I prefer a scratchy dip pen. It feels more authentic to me, and for kanji, a scratchy pen forces you to make your strokes in the correct direction. This does not. Some folk like super smooth, and this one is about as smooth as I've ever seen. The balance is perfect for this pen. Yes, I know, natural materials will vary pen to pen, but the one I have is exceptional in how balanced it is.

The stand is plain, just a glass-like square with a pen holder sticking up. Absolutely nothing to write home about.

At the time of this writing the description said the ink bottle was empty, but it has black ink. Again, nothing to write home about. I wouldn't put it up against say a Noodler's ink, or a Platinum carbon black, but it's fine. It does its inky job.

The notebook takes A6, six hole refill paper. This was not mentioned in the description, and I think it's important information. You need to know the size of your notebook after all. It has a wrap tie, is very soft (like you could roll it into a tube, though I don't know why you'd want to) . It has a leaf pattern embossed on it and closes with a leaf closure on a strap. Pull it a bit or it will clasp in the back. I don't know if it's leather, but it smells like it is.

It's earned a place on my desk. Other nerdy confession. Working from home for months, I've gone back to dip pens. I refuse to grow up.

title: High quality and pleantiful
text: These are nice and study. Good craftsmanship. No sharp points to tear or groove paper. I've been using them for a while now and have had no trouble at all. There are a lot of them, so this set should see most people for a good long time.

title: Very sturdy; beautiful
text:
Usually these oddly shaped metal ones fall out, but this one has done a great job staying in place in the book, which, after all, is the only actual value a bookmark provides. The rest is meaningless without that. The rest being how absolutely beautiful this one is. How sturdy. How well made. I would have expected the ball to be at risk of coming off, but it's quite secure. My cat tested it. My cat is in charge of durability testing around here, and she takes her job very seriously. I can assure you this has survived no fewer than forty bats and three chases across the floor and is still in perfect condition.

I am very much in love with the digital book for portability, but under the current circumstances, pulling an old print book off the shelves has been a comfort, and a charming bookmark like this pairs well with a nice cup of tea and a favorite old read.

title: Magical
text: It's an incredible notebook, with an almost magical feel. I'll be buying another once the world is back to normal and I can go back to playing a mage in my D&D group. This will be perfect for notetaking there. The evil in me wants to bring one into the office for meetings.

title: The most reliable pen I've ever owned
text:
These are the gold standard for disposable technical pens. They perform comparably to the Rapidograph, but for the fact they cannot be refilled. If you get into bullet journaling, you'll see tons of recommendations for these. Inktober, or ink drawing in general? These are recommended all the time. Art journaling? I see these on the supply list of half the classes I've taken. Urban Sketching? Granted, that crowd loves the Lamy Safari/Al Star, but these show up a respectable amount of time as well. You'll get that for a lot of Sakura's products because they make really good stuff, but especially the Microns.

If you're getting into any of these creative pursuits, you will want these. And there's a reason everyone keeps recommending them in book after book, video after video, and class after class. It's because they work so well. They produce a strong, even, reliable line. And here I'll compare them favorably to most refillable technical pens. I've had the Rotrings skip. I've had them blop on occasion. I have never had that problem from a Micron. If I needed a pen to be reliable, I'd set my expensive technical pen aside and grab a Micron.

If you want a workhorse writing pen, one that writes on all kinds of papers (I'm right now using a parchment journal that is a little funny with fountain pens) this will work. Works on rough or smooth paper. I've gone through dozens of these and never had a problem.

title: Excellent notebook
text:
I can't wait for the refills to go live on this. Such a clever idea.

The paper is excellent. I'm using the one I have as a journal and I'm thinking of getting another to use as a sketch book. It handles fountain pen ink very well. It can handle erasing, but you need to be very gentle. Heavy scrubbing is not good for this paper. I wouldn't go so far as to use it for urban sketching. I don't think it would support watercolors very well. That's not to say I tried it and it didn't, only I don't think it will. If you've had good experiences with that, please let me know.

It's beautiful. It's got a rustic charm. It's just a great, fun notebook.

ETA: After writing this review I broke down and tried painting in the notebook. And then I bought three more. It's perfect.

title: Light ghosting with very dark ink; removable cover
text:
The liquid glitter part is a book jacket, so you can slip it off and slip it on other notebooks if you want to.

The notebook itself is of a decent quality. I'd call it closer to wide ruled than college ruled, but that works for me. The paper can handle fountain pens well with no feathering. I'm using a medium nib Lamy with Carbon Black ink and almost no ghosting. That's a pretty dark ink, so some ghosting is common. This is less than usual. If you're using this as a BuJo and any amount of show through is a problem, this won't work for you. If you want a diary or notebook, this should be just fine.

title: Unusual in its purpose, but an interesting idea
text: It's not really a journal or a sketchbook. It's too full of bits of show imagery and such to be useful as such, but too full of "fill in the blank" exercises or semi-blank pages to be a show art book. It's kind of a hybrid that invites the reader to be a participant in the creation of a unique and personalized piece of memorabilia/journaling. If that's what you're looking for, then this is perfect. If you want more of a general purpose notebook of some kind with a bit of Supernatural thrown in, this isn't that.

title: Cute, so far everything is perfect. Cat resistant.
text:
It seemed on the small side, but it stays in the book well, at least now when the not in use book is sitting on the desk. Once it's in the bag and on the go, I'm not so sure. If there are problems, I'll come revise this. So far, I think it will be fine.

The charm is well made and quite secure. My cat had a go at it and no damage.

I love it. I think it's adorable.

title: A must have for writing in hot environments. High school me would have hoarded these.
text:
I don't know how pens can be sheer, and I don't think a pen with a fan is supposed to be cold, so I can't rank it highly in those areas. For what it should do, it's great. It writes well, and there are ample spare cartridges. It takes a moment to get the pen started, but that's pretty common. Twist the bottom section to retract. Twist the top section to get access to the battery compartment.

The fan part is cute. It reminds me of those handheld fans we had as kids. It comes with two batteries, but the pen takes one (AAA). It also comes with a spare blade. I can't imagine wearing it out, but so it is. It might help if the blade breaks or something. It works as well as those little fans did back when, and I for one depended on them in high school. If you're writing with the pen while the fan is going the breeze will come and go.

Overall, I think this pushes just past the barrier of gimmick into the domain of clever and useful.

I'm thinking of using these as stocking stuffers. They're very nice.

title: Beautiful and good to write in if you're not too precious with it
text:
It's a perfectly good notebook for people with the right mindset. I know way too many people who are precious about their notebooks. My boyfriend keeps buying practice sketchbooks to work in before he uses his real sketchbooks, only they instantly turn into real sketchbooks, so he needs practice sketchbooks and... Yeah, this notebook is horrible for anyone with that mindset.

I think it's perfectly lovely as a journal. It holds the ink well. It doesn't feather. It doesn't give me trouble. I haven't tried any heavy application of anything, not even ink sketching, in it, so I can't say how well it would hold up to that kind of treatment, but for me, it's not that kind of notebook. Maybe I'm being a little too precious about it.

I like this. I will buy another. I will give these as gifts (just not to my boyfriend). They're absolutely lovely.

title: Good for fountain pens, dip pens, brush pens, honestly anything
text:
I'm going through an odd pen phase during this whole social distance, stay at home thing. I've been playing with thick pens, dip pens, brush pens, all the pens. Yeah, I'm kind of bored.

This notebook puts up with all of my nonsense. I can do dip pen or cartridge calligraphy in it with no feathering. I have a lot of trouble with that on some paper because I use a very broad pen and I have almost no skill. If you tend to lay down a lot of ink and don't want feathering, this is a great notebook.

Gel pens it likes. Ballpoints it likes. It really doesn't work badly with anything. I took out an old fletched feather, a glass dip pen... It works. My old notebook, and granted that was a dime store notebook, kept catching on the feather and making micro splatters. That is a sort of common problem with some feathers. This one is perfectly smooth.

To be honest, if the world were normal I would be taking this when I got together with my stationary loving friends and showing off how awesome this notebook is. I'm buying more of these.

I've done extremely light washes and ink drawings in it, and yes, I know, it's not technically meant for watercolor and this is absolutely the wrong notebook to use for that, but that's a common thing among the BuJo and Sketchnoting communities, and I find it holds up as well as some of my more expensive notebooks. It's not perfect, but it's reasonable.

title: Good for BuJo, crafts, art projects
text:
These aren't so great for a main writing pen. Some are dark enough, but not all. They are great for putting decorative accents in a BuJo or an arts and crafts project. I use them to add shadow highlights to lettering and borders. They make a smooth line for fauxligraphy, which is fun.

They offer consistent ink, no skips, no issues. They are a quality ink, little feathering, little bleeding depending on the paper. They offer excellent control.

title: Small, but excellent
text: It's small. No getting around it. It's smaller than an A5 notebook, and that might be an issue for some. That said, it's perfect for those situations where you want a smaller notebook. It's sturdy. It always ends up on the bottom of my bag with heavy stuff on top of it, but it has held up perfectly. I use it every day, and at this point, I'd be lost without it. Great notebook. My only issue is I use it so much, I keep running out of paper.

title: High quality
text:
It's packaged quite well for a fancy presentation. Clearly, this is meant to be a gift for the writer or artist, and they will love it. The strap was a bit hard to figure out -- and I've used this type of closure before -- but after a few minutes it made sense. That's the worst I can say of it.

It handles everything I've thrown at it from the pen perspective, up to a black Tombow, with no ghosting. I did a light watercolor wash and while yes, it buckled (it's supposed to buckle) it held up as well as I would hope. This is a kind of paper stress test, I know, but it passed with flying colors.

I can't say it lies flat when open, but well enough I can do a two page spread no problem. It feels nice. It's well made. It's really everything one could ask it to be. I'm happy with this notebook and plan to buy more like it.

title: Not great workmanship aside from the leather.
text:
I can see its charm. It looks old world, hand made. I'm okay with it, but I don't love it.

First, the front page came stained with what looks like whatever they used to color the cover. I have half a fingerprint on it.

Second, the book came bent. It not only doesn't lay flat open; it doesn't lay flat closed.

Third, the cover has what looks like scratches or grooves it in. I don't mean the lettering and the footprints. I mean the odd mark here and there that does not seem intentional. The footprints are really cool.

Fourth, the sewing seems wrong. When you open the book to a spot between the seconds, then the entire thing lays very flat and you can see a substantial amount of the inside of the spine between the sections. I can see people might like that. I just am not a fan of it. That said, if you mean to gesso these pages, tape things to them, do collage, or do anything where the spine needs more room, then this book is right for you.

Fifth, the paper isn't of quality. I'm getting ghosting with a Micron. Microns don't ghost. It doesn't stand up to much of anything -- heavy erasing, dark ink, I wouldn't try something like goache without a gesso (and yes, I do normally paint in my notebooks, and yes, I know it warps them, but I also know what to expect after all these years of doing that). I'm not dinging it for not being something it never intended to be, but I do expect to be able to erase and to write with a blank ink pen in this.

The cover design and the work in the leather (minus the scratches) is incredible. I absolutely love the subtle design. That's the best part of this. And the latch is really awesome and works as you'd expect.

title: Same quality as Canon's own brand
text: I had no issue with these. They work exactly the same at the official ones from Canon. They install no problem. They print no problem. They last roughly the same amount of time. On the level of quality, they are identical. It comes down to price which to choose. I used them for documents, for stickers, and for iron ons for T-shirts, and in every application they were perfect. I have nothing to complain about. They're great.

title: A solid, basic ink
text:
I filled a Waterman with this and had no problem. The ink is about as you would expect, no issues, no problems. It started well. I used it up without any concerns whatever.

Keep in mind, there are luxury inks out there. Noodlers has "bulletproof" ink that, while totally fountain pen safe is both waterproof and archival. Indeed there are many archival inks out there, scented inks, even inks that work in arctic conditions. If you're looking for the best ink, you'll look there (and may need a converter for your pen).

This is a workhorse ink, plain, simple, and gets the job done. It's good for your day to day needs. It's a good value, and I wish it was around when I was in college and going through about a cartridge a day. For that purpose, it's perfect

title: Quality pen, decent paper, nice office gift
text: The pen writes smoothly, black ink and I think a medium point. The pads are pretty much as pictured. The paper is of a reasonable quality. It doesn't feather much with a fountain pen. The bound notepad is quite small. The other two are normal enough for memo pads. This is a perfect secret Santa for the office.  It came perfectly packaged, so no dinging on the corners. I like it.

title: Gentle for an electric eraser
text:
This thing comes with a lot of refills. I've yet to run out of them, and that's surprising. It's gentler on the paper than most electric erasers I've encountered, but parse that fully. Electric erasers are not usually gentle. Indeed no erasers used by rubbing are going to leave the paper perfectly intact, so if keeping the paper's texture pristine matters, say for hot press watercolor paper, grab a kneeding or putty eraser, and press down then lift for the gentlest treatment.

That said, for what this is, for what it is meant to do, it does it quite well. I've used it perhaps excessively on the Blick sketch pad (cheap lightweight paper, 60 pounds, meant for sketching, not the kind of endless reworking I do with it) and it has not damaged the paper significantly. Another electric eraser has, and I've done some damage by hand with a white vinyl eraser. Here I should point out this is not a flaw with the paper per se. I'm a raw beginner and I erase excessively. But this eraser is kind enough I can get away with overuse with no problem. Artists who know what they're doing will find this meets their needs. Beginners like me will find it unusually forgiving.

title: Great value
text: It's good paper. I've used it with my Tombows, which can be really hit or miss with printer paper, and I've had no issues. Otherwise, it feeds well, it doesn't jam. It doesn't smear. It doesn't give me any trouble. It's just a whole lot of good paper at a great price. For most uses, this is a great value. Back in the day, I might have turned my thesis in printed on this with no concern at all.

title: Great fountain pen; not a calligraphy pen at all
text:
It comes with a converter, which surprised me, and with an ink cartridge, that looks like a standard short, the kind you'd put in a Mont Blanc and the kind Waterman sells as a short cartridge. I'm not sure if it will take a long, but I'm thinking it might given the length of the converter.

At first it was a little skipping and didn't write well, and then I dropped it, and now it's perfect. I think the nib wasn't saturated will enough. I don't advocate dropping the pen, but I do advocate giving it a little time to get settled in before judging it. It is a dream once you get it going.
