title: Updated: terrible fude nib, excellent communication and CS + M nib
text:
Update: changing review due to excellent customer service and very nice M nib.

I ordered the fude nib. It was very bad, as one can see below in my older review. I tried to return it, and the seller reached out to me to try to help me get the pen to work, but nothing worked. As a last resort before having to return the item back to China, the seller suggested that I try another nib - they sent me an extra feed and two Medium nibs. I slid one of the M nibs and voila, it works perfectly. The M nib for this pen is much smoother and higher quality than other M nibs I've tried. This pen has turned from junk to easily a perfect $200 replica pen. I'm excited to be able to travel with this vacuum system, and the CS has been very swift in their communication. As they sent me a refund before I could tell them that I received the M nibs, I alerted them that I would like to keep the pen after all, so they made separate accommodations for that as well. A++ customer service.

The build quality looks solid, and it's very heavy. It looks like a very expensive pen. The vacuum mechanism holds a lot of ink. It could be potentially a great pen, especially at this price point. Unfortunately, this pen has given me nothing but frustration and pain. The nib has a really hard time starting, and I've had to manually pry the tines apart quite a bit to get the ink to flow several times. It takes a while for the inkflow to start, and once it starts, the inkflow is very inconsistent, gushing here and dry there, dry for the most part. Trying over and over to get it to flow and then having it stop again, repeatedly, is the story of my life with this pen. It's extremely frustrating, not to mention tiring on my arm - the whole point of fountain pens for me was to lighten the burden of muscle fatigue, but this pen is proving to be more labor and work than other pens, and not pleasant at all to worry about when it will stop flowing again or what to do this time to make it flow.

title: Pretty journal, pen is a hit or miss
text: The journal is very pretty for the price I paid. I bought four of these - two pens worked, one works quite well; the two others did not work at all, so were sent back.

title: Great value at a discount
text: This is a tiny little journal with very fat pages. It looks fatter than it needs because the pages have been wetted, and then dried out, resulting in crinkliness. It might not be your cup of tea especially if you're writing with a fountain pen that needs to hit a sweet spot at all times - it will make you derail and use very little of the pages, since it's a small book. That said, at the discounted price I bought it at, 400-ish pages is a great value. The paper is thick enough to not bleed or ghost even with wet pen inks. The leather isn't high grade enough for me to want to rebind this book after use, but it's a perfectly giftable journal for antique lovers and those that want to infuse a bit of romance into their writing.

title: Beautiful leather but flawed sizing
text:
I had bought a competitor's leather cover like this and compared against this item. This seller makes beautiful leather products, and true to my expectation, the leather on this one was much more beautiful. It also had more realistic dimensions -- the cover was bigger than A5, so it actually was able to hold an A5 notebook inside. That said, I still returned it because it could not fit my A5 notebook due to how shallow the spine is. It accommodates only a very thin notebook - otherwise the cover does not come close to closing at all because of the stiffness created by the layers of pockets.

I imagine this will reach a bigger market when it's able to hold a thicker journal and adds a horizontal strap across the top to hold a notepad if desired instead of only typical notebooks. I can't imagine many people using journal covers to hold so many credit cards or stuffing their balled-up earwires into, so a better use of the pocket material would be to create sleeves that hold more pens and sheets of paper instead of having so many card slots.

title: Perfect Design, but Flawed Sizing
text:
The design of this cover is excellent. Plenty of pockets for pens and sheets of paper, a sleeve for a typical notebook, and a slot for a vertical notepad. It's hard to find notebook covers that accommodate both horizontal and vertical notebooks/notepads. I would have loved to keep it, but unfortunately its sizing was not realistic for its purposes. It is too small to fit any typical A5 notebook despite being sized as such, because the maker did not take into account the extra material required to hold an A5 after the stitchings are done. It's measured exactly like a notebook, so of course when the stitches are completed, the room inside is smaller than an A5. If you want to make an A5 sleeve, the leather needs to be bigger than A5 sized, and the makers of this thing don't seem to have thought of that.

I would love to come back and buy this if they make this more realistically sized. I can't imagine many people actually using notebook covers to hold their credit cards, or stuff a balled-up earbud wire into, so a more useful consideration for the material would be to perhaps use the extra leather for holding more pens or sheets of paper, or accommodating a thicker journal -- currently this holds a rather thin journal at best, due to the shallowness of the spine.

title: Good set, very wide nib, not easy to hold
text: These are a good set for the value if you're into large lettering and using these as highlighters. For beginners, it might be a bit jarring because these write HUGE. The handles are not at all ergonomic, however, so if you plan on using these for long stretches of time, I'd recommend going for another pen that has a more ergonomic design.

title: Defective nib
text: I got this because I heard a lot of good things about this pen. It looks fine, but did not write well. I didn't even put ink in the pen - I tried only dip testing it - and the nib just wouldn't write in a single line. A lot of blurred, double-lined strokes. It's a pretty pen and I appreciate the dropper coming with it but it looks like it needs better quality control.

title: Light, watery, easy to wash and wipe.
text: This ink is a very light blue. So if you're looking for something dark, this isn't it. It's a pretty color, but definitely not for writing checks or signing documents. By light blue I don't mean sky blue - it's just a type of blue that is not very saturated. It's very watery in color and consistency. Following the advice of some ink experts, I got this to add to my Parker Quink Black ink just to see what the fuss was all about - apparently you're supposed to use blues often so you can get a sense of the baseline to compare all other inks on. Well, it worked, because this blue ink taught me that Parker Quink Black is much smoother than this one. This blue is lovely, especially inside a demonstrator pen, but it has been giving me quite a bit of feedback on my 1.1 stub nib, same as the Broad nib with a Black in it. I mixed the black into the 1.1 stub, and voila, no feedback at all, smooth as glass. I imagine that the black is higher in viscosity and therefore smoother because it's more water resistant. This blue is probably a very lovely choice for making art, or just for enjoying the color, or for those that don't mind feedback. For people like me who switched to fountain pens to have as little feedback as possible when writing, the Parker Quink Black is the way to go. Incredible value for the money. This blue is more expensive and drier, but it has taught me this valuable lesson, so it's still worth it. I might keep mixing it with the black to create a blue-black of my own liking.

title: Great value, writes much smoother than Quink blue
text:
This value-priced ink is a great offering for someone like me who just needs ink to use and isn't finnicky about shimmer or shading or whatnot. It's black as it should be, works well on all kinds of nibs and pens, and is good value for the money. It's relatively water resistant for your check writing and signature needs.

I had this ink in a Broad nib and had the Parker Quink Blue (washable) in a 1.1 Stub nib, and both felt quite a bit of feedback. As an experiment, I mixed the blue with the black in my stub pen, and boom, it writes like glass. Now I know that the stub is indeed a smoother writer than the broad - it had been the ink that was the problem. This black ink has higher viscosity, if I were to venture a guess, and therefore writes smoother, since it's less washable. On the right nib, this ink is proving to be an effortless writing experience, which was the whole reason I bought a fountain pen to begin with. Definitely recommend.

title: One completely defective nib; trying to open the pen broke it
text:
For a pack of piston pens, this is a great deal. That said, there are some serious quality issues with these pens.

I can only use one out of these pens normally, so I paid the price for basically one pen instead of six. Most of them have mediocre nibs, while one of them has a completely unusable one - the tines are misaligned so that it draws two lines instead of one when using a stroke.

They all have very tight caps. Which is fine on a well-built pen, but on this one, when I heaved to pull the cap off, the cover for the piston flew off instead. The opening line for the cap and that part are both at the same place, so it's anyone's guess as to which part will go flying. Of course, said part is supposed to have threads for screwing, but they did nothing to stop the entire thing from just popping off. Thankfully it didn't destroy the pen YET, but it makes me have severe doubts about quality if upon a single use, the pen cannot handle the pressure of trying to open the cap and ends up completely sanding off its screw threads.

So with one nib out of six being unusable, one out of six already having come apart just from opening, most of the nibs being mediocre, and all of the six having the same build quality that can break any moment from trying uncap... I'd say take your chances. Only buy if you're ok with throwing the money away.

Gave two stars instead of one because it IS a good value IF it didn't have egregious issues right out of the box - and it's not every day you get a piston filler at this price.

Update: They all leak. Reduced to one star as they are all completely unusable by the second week.

title: Great value, quality is mediocre
text:
I admit I'm not an expert at fountain pens, so this was a bit difficult to get used to - I make big strokes across the page and found this pen difficult to handle because the ink would not flow. That's not the pen's fault - that's how fountain pens are. For being a fountain pen, this is incredibly accessible for the modern city dweller who only thinks of them as distant relics of the past, perhaps a luxury they cannot indulge in.

The only thing I DO fault the pens for is that all three pens went dry on the second day. They all flowed well on the first day, but on the second day, all three were faint. The caps were on the entire time they weren't being used, so I'm not sure what the problem is. Perhaps it's a hit and miss, since there's got to be a hidden cost to manufacturing things like this at such a price.

A word of caution - these are "medium", and when they have good inkflow and the proper angle, they do compare on par with the Pilot G2 0.7mm "medium" gel pens. But a slight twist in your hand or a slight off angle, and they become much finer. I might go with a broad nib next time when I upgrade -- Pilot is a Japanese brand, and apparently Japanese brands have a reputation for being much finer than western brands even though they use the same terminology.

title: Excellent craftsmanship and design, but leather color and pattern is off.
text:
I love this leather. It's thick, dense, squishy, and rubbery in a good way. Something you'd feel safe banging around inside your bag, your car, carry around, what have you. The paper is similarly dense, thick, and smooth. It's a delight to have. It's overall an extremely well constructed piece of art, and it made me excited to carry this around with me to work meetings.

Sadly the reason I returned it was that the color description was way off; instead of dark brown, or even brown, this leather is very red. I got two sizes of this and both came in the same red color. The leather also has a strangely dotted pattern, as if they hadn't sanded away the follicles from the hide -- I mean, if you're going to sand it down to be smooth anyway, why not get rid of the porous looking leopard print too?

I appreciate how sturdy this looks, but I would love it more if they offered something without the faint circular marks, and something that's dark and lustrous instead of reddish and powdery. I also love the closure - I'd be back in a heartbeat if they offered this in a refillable design. A refillable style would be a dream.

title: This is the real deal.
text:
I'd bought and returned a lot of leather journals, disillusioned by many that claim to be "full grain" "buffalo leather" and are still sanded down to oblivious, dull and dusty, stiff as cardboard, or smelling of toxic fumes. This, right here, is real buffalo leather - and it's the only one I'd see and at first glance say "yes, this looks like buffalo leather and has retained its unique properties that made me search for buffalo leather in the first place". It's got the large, bold grain and patterns that aren't artificially created by scratching up and pulling; it's the first to really smell like real healthy leather (I'd been starting to think maybe I was crazy, with the many journals that claim to be 'leather smell' but smell like toxic chemicals'); it's wonderfully soft and naturally napped in the underside; it doesn't have the oiled-up stiffened look that is designed to make it look artificially distressed as quickly as possible -- don't get me wrong, I do love scratching up the stiff, luscious leathers, but this one looks REAL -- the rivets is strong without flimsy stitching; the strap is thick, spongey, beautifully soft; the asymmetric flap really adds to the natural look; and the pages are thick and hefty, and do not collapse into a thin shallow puddle.

It's beautiful, it actually LOOKS like what it claims to be, its minimal processing shows that it's got quality leather to begin with that doesn't need much covering up, and really lets the natural beauty shine through. If the seller offers different closures, refillable styles, or differing sizes, I'll be back to snatch up every one.

title: Surprisingly lovely, clever design, the most realistic 'rustic' journal
text:
I actually didn't expect much from this, because it felt overpriced for leather that didn't look great in pictures - there's rustic, and then there's dirty and dingy, and the leather looked like it fell into the second category in pictures.

Make no mistake; this leather is not glossy, lustrous, or textured. It's sanded down to the point of feeling like acrylic or velvet, not quite thick enough to be spongey, and does look... well... dull. But it is soft and floppy; it's got the crazy horse look without being stiff; and the way it's super soft and looks dull while also carrying the spots of distressed looks makes this look legitimately aged, as if it's lived through centuries of being banged around in a pirate's basement. The key that's shaped like a compass doesn't hurt either - it's unique and beautiful. It doesn't look like a new journal that's just been hand-crafted to look old, and made with stiff new leather that's oiled to quickly take on looks of distress. It looks like something that's been distressed to the point that it can't be easily distressed anymore, like your softest worn-out jeans. And the fact that it's paired with equally old-looking paper does wonders to complete the look. I'm not one for finicky wraparound strap closures because they feel pretentious and unnecessary, but for something that looks so legitimately old, I start to suspend my disbelief as I wrap and unwrap this thing, careful not to spoil the old, tattered-looking pages, and it starts to really feel like an age-old treasure.

On the wrapping: this is the only leather journal I can legitimately say serves its purpose in being the hassle-y wraparound strap closure, thanks to how genuinely rustic it looks. It's also incredibly useful in the kind of A5 variations it can take - extra thick and extra narrow can both fit, because the sleeves are open ended and the elongated flap offer flexibility in sizing. Which also justifies and necessitates the wraparound closure in case of ill-fitting paper spillage. If I like a leather journal, I usually ask that the seller consider a closure that's more hassle-free, like a short strap on a loop, but I don't know if it will have the same effect thanks to how rustic and purposefully hassle-y this journal looks -- maybe some decorative x-shaped stitching can work.

The paper is also unique; most refills don't have this deckled, aged look unless you bind them yourself. Most leather journals that have this aged, wraparound vintage look do not allow for refills. But this seller makes it work, and is the only one to do it so far around these parts. The refillability, along with the authentic look, makes this journal a winner. Of course I'd have to only buy the deckled bound refills that only this seller offers so far, but if you're going to make-believe, you might as well commit.

A minus, though: it doesn't look very sturdy. The thread used to stitch the leather looks incredibly thin and fragile. I'd also like to see a version of this design that's made with more lustrous, less sanded-down, top grain pull-up leather. If you're looking for something that looks actually "nice", this might not be for you. It IS sanded down to oblivion and feels ready to fall apart.

title: Good leather, beautiful paper, smaller than claimed
text:
The only ding against this is that, like most of the leather journals that come from this seller, this seems to run a bit small. It's about 1/4 of an inch short of all claimed measurements. I'd love to buy more from this seller if the journals come in their true sizes, but so far they've all consistently been smaller than they claim.

That said, the leather is prettier than it looks in pictures. I was hesitant about the "peanut brittle" color because it looked like a scratched up, cracked, hard thing in pictures. But in reality, the leather is soft, doesn't have harsh crackles on it, and spreads lightened creases beautifully when folded. The color is lighter and softer, more like sand / caramel than a solid brown like in the pictures. The paper is beautifully aged. Unlike another journal type I purchased from this seller, which had beautifully luscious dark leather but smelled of toxic fumes that made my eyes water, this one was unassuming and perfectly healthy smelling.

I took a chance on this because this particular color was on sale, and for the price I think it's worth it. But because of it not measuring up to its claims in dimensions, I wouldn't buy this at full price. Also, it's not going to be as thick as in pictures if you get anything bigger than a 7x5. The picture is obviously that of a 7x5 or smaller notebook; if you get an 8x6 or bigger, size dimensions of the leather will change the ratio of the paper thickness, and it will look much more shallow than what you imagined.

title: Winner.
text: There are countless 'antique' 'vintage' 'book of shadows' leather journals out there with leather straps and keys attached to them. I've found this to be not just the cheapest and best value, but also the most beautiful of them all. The leather relatively thin and not all that squishy, so if you're looking for a spongey, thick, dense kind of leather (which I also love), this is not for you. It's thin, crisp, and glossy. It's not dusty or dull like most of the others. It's a rich, vibrant color, oiled and pulled for a true crazy horse look, and the gloss looks luxurious. Oh, and it actually measures up to the size it claims to be. I'm not a fan of these wraparound journals because they're finnicky to handle, but this one I just could not let go. It outshone all the others and made me end up returning them all so I could clutch this one in my grabby hands.

title: Great paper, slightly small and not embossed all the way
text:
The paper in this leather journal is very satisfying. Thick, soft, and fills out the journal beautifully. However, they don't measure up to 1.5inches as claimed. The leather journal barely fills out its dimensions, and the embossing is nowhere near the clarity of the pictures shown; it's done very shallowly. The leather also doesn't look as plump as in pictures.

I've bought from this seller before on another leather journal with beautiful luscious leather and engravings in the pictures, and also ended up returning it because it was smaller than claimed and the engraving was very shallow and looked unfinished. This journal had similar problems.

If the artists providing the work here could add a bit more finish to the final product and cut fewer corners, these products would look dramatically increased in value, even if they end up costing a bit more.

title: Very very thin and flimsy.
text: This was so much thinner than it looks in the pictures. Returned.

title: Pretty good value, but it's narrow.
text: It's a good value, but mind you this is not standard A5 size. It's a bit narrow, so if you're using a nice leather notebook cover, it won't fill it out and will leave a weird saggy space at the ends.

title: Good product made unusable by horrific chemical fumes
text:
You know what this journal smells like? Toxic, leaded, crude gasoline coming out of car exhaust.

I am sensitive to smell and often have to pass on leather journals that smell of toxic chemicals and claim that the smell is simply a leather smell (it is not. I know what good leather smells like.), but this journal is not within the same plane of existence. This smells downright toxic, like someone burned a rubber tire at it.

It's a real shame, because unlike the last journal I tried from this seller, this one is actually quite nice. The leather is the same color on both sides this time, it's not dry like cardboard (but it IS a little bit rubbery), and the wrap is decently soft. The color of the mocha is a rich, handsome color. It's not glossy on the surface like in the pictures; it's more matte. The pages are lovely with light, dotted lines, which are rare and a real joy - if I were to be able to use this at all thanks to the fumes that are burning in my throat.

Update: I dunked it in a box full of tissue paper overnight to absorb the smell. Afterwards, the tissue absorbed the smell and also smelled horrific. And the journal smelled no less horrific; it immediately made my eyes burn and water when I approached. I love the look of this and wanted to give it a chance but decided I don't want to invest so much effort into being able to use an unusable product, so sadly returned.

title: Pretty leather, mediocre paper
text:
This leather is quite pretty - it's not exactly thick or dense or even all that soft, and feels a little dry in the inside, but when you fold it it spreads beautiful lightened crease marks like those high quality aged buffalo leathers. It's the only journal of its kind among many that I've found on Amazon that has this look - dark at first glance, and instantly gaining a gentle spread of creases (not just scratchy, harsh fold line) when you fold.

That said, the leather doesn't have the full grain on it - it's sanded down, so the hand feel is decent but nothing to write home about, and like many of its contemporaries, this journal has a dry, powder-dust feel. Pages are meh; not aged but just dark colored paper that's been dunked in water and dried with water stains. For once it's got a true 9x6 size as it claims, and the wraparound cord, while a bit thin, also has that nice creased look and is soft to the touch. I'd like this to come in a different closure - something that isn't fussily wrapped around and around - and hopefully the seller offers the leather in a bit softer, thicker varieties in the future, and hopefully even refillable... with better paper. The smell of wet moldy paper is what caused me to return this.

title: Not quite there
text: It looks good in pictures, but the paper is as stiff as cardboard. The leather isn't much better either. It feels almost like plastic. It's also not quite A5. Had to return.

title: Great idea, execution has room for improvement
text:
This journal looks beautiful in pictures. I bought it despite having similar journals because I love the simplicity of the strap that doesn't require winding around and around like a lot of other journals out there. It was also not stingy about the length, and the extra length made it stylish. It looked soft and well cut. In person, the strap is good. But the rest of the body is very stiff; it's glued into what looks like a love child between cardboard and kraft paper, probably to give it some more sturdiness and prevent from flopping around. But to me, this glue + cereal box material totally ruins the soft handfeel of leather, which is the reason I got a leather journal in the first place. I'd rather have leather that's stiff and firm enough to hold its own, or just live with floppy leather that's thickened with an extra sleeve or card slot. It felt like fake leather due to the stiffness, so I returned it. I see that the leather can be very nice, judging by the quality of the strap, so if the seller takes out the cardboard and glue and and adjusts the size to be a true A5, I'd be the first to come back to snatch this up.

Oh, and it's narrow. Doesn't quite measure up to the A5 journals that I have.

title: Beautiful leather; heavy, thick, sturdy, well made. Paper is a bit thin.
text: The leather on this is superb. Heavy, thick, sturdy. It's very pleasant to handle, and has a pleasant heft to it despite being small. I also enjoy how easy it is to open and close, without the long wraparound strap that most leather journals have. That said, the paper is pretty thin inside; you'll finish writing in this in no time. I'd love to see a bigger version of this, or even better, in refillable versions.

title: Soft, but not very thick or lustrous like in pictures.
text:
Edit: I was charged money for this two months after returning it because "they never got it". Unacceptable.

I like the handfeel of the leather because it's soft and blends seamlessly with the aged paper inside. But unlike the raving reviews, this journal I got has pretty thin leather, with noticeably thinner strap. The leather is also not sturdy, thick, and lustrous grain like in the photos of other reviews I see - it's dry and dusty. Maybe I got a dud, but I'm not sure I want to try ordering another one just in case it's different. I like how easy it is to handle with the short strap, but this doesn't look like it will hold up very well over the long term.

title: Beautiful leather, but would not hold up
text: I really wanted to keep this journal because the leather is very beautiful, thick, and supple. Unfortunately the cut that serves the leather cord closure is made so close to the edge of the book that a few tugs and it would simply tear open, and I couldn't justify spending this kind of money on a book that would last only a few uses. I would be happy to come back to buy more if the seller offers a different closure (maybe a shorter strap instead of a wraparound). Overall well made.

title: Beautiful leather, true to size, but had a huge cut on the leather
text: I really wanted to keep this one, because it has beautiful leather, has truly aged-looking paper instead of normal paper dunked in water, and is true to size for once instead of being barely 8x6 despite claiming to be 9x6. Everything about it was perfect, except that if you open the journal, there was a huge cut going all the way across it, as well as a three-digit number cut into the leather. Completely ungiftable.

title: Very pretty color, looks nice and smooth. Leather is unfortunately stiff.
text: I'm torn on this and really wanted to keep it, because the color is very beautiful. It's smooth and takes scratches beautifully, and is a good price for a moderately rare find. Unfortunately I couldn't justify keeping it because the leather, while beautiful colorwise, had a very weirdly smooth texture that felt more like rubber or cardboard. Hopefully I had a dud, because I would be happy to come back and try another one just in case.

title: Looks nice, but is smaller than it says it is. Paper thin strap.
text: It's honestly pretty nice. Decent leather, good binding. The strap is unfortunately paper thin, and really stands out from the rest of the package. It's not as big as it says it is, so I had to return it.

title: Pleasing aesthetic, a bit too small, leather is low quality
text:
The aesthetic is stunning, especially from a distance. But inspected up close, one might understand how such a beautiful book can cost so little; they have to cut corners somewhere, right? First off, this isn't truly 8x6. It's smaller than that. The closure isn't easy to use; you have to press it pretty hard, and the flap isn't attached around the book so it flops around awkwardly when you open it.

The leather is the lowest quality leather I've seen in these leather bound books. The exterior is shiny and slippery like vinyl, not the kind of smooth lustrous grain you find in higher quality leathers. It is bleachy white inside, and paper thin; the flap closure was thin and stiff and I thought it was cardboard at first, not leather. The paper doesn't look so much "aged" as it looks "caught in rain and dried badly later". Water stains everywhere on normal paper, instead of soft textured paper that is carefully stained and ripped like in most other journals like this.

I had high hopes for this book and was hoping to move onto even bigger, more expensive books made by this seller with these interesting aesthetics, so I'm a little discouraged. I might try one more - I really hope it lives up to the hype. Still giving three stars because the design and thickness are nice and unique ideas; they just need better quality execution.

title: Beautiful aesthetic, medium strength band, slightly small
text:
The look of the book is superb. For a traveler's notebook - which are known to be lightweight finnicky things- this journal really adds gravitas with the deckled paper and you can't even tell by a glance that it's a traveler's notebook held together with flimsy elastic.

Which makes the elastic a bit of a shame, because it can't handle the weight of the nice paper inside. The leather is also a little bit stiff - not thick buffalo stiff, but more like rubber stiff - but it's really not bad; it's quite decent. I returned it only because it's a bit small to be calling itself an A5 size. It doesn't quite fit a regular A5 inside because it's too short. If this seller offers regular A5 sizes in this type of notebook I'll be the first to snatch it up.

title: Beautiful leather, but small and loose
text: I returned to this seller because their travel sized journal had one of the most exquisite leathers I've seen sold here. This journal also has the same beautiful leather - waxed and glossy on top and soft suede on bottom and altogether very supple and spongey - but it is not 8x6. The paper measures closer to 7x5. Shame because I'd return to buy in a heartbeat if this seller sold something truly A5 sized or refillable. Also, the binding was very odd. Cords look like waxed shoelaces, and are loosely threaded, making the pages almost fall out.

title: Good value but not A5
text: I bought this because it claims go be A5 size. It is not. Too narrow to fit a standard A5 cover properly. Good value if you don't mind that though. It's also a little shallow.

title: Pretty leather but paper is like cardboard, and a bit small.
text: I thought this would fit a standard A5 that gets tossed around with 8x6 sizing. But this is too small for A5; while the leather is pretty, the paper is thick and stiff and feels more like cardboard than craft paper. I know paper tends to run a bit thicker with these types of journals, but this was cereal box level.

title: Beautiful leather, but too small
text: This is one of the best leathers I've found in a journal. Unfortunately, it's not actually 6x8 in paper - the leather barely makes it there and the paper is more like a 7x5. I really wanted to keep it but it was not the A5 that I had thought it would be from the 8x6 description.

title: It's less clear and smaller than in pictures
text:
Edit: I've returned this two months ago and Amazon sent me a message saying they didn't receive it yet and charged me money for it. Unacceptable that I had to sit through customer representative queues for this.

I had been eying this journal for a long time, and was so excited when I finally decided to order it. From the pictures, the color of the leather and engraving are so beautiful. Unfortunately, the real thing that arrived had a very shallow etching of the picture, looking almost unfinished like a rough sketch. The size is also not a true A5 size - it's very small and would not fit any standard A5 refills. I was really sad to return it because the color is pretty and if executed well, it could be a gorgeous work of art that would put all my other leather notebooks to shame.

title: Beautiful leather but NOT A5 as claimed

title: Best ergonomic solution
text: I spent $$$$ on an expensive chair just so that I might have armrests that adjust back and forth and side to side as well as up and down. But alas, it's still not narrow enough for me, because most chairs are made for bigger people. Enter this little gadget, and I have my own customizable armrests. I might actually buy a chair without any armrests at all next time so that there would be nothing in the way of these little things. They follow my arms everywhere at the perfect height, and are cheap to boot compared to my fancy, ill fitting chair. The only downside is that the they are obviously less sturdy, and will wear out in a while. And the elbow cups are not padded, and will smudge your elbow black and/or give you pain after a while of pressing into them. I bought little sheepskin bits to pad the elbow cups because I know from experience that messing around with too much softness (memory foam) can actually cause injury.

The tie and the leather are overall a little bit stiff. I can't imagine needing to replace this for a long, long time. The included journal is beautifully made paper.

title: Decently supple and thick, a little dry-feeling, hard to close
text: I overall think this is a great product. The closure was what won me over; it seemed less finnicky than the fashionable journals with the wraparound straps. But when you let go, the strap is only attached on one side of the journal, so the rest of it hangs down loose, which makes it just as finnicky and even more awkward because the strap is wide and floppy. If the closure strap were secured on both sides of the journal, I might have kept it. Overall the leather is decent; it seems sanded down, but has decent thickness and is relatively supple, but it felt a little dry perhaps because of the powder/dust that was coating it. The closure was also a little hard to close, and I needed something that was quick and easy. The color was nice and dark and rich.

title: Sturdy, well made, great value for the money - just not very pretty
text: Honestly this is a great deal. For the price you get thick, sturdy leather in a rich color, a nice artsy looking pencil, and some more leather accessories thrown in, plus a nice gift box. It's an amazing gift if you want to give it to someone. For me it simply didn't work because the clasp was very big, heavy, and hard to clasp closed. I chose this clasp in hopes of having an easier time opening and closing my journal compared to the wraparound leather strap ones, but this one was just as much work, with actual WORK - it's hard to maneuver the clasp when in a hurry and on the go. The leather was also a little stiff - not exactly dry, but not rich and supple either. It had the smell and touch of sawdust all over it, like it just came out of a workshop. It adds charm and feels genuinely handmade in dad's garage, which I appreciate. It just wasn't for me this time around. I would love to see more creative designs like this coming out of this shop though.

title: Nicely made, but materials are not the highest quality
text: I liked the idea of this journal because it seemed easier and less fiddly than the ones with the wraparound straps. I also liked the idea of the organic looking cover that's uneven on top. But in execution, the leather seems like split leather, not very thick and very sanded down; the hardware is rusted and very hard to clasp together, and already has a huge dent under the clasp parts; the little pocket on the bottom looks like this was originally made for one of those wraparound strap leather journals with keys to put into these pockets, but the maker changed their mind last minute. The leather's hand feel itself was decent - it was supple and soft. It just didn't feel like something I would reach for over and over again.

text: I don't know what it is about the passport sized refillable journals on Amazon, but all of them have beautiful leather compared to their bigger counterparts. The wrap is also the same quality - beautifully supple with a glossy, smooth top side and a soft, sueded underside. title: Beautiful.
text:
I already had a beautiful travel journal just like this, but I bought this at a higher price because it was one of those rare journals that have a leather closure. I love the soft, supple, sturdy all-leather closure that's not finnicky like elastic bands or a giant hassle like leather straps that wind around and around. The closure is a little tight at first, but the friction is what makes it work, and it's lovely. No corners cut. Lustrous, supple, beautiful leather. If they ever have burgundy or dark chocolate brown in stock, I'd come back to buy again. Please make more leather journals like this but in different sizes! I'd buy in every size.

Update: I returned this because the included pen holding metal thing was not working out, and it was difficult to secure a pen. Would be nice to have a leather pen loop attached.

title: One of the most gorgeous leather pieces I've seen.
text: I'm very picky about my leathers, and have returned a dozen leather journals because they're simply too thin, hard, stiff, rubbery, what have you. This leather is the first I've held and not wanted to let go. I actually bought more that are similar to this in quality, but the color and lustre of the leather on this one cannot be beat. Rich color, luxurious smooth to the touch, supple and thick, with a smooth luster that takes scratches beautifully. I want to buy more even though I don't need them. Please make more journal covers of all sizes and styles with this quality of leather! I ended up buying another TN just because the elastic on this is finicky to handle and wanted a short strap with loop for closure instead of rubber bands or winding leather strips. I'd love for this seller to offer different closure styles.

title: Soft, but not durable.
text:
This is a good example of "you get what you pay for". You want a handbound buffalo leather journal with handmade paper? Then you're gonna get it, but with paper thin leather, flimsy stitching, and scratched-up surface. I don't blame them - it's a ridiculously cheap price for something that's definitely a luxury item. I'm amazed that the leather is holding up at all to any kind of touch, thin as it is, and am afraid to touch the stitching because it's so flimsily done. It looks like they split the hide at least four times, if not more, to create this and other replicas of it.

But if you're looking for barely-there leather that is as thin and soft as paper, this is it. The paper is beautiful and pleasant to touch. The hand feel of this journal is very pleasing, if you like something that feels less like paper encased in leather and more like one giant, fluid, supple thing that feels the same inside out. It's too flimsy for me to gift to someone, and because I tend to replace papers and reuse bound journals, I had to return it as I don't see it lasting beyond the first rebinding.

So my arms were always floating uncomfortably midair, not quite able to smoosh it down completely but not fully supported either, and this gave me brand new muscle pain in parts of the arm that have never had pain before, and it got so bad within half a day I had to take it off. Can't return it because I threw away the packaging and trimmed off the extra velcro strap (you can do this, people, instead of complaining that the straps are too long) and I don't mind because that's on me. But I do wish there were more ergonomic considerations that went into arm padding than "SOFT AS POSSIBLE!!!" because that is not good for you.

title: This is just the HP OfficeJet Pro 9010 with a different number.
text: When you go to set this baby up on the wifi, etc. , you should realize that your are looking at an HP OfficeJet Pro 9010. Don't bother trying to find the 9015 that you purchased from Amazon.  While that is the number on the actual printer, as far as the app is concerned it is a 9010.  I tried customer service but they never gave me an answer.  Google the question and found several folks in the HP community support who had discovered the same thing:  "Ho, both models provide the exact same capabilities, only the color and marketing specifications are different, there are no changes in the features or capabilities of both models." Another member posted that the 9010 was the European designation for the American 9015.  All a mystery to me.  Marketing I guess?  I thought I was purchasing a newer better version of the same old thing.  Fortunately the 9010 (or 9015) is a good little workhorse.

A month later I need to replace another empty cartridge (as expected) but when I loaded the new out of the box cartridge into my printer, I got the replace the empty cartridge notice.  Fortunately I checked the ink in my print screen and found that the cartridge was showing as full.  This happened two more times.  So the caveat here is don't assume that you got a bum cartridge no matter what your screen is saying, you have to repeatedly check and replace your cartridges for them to read correctly.

title: Works Great--Saves Money--Easy To Use
text:
Worked great! This package comes with the three ink supply tanks, a manual drill to open up the tanks in the cartridge and a set of very good instructions.

If you follow the instructions, you will be able to refill a cartridge easily. The color quality of the subsequent prints I made was as good as I get with a Canon branded cartridge. I did find that the low ink indicator on the printer stay on after refilling and reinstalling the cartridge. The instructions detail a method to reset this. I followed it but the indicator light did not go off. This did NOT keep the printer from working and making very good prints.

SUGGESTIONS:
1) Get some vinyl (or other material) gloves because some ink will get on your fingers when refilling--not a lot.
2) Cover the work area where you're going to refill the cartridge with a sheet of aluminum foil, then a layer of plastic wrap and finally a paper towel or two. This will prevent any spilled ink from staining a counter top, table top or desk. I recommend doing the whole thing in the kitchen sink since accidents may happen--not the fault of the product as much as human clumsiness.
3) Wipe the cartridge with a damp paper towel after refilling to remove any stray ink.
4) Cover the holes you drill with a small piece of clear tape (like Scotch Tape) to prevent the cartridge from leaking after you put it back in the printer. I didn't find this in the instructions, yet from prior experience refilling other cartridges knew this to be necessary.

While reviews on this product vary a great deal, I found that being careful, covering my work area and following the instructions gave a very good result.

text:
The quick version:

-Some are just highlighters, others are beautiful.

-Great packaging

-Test you paper before committing to use.

The Whole Story:

I bought these to use in my scriptures, both for highlighting and for artwork in the margins. I like that they're dual ended and the packaging is great, seems sturdy and can fold into an easel for convenience. Some of the colors, like smoke blue, vermilion, gold and magenta are vivid and lush. Others, like green, blue, yellow and orange are more like your average highlighters, they somehow manage to be faint while still burning your retinas. So, since I only use retina damaging highlighters for editing essays (I'm going for relaxation and peace while studying the word of God) some of these either won't see much use, or will make their way into the family school/work supplies. Others will see some action in one of my books, but I think I'll continue the hunt for good bible markers and mostly sick with my prismacolors for the time being.

I tested them in an inconspicuous spot in 3 of my books and had varying results. You can see in my pictures that first I tested it on my new NRSV Catholic journaling bible and you can see where I wrote on the back of the pages although it didn't bleed through onto the next paper. Next I tried it in my Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints journaling BoM. It didn't "ghost" onto the reverse. Last I tried it in my KJV Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints quad. It also ghosted through like my Catholic bible, but didn't bleed onto the next paper. I haven't tried it yet on my NIV, but I'll definitely test it first.

title: Nice planner! Suggestions for improvement, but definitely a repurchase item
text:
Nice planner for the price!

Things I like:
- Plastic front and back covers. Won't fray or tear like paper.
- Great size. Thin and small, easy to pack into my daily work bag, but large enough that I'm not trying to reduce my handwriting to fit.
- Has a page for weekly to-dos/goals/habit tracking, and then another page for tracking events and goals for individual days. I like being able to break things into macro (weekly) and micro (daily) tasks.
- Also, is it weird that I like that this planner starts the week on Monday? It's called a weekEND for a reason, I don't know why Sunday is considered the start of the week in the US. I enjoy taking 10 minutes on the couch on Sunday evening and flipping to the next page to start planning out the next week.

ANYWAY, some possibilities for improvement:
- A daily water tracker. My doctor wants me to track my water intake, but I don't want to draw little checkboxes on each day to mark off how much water I've had. The bottom line on every day could be removed and replaced with water tracking checkboxes.
- Monday - Friday has its own square, but the weekend is consolidated into two. I just draw a line through half and make the top Saturday and the bottom Sunday, but it would be nice to have two separate areas for each day.
- An extra page at the end of each week to track things that went well, things that need improvement, and a gratitude journal. I use a separate journal for these things, but if I could have both my planner and journal packaged into one book, that would be amazing!
- Some sort of bookmark. I bought a pack of magnetic bookmarks on Amazon and am using one to mark my current page in the book, but it would have been nice to get one with the planner itself. (Now I have nine extra magnetic bookmarks I don't know what to do with, since I don't ever read nine books at once.)
- A pen loop, even if it's an adhesive one. Again, I could get a pack of 12 on Amazon, but then I have 11 extra pen loops sitting around.

All in all, I'm really pleased with this planner and will be buying another one next year!

title: I love this thing
text:
I was initially skeptical about buying a portable scanner for $178, but I've been trying to clean up the clutter in my life and paper is one of them. I also scan all my receipts from every purchase I make and keep track of my spending in a tracker so that I have a clearer understanding of where my money is going each month. I was originally scanning everything with my HP printer, but it was getting to be a real chore. I'd have to sit at my desk and put each paper through the scanner (which was LOUD and slow), then crop it, name it, and save it. It was mind-numbingly boring. I decided to take a chance and purchase the Doxie Go SE and I'm so happy I did!

Now I can sit comfortably at my couch with Hulu or Netflix on and scan away. The scans go through the Doxie quickly and quietly and get sent to an SD card (like the ones we used to put inside digital cameras before smartphones took over), which is included in the package. Perhaps my favorite thing about the Doxie is that it auto-detects the size of what is being scanned. I'm able to go from scanning 8.5x11 papers to the small receipts from gas pumps to a standard sized receipt from Wegmans without having to crop ANY of it. It's one of those things you don't appreciate till you don't have to do it anymore!

Then when I am done scanning, I pop the SD card out, put it in my laptop, and the Doxie software imports the scans. Another one of my favorite things about the Doxie software is that after each image is imported to your computer, it is automatically deleted from the SD card! So I don't have to worry about clearing the SD card myself or having the same files imported the next time I use the scanner.

The Doxie software is pretty easy to use, although I'm pretty good with computers so I'm not able to speak to its ease of use for those who aren't as comfortable with PCs. I use the software to name all the files, crop them if I need to, rotate them if necessary, and "staple" pages together. I have noticed that when stapling a lot of pages together (such as the product manual for my expensive electronic toothbrush) the software can freeze sometimes, but it always unfreezes eventually. It's a very small hiccup in an otherwise incredible product.

You can then choose to save files to your computer as a JPEG or PDF, or upload to a cloud storage service. I've been saving to my PC since I upload my receipts to my tracking software so I can't comment on the process of uploading to the cloud. Another great feature about the Doxie software is that when you save a scan to your computer, a green checkmark shows up on the scan so you know it has been saved and that you can delete it from the Doxie software. (Doing so just deletes it from Doxie, not from your computer.) This is nice so you avoid wasting time on trying to save scans that you've already saved to your PC but forgot about (helpful when I was scanning an entire month's receipts the other night). If you haven't already saved the scan, there's no checkmark and Doxie will warn you that it isn't scanned before you delete it.

Charging time was quick. Doxie comes with a USB cable but no outlet adapter to plug it in to. You can charge it by plugging it into a USB port on your computer, or if you have owned a smartphone at any time, odds are you have a few outlet adapters lying around anyway. You can plug the USB cable into one of those and charge Doxie through a standard outlet.

I would have liked to see the Doxie available in a few colors other than white. Most of my office accessories are black, and it would have been nice to have some fun color options like blue, purple, etc.

I can't believe the longest and most passionate review I've ever written on Amazon is about a portable scanner. That should speak to A) how much I am type A and like organization, and B) how easy to use and high quality this scanner is. I'm so happy I bought this scanner and believe I will be using it for years to come. And when this one dies or becomes totally outdated, I'll keep buying Doxie scanners as long as the company is making them!

title: I'm actually surprised at how nice this is.
text:
Honestly, I was looking for a cheap table to hold my laptop while I work. Sometimes, I like to work while laying down in my bed and I hated having my laptop on my lap.

I ordered this table because it was well reviewed and looked sturdy. Plus, I don't like the look of the wooden tables that were shown.

I wasn't expecting much when this showed up. For $25 or so, I assumed it would be on the cheaper side of things. Honestly, though, it's well made, light weight but sturdy, and has a nice finish. I like the color (I got grey.)

I do have a few nitpicks, though.

There's no locking mechanism for to keep it unfolded. That means you either have to lift it with both hands or take everything off of it if you plan on lifting it. Also, and this is more of a personal taste, I'd love it if it were 2-3 inches lower. The legs on it feel sort of long to me. Again, that is a personal thing, and depending on how you use this table, that might not matter.

Finally, we'll move on to the only part I'm unhappy with and the reason I gave this product 4 stars instead of 5.

The seam down the middle, where the two halves meet is raised. For some reason, this wasn't apparent to me in the pictures. Regardless, this means that your laptop likely won't sit 100% flat if you place it directly in the middle. My MacBook doesn't wobble too much on it and it's perfectly usable, but it is noticeable and slightly annoying. For any other use besides typing on a laptop, I don't see the raised seam getting in the way of anything. But, the only reason I bought this table was for using my laptop in bed. I don't plan on using it for eating, etc. That means it's not quite suited for the primary reason I bought it.

Lastly, I found that you can also leave it folded and use it as just a flat surface on your laptop. That's pretty nice too.

title: Great double-pocket multi-colored dividers w/ tabs to label & store important papers
text: There was nothing that I disliked w/ this product!  It was perfect for my organization of important papers that required easy access when combined in a notebook.  Divider pockets were used to add visible tabs that labeled the content papers behind each tab.  But the double pockets (one in the front; and one on the back of each divider, allowed me to slip in papers of most importance on the single divider (in front & back pockets, and then add papers related to the stick-out tab behind each respective divider.  Each divider is hole punched to fit into a large notebook (sold separately). To be used w/ these pocket dividers, I bought different widths (1”, 1-1/2”, & 2”-wide colored notebooks that have a transparent plastic cover on the notebook front, so each notebook can have its Major Topic identified on a piece of paper that slides into the top of its outer cover. For examples of the double-divider uses, I have one notebook labeled MEDICAL, with many tabbed double-pocketed dividers inside that list my doctor and surgeons’ names. This enables me to easily locate information papers that I’ve acquired under each doctor.  I do the same w/ these double-pocket plastic dividers re: “types of bills received each month” store them in a smaller colored notebook. This type of organizing diverse paperwork saves me a lot of time, when I need to locate information in my colored & titled notebooks filed on a bookshelf.

Silhouette Cameo 4 settings I used:
Blade 2 (To cut through the paper I would use 4)
Force 20
Speed 3 (for intricate designs)
Passes 2

text:
The only reason this is not a 5 is because of build construction. This entire unit feels like a model airplane put together with paste. It is very flimsy. Now moving along..

Out of the box, setup is incredibly easy once you get by the countless blue tape pieces holding some of the flimsy panels in place. The software setup and wifi connection was also flawless. In fact, this helped me deduce I was having connectivity issues with my extender by way of the PC not syncing with the printer immediately. The LCD is very low quality but functional enough to do what had to be done. Printing 1 or 2 photos 4x6 were very good quality as compared to my old HP 8500 OJ Premiere. I was pleasantly surprised to see options I did not even plan for such as CD printing and faxing. (even if unlikely to use anytime soon)

I think people need to balance value with purpose. This is NOT a high end printer for a small or medium business. This is a fantastic printer for a kids room for school projects and selfies. Just make sure the kids treat the unit gently.

Update 1/7/17: This printer was rarely used. I would say max. 30-50 sheets over a period of less than 2 years. Ran into a perm. jam error that I cannot clear no matter what I try. Every part that can be removed, has been removed. This printer is complete garbage. The warranty has some vague 3 year coverage and will contact Epson to see if they stand behind their product.

title: Bigtime $ savers! (with the occasional "surprise"
text: Yes...I like the fact these are around one-third the price of Epson-brand cartridges, maybe less, IDK. There are trade-offs sometimes, however. Like when you install them and black ink pours out on your print job and you have to replace it with another one that hopefully works only to discover your print head requires roughly 10 cleaning cycles in order to print a decent copy...Whew!! Even after all of that, I'd STILL go with these over the brand any day of the week and twice on Sundays.

title: i'll never buy brand ink again!!!
text:
When I used the name brand ink, i would dutifully replace the cartridges when the ink monitor said i was low. After awhile though, I noticed I would receive these notices that my ink was low, even though I hadn't printed anything for a long period of time. I think they just send out these bogus alerts to get you to buy more ink. From now on, I'm running it until it's dry. The Epson printer really did want to accept the EZink cartridges. They were flashing all kinds of hazard warnings and threats that they could damage my printer blah, blah, blah. Ignore all of that. The ink cartridges work great. With the brand cartridges I had to run a head cleaning function if I hadn't printed in awhile. Then I would have to print 3 pages before I could come up with a decent looking page. Not so with these, perfect page right from the get. I will be going with these from now on.

UPDATE: March 26th 2020.

I wanted to update this product because I think it is the perfect solution for people who still use brand cartridges. I purchased 2 boxes of these back in July 2019. I purchased 2 based on who much I used brand ink and let me tell you, my ink levels from the first box I installed back in 2019 have barely budged! All of the color levels are 100% and the black level is down to about 90%! Unreal!

I don't print a ton, but the burn rate is incomparable. It makes me wonder if the brand cartridges are on a timer so that after being in the printer for a given amount of time, they signal that they are low. I know that sound conspiratorial, but I have no other explanation.

Anyway, these definitely are superior the the brand and are certainly worth giving a try!

title: Slimy business practices
text: The VOIP service is fine. Here's the problem: After years of using the service with Ooma, I was offered a significant discount on my overall cable bill if I added phone service (the entire bill went down by $40).  I ported my phone over (which had to be done through Ooma). They continued to bill me for the ported service every month. When I finally discovered this after 6 months, they told me that it wasn't enough to port the number to another service; I had to make a separate call to "cancel the service'. Obviously I wasn't using the service, since the number was ported. After calling to complain and having to argue with them, they refunded 4 months of the fees. But their premise is nonsense. Once you port your number, you're not using their service any more. I was never notified I had to make a separate call to "cancel" it.  Basically, continuing to bill someone in this circumstance is theft (in my opinion). And once they were notified, they failed to refund the full amount they stole from me.

title: Wifi Direct is useless!
text: I bought this for a tad cheaper at an office supply store.  I have been loyal to Brother printers for many years now but I gotta say Brother missed the mark on this one.  I bought this printer specifically because it had Wifi Direct which I needed to to print from my Ipad at work.  The instructions to set up Wifi Direct are confusing and lacking!  I finally figured out that I had to manually set up a Wifi Direct network for my Apple device to connect to which was a tedious process that involved inputing a generated password from the printer into my Ipad.  But that was OK, I was done.  I had my Wifi Direct set up and I was finally printing from my Ipad.  Then, about 10 minutes later, the Wifi Direct network disappears and my Ipad can no longer print.  I had to go through the entire process again.  I print throughout the day and need Wifi Direct because of the way our office is set up...THIS WAS NOT GOING TO WORK!  In conclusion, set up was NOT straight forward (even for connecting printer to a wireless network) as some of these reviews will have you believe and if you want to use Wifi Direct it is hard to figure out and does not stay connected.  After reading up on the subject, Brother suggests in its manual to use Wifi Direct as a "temporary" way to print.  Other brands of printers simply have a setting to leave Wifi Direct running so you can connect any time.  Very disappointed!  Hope this review helps someone as I saw no other reviews that mention Wifi Direct.

title: Very Cute and Writes Well
text: I picked this up from my mailbox and thought the box was very cute. The pens are also super cute, but definitely thicker than I had expected. The clip is very nice and tight, but keep in mind that it is a slide on; you do not open the pen clip. There was a wax tip on the pen when I first clicked it that I removed and the ink flowed smoothly and freely. I really like these pens and will likely purchase them again when I need more.

title: One Major Flaw
text:
This is super gorgeous. I love the rose gold color. I unpacked it immediately when I got it. The box was very pretty as well. It works very well holding and organizing all my various pens, notebooks, sticker pages, etc. Overall, I would recommend this wholeheartedly if it wasn't for one major flaw:

The drawer at the bottom doesn't fit exactly in the slot. It does not close all the way and does not sit flush against the rest of the organizer. While this doesn't really interfere with its utility, part of the huge draw of this organizer is its aesthetic, and to me, it takes away a bit of the glamour. If you can live with that though, then it's a really lovely piece that works well.

title: Simple
text:
***Disclaimer: This item was received for free in exchange for an honest review.***

I love these. I really liked the design of many types of chore charts, but I didn't like the idea of listing things as "chores" because building better habits is already a pain in the butt, and labeling them chores just continues to encourage me to be in a negative headspace. A lot of the chore lists were also geared toward children, and while I'm a huge baby, that doesn't change the fact that I am actually an adult. So I liked the more minimalist design of this. The least quality part has honestly been the adhesive for the market attachment. It was difficult to pull off the cover to stick the adhesive part onto anything. However, once I stuck the holder onto things, it stayed on just fine. The next morning, one of them had fallen but all the others have stayed on so far.

It does feel a little cheap, but honestly, for being so inexpensive, I think it's probably a good value, and it is exactly the kind of thing I wanted.

title: Large Dot Grid is a Deal Breaker for Me
text:
Pros:
-Sturdy cover
-Nice binding and lay flat design, seems like it will hold up to daily wear and tear
-Nice elastic strap
-Paper is cut so the dots are straight and evenly spaced on the page (I've tried some dot grid notebooks where the grid slants... a travesty!)

Cons:
-The dots are .25" space, so you have 30 x 19 squares on each sheet of paper. This is not enough "grid" for me. I do two different monthly task tracker spreads in my bullet journal, and I won't be able to use this notebook because there simply isn't enough grid space to chart those, and I find them extremely useful. So, that's my personal deal breaker.
-I used with staedtler triplus fineliner pens and the black bled through. Like a lot. Like you probably only want to use one side of the paper, a lot.
-I'm not sure how I feel about the "off white" color of the paper. It's nice, but I think I'd prefer white.

Interesting:
-The last pages of the journal is a strange index that you can use to match up with whatever page numbering system you use in the bottom corner of the other pages, where they've put a large box for numbering. I like the index idea but I dislike the big boxes for page numbers, they're just in the way for me.

Overall this a quality notebook, it just wasn't quite right for what I want to use it for (mainly the grid size being too large). But if that's not an issue for you, it's a good quality notebook at a good price and I'd recommend it.

title: Nice Printing at Moderate Cost but Terrible Durability!
text:
It is obvious that HP makes ink cartridges on the cheap. I barely use them and after only a few color printings, I am already out of ink. It is probably a combination of cheap cartridges and printers not optimized to efficiently use those cartridges. On the other hand, when I do print, the documents have a nice crisp image for graphics and text. I recommend ordering multiple packages simultaneously just to save you the hassle of ordering multiple times, especially if you print a lot of stuff.

Do not be cheap in purchasing the HP only authorized cartridges either, as the cartridges are chipped or the printer is programmed to work with specific brands, you WILL waste your money otherwise.

title: Half-slide scan problem: SOLVED
text:
I decided to digitize my Dad's 3,600 slides, and I struggled with the decision of whether to do it myself or send them out to be scanned by one of those scanning companies.  I concluded that the most time consuming part of the job would be to figure out what was on the slides and get them sorted into logical groups, and I needed to do that part myself anyway.  So, sending them out (and spending a lot of money) wouldn't magically make this easy.

I have to admit that my first instinct was just to "throw money at the problem", and send them out without doing any sorting first.  The scanning company suggested that I just hire them to blindly scan everything, and then sort the images out on the computer later.  They recommend that because that suggestion is best for their business.  (This is because the pain of sorting would prevent many people from doing the job at all. And if you tell people they don't need to sort, they're more apt to plop down the credit card.)  

However, there's a serious flaw with that approach.  In the case of my Dad's slides, there was a ton of information written on the slides themselves about what they were, and when they were taken.  That information isn't included with scanned images, so I would need to sort the images on the computer based on information on the physical slides, and keep correlating back and forth between the two. That's a daunting task that realistically I would never do.

So, I had two choices.  Either scan them blindly in bulk, and accept that I'll forever just have a big random mess on the computer (with no idea what anything is), or do all the careful sorting first, independent of how they got scanned.

Well, I knew I didn't want a mess, and I didn't want to lose all that information written on the slides, so I decided to do the careful sorting first.  And as long as I was doing all that work myself anyway, it didn't seem like too much more work to scan them myself, particularly with an automated machine like this.  Furthermore, even with the cost of the scanner, doing them myself would be vastly cheaper.  Sending out 3600 slides to be scanned would have cost thousands.  Also, the scanning service I was looking at charged a lot more for higher resolutions. 

Doing it myself meant that I could scan them at as high a resolution as I wanted, without it costing me a penny more.  And if there were any images that I truly loved and wanted to re-scan at even higher resolutions, it would be easy to do if I have the scanner right there.

Ultimately, purchasing this batch scanner was a no-brainer.  It was by far the best option I found, and vastly cheaper than sending the slides out.

Overall, I'm happy.  I succeeded in getting all the slides scanned, and I'm pleased with the results.  It was a huge job, but I found that it was kind of fun, too.  It was cool to see all those pictures of my parents when they were young, and pictures of myself as a kid.  I even learned a few things.  My one big regret is that I didn't do this when my Dad was alive.  There were so many interesting pictures that undoubted had a great back story he could have told me.

Anyway, initially I had a love/hate relationship with this scanner due to the half-slide scan problem described below.  However, after I solved that, everything went very smoothly, and it was pretty easy.  If you're looking for a final recommendation, I would tell you to buy this scanner, and use my half-slide scan fix.  If you want to scan a bunch of slides, I think this is by far the best approach.

---------------------------------

Half-slide scan problem:
Let me tell you, I pulled my hair out over this problem.  There's a little arm that pushes the slide into the scanner.  The arm is thin, because it needs to pass through the slots in the bottom of the tray.  (Well, I call it the "bottom".  It's the bottom when it's sitting on the table and you're loading it, but it ends up being the side of the try inside the machine because the trays lay sideways, just like in an old slide projector.)  Anyway, this thin arm pushes on the thin edge of the slide.

The problem is that for 10%-20% of the slides in the tray, the arm would slip off the edge of the slide while the slide was being pushed, and the arm would either slip behind or in front of the slide.  At the point where the arm slips off, the slide won't move any farther.  So, you end up with the slide half way into the scanner, and you get a nice scan of half the slide. 

This was a huge pain, because on every tray I had to check the images afterwards, and then find the 5-10 slides in the tray that needed to be scanned again.  Then load those into a tray and scan them again.  But sometimes I'd get half-slide scans on that second pass, and I'd need to do a third pass.  It was very aggravating and time consuming.

The problem wasn't the slides themselves.  I did some experiments where I ran the same tray through twice, and a different 10%-20% would fail.  It was random.

I contacted the company, and they sent me info instructing me to bend that arm.  However, this arm isn't designed to be bent, and if you break it, that's not covered by the warranty.  Even so, I attempted this approach and wasn't able to solve the problem.

The slide is much thinner than the slot in the tray, so there's room for it to flop back and forth, and perhaps it's not surprising that the thin arm can slip off to one side since the slide is so loose in the slot.  

My first idea was to make the arm thicker with some tape, but that didn't work because the arm would jam as it passed through the narrow slots in the bottom of the tray.  My next approach was to find a way to make the slides thicker, so the arm wouldn't slip off to one side during the push.  However, I couldn't come up with a practical solution, and any solution like that would mean doing something to thousands of slides one by one.  That was not the right direction to go.

The epiphany came when I realized that I could solve the problem by modifying the tray such that the slides stayed in the center of the slot while being pushed.  This is a significantly better idea because I would much rather modify my 3 trays (150 slots), than modify thousands of slides.

After a considerable amount of brainstorming and experimentation, I eventually solved the problem using bobby pins.  By sliding a bobby pin onto each fin of each slot, the slides were held exactly in the center of the slot, and the arm could push them all the way into the scanner without the arm slipping off the edge of the slide.  This turned out to be a very easy and graceful solution.  The bobby pins were cheap and quick to install.  And they could be easily removed later if desired.

There might be different sizes of bobby pins, but I used what I think is just the standard size.  I got them at CVS.  I needed to cut off the flared tip of each one, but then they worked great.

Before I discovered this fix, I painfully struggled through about 500 slides, with 10%-20% failures in every tray.  After the fix, I did another 3,100 slides with literally only 2 half-slide scans.  Upon further investigation, those two cases were caused by slides that were severely bent.  Other than that, the fixed trays worked perfectly.

At one point, I considered the possibility of using a "compact" tray, because the slots are narrower.  However, in the reviews of that tray, multiple people said that the compact tray did not work with this specific scanner, and caused it to jam.  So, I don't think the compact tray is the right approach.  But the bobby pins completely solve the problem.

Dust removal:
The scanner has a feature where it uses the IR data collected during the scan to identify dust particles on the slide.  (The heat from the lamp doesn't pass through the dust, so the IR image shows exactly which black specs are dust, and which are actual black portions of the photo.)  Then the software repairs the image at the points of dust by using the information around the dust spec.  This feature far exceeded my expectations.  Some of my Dad's slides were extremely dirty, and this feature was able to clean them up amazingly well.

HDR:
The scanner has the ability to make two scans of the same slide at two different exposures, and then combine the information to get an improved image.  One exposure would be better in the lighter parts of the image, and the other exposure was better for the dark part.  In theory, if you take the best from both, you can get an image where the light parts aren't washed out, and the dark parts still have plenty of detail.  Unfortunately, I was very disappointed in this feature.  It sounds great on paper, but I couldn't get it to make much difference in my scanned images.

Multi-sample:
I was similarly disappointed with the multi-sample feature.  The scanner can sample the same point multiple times to get the best possible values.  This can theoretically increase the effective bits-per-pixel quality, and reduce noise.  However, I could never really see any difference.

Jam:
Prior to my half-slide scan fix, I would sometimes end up with serious jams where I couldn't even pull the arm out manually.  When that happens, you need to pop off the cap on the top of the machine and reach down in there with tweezers to pull the slide out.  The hard part comes when you want to put the cap back on.  It fits in there a certain tricky way, and it would sometimes take a while for me to get it back on.  If you ever need to take that cap off, I recommend you examine it very carefully as you are removing it, so that gives you a clue of how to put it back.

Loading the tray:
When I loaded the tray for the very first time, it wasn't obvious to me where to put it.  The manual talked about pushing it forward towards the arm (with the arm in the pushed-in position) until "it clicks".  Well, I never heard any click, but it turns out you just need to push it up against the arm, and you're good to go.

Quality:
The scanner can go up to 10,000 DPI, which sounds cool, but it takes a very long time to scan, and the files are insanely big.  I don't think it makes sense to scan the bulk of your slides at that resolution, even though the scanner can do it.  However, there might be a few very special photos you'd want to re-scan at this resolution.  For the bulk scanning, I used 2,500 DPI, which seemed to be the right balance between quality and time/space.  I also had the scanner save each image in both JPG and TIFF formats, which are good for quick viewing and later tweaking respectively.

Colors are a little flat:
I feel like the colors in the images from this scanner are a little flat. Looking at the images, I feel like I want to find the "saturation" knob and turn it up.  Unfortunately, there doesn't seem to be a saturation knob.  I'm living with it for now.  I believe I could go back later and tweak the tiff files to adjust the colors (although that sounds like a lot of work).

Glass Mounts:
Some of my Dad's slides were mounted with the film between two pieces of glass in an aluminum frame.  I was told these are called "glass mounts".  They are much thicker than the cardboard slides.  At first I was frustrated that the machine kept jamming during batch scans, but when I contacted Pacific Image they told me that the scanner doesn't support glass mounts.  Later I found a little note in the manual saying the same thing.  Although the scanner doesn't support those, you can still scan them by turning off the batch mode and moving the arm in and out by hand between scans.  

I set the scanner up within easy reach of my computer, and let it run next to me while I worked.  Every couple minutes, I would manually pull the arm out and back in, to load the next slide.  It actually wasn't that inconvenient.  Keep in mind that the Pacific Image person told me that since the scanner isn't designed for glass mounts, if I damage the scanner (or cause excessive wear) when scanning those, that would void the warranty.  I didn't see any problems, and I did several hundred glass mounts this way.  Note that you need to remove the half-slide scan fix bobby pins from your trays in order to load those thicker glass-mount slides, so you might want to do those last (or first).

---------------
Well, that's all the important info I can think of.  I hope you found this review helpful!
