title: OUTSTANDING STARTER SET OF TEMPLATES
text:
OVERALL -- A good variety of robust templates, suitable for children as well as adults and even professionals for some uses. Extremely cost-effective as a learning tool for kids who have never seen a template before, and who like to draw.

PROS -- Price. Variety of applications, from drawing basic shapes, to home layout / planning, mechanical drawing, sketching (French curve), flow charts / logic diagrams. Well packaged, each in a clear sleeve, and all came in a plastic case with a slide-closure.

CONS -- Thick compared to most templates, and not flexible, so professional users may not be used to the offset from their drawings. Units are metric measure, not the English engineering system more common in the US. Collectively, these disadvantages are not reasons to avoid purchase, if you need templates.

SUGGESTION -- Some users might benefit (greatly) with a small pamphlet in plain English (not a poor translation) included in the case, that demonstrated the use of some of the more unusual templates. (E.g., hex nut template, sinusoid forms template, partial oval template.)

title: WHY DID IT LEAK?
text: Amazon Prime got the pen here right on time, but when I opened the envelope and the box inside, I found that the BLACK-DYE INK from the loose cartridge in the pen had leaked on the inside of the pen. Moderate cleaning job and ink-stained hands later, things are restored to expectations, except I'm OUT ONE CARTRIDGE. Now, I've had pens shipped for a month from Japan that survived intact -- WHY DID THE ONE SHIPPED OVERNIGHT IN THE U.S. LEAK ? You'd have to shake the box violently to dislodge the little steel ball bearing at the tip of the ink cartridge enough to do that.... 2 STARS.

title: THE NIB CAN BE USED IN OTHER PILOT PENS
text: For example, it fits the Metro, the Plumix and the Prera. I used the Kakuno metal-nib portion to replace the nib in my Prera, which had been damaged. The $11 cost of the Kakuno helped me to avoid the $32 charge Pilot wanted for a new Prera nib ! (It's also more than a new Prera on AMAZON !)

title: PERFECT FOR A LIGHTWEIGHT HAND
text: A tremendously smooth writer, the Prera demonstrator is a good-looking fine writer. I got my first years ago for $70.  The approx. $30 price for THIS one is just "gravy." It writes as smoothly as my 18K gold nibbed Waterman Charleston, for a LOT less money.

title: GOT MINE AT OLLIE'S
text: Not quite 6 x 9 (a few millimeters short), it's a 400-pager though, and OLLIE'S box store was selling them for $2.99 EACH !  Under those circumstances, I rate the ones I bought 5-star !

title: INEXPENSIVE can still be USEFUL
text: The pens (and extra converters) I ordered arrived on this date.  I have inked one pen -- the check-pattern -- thus far (Levenger EMPYREAN, a dark blue ink), and it writes smoothly, a little broadly for a medium nib. It's similar to results from Waterman Experts I bought at the turn of the century.  The pen is heavy, as commenters have noted, but not unpleasant. When the cap is posted, the pen feels somewhat unbalanced (toward the back end), which may be an issue that's difficult to get used to. If the other four pens perform similarly well, I'll change to five stars in time. If not, I'll lower and let folks know the reasons.

title: GOOD HOLDER, BUT NIBS ?
text: Treating the nib + holder as a set, they work well together, but scratchy. The result (for me, a left-hander) on 24-lb paper was like an extra-fine nib in width. By experimentation, I found I could flex the nib easily and vary the width of the stroke. Most positive aspect:  the way that dipping the pen once can trap enough ink in the nib to write more than one on of words. The holder I perceive to be well-designed. I used Noodler's Dragon Napalm, an orange-red ink, and an old bottle of Waterman Florida blue. READER -- let me know if you have a suggestion about a nib for the Tachikawa T-40 that would produce a broader line. I'd then consider making that nib-holder pair 5 stars.

title: CONSIDER THE PLATINUM 3776
text:
Short version -- Well-packaged, well-timed (vs. delivery prediction), well-priced, and well-designed. WELL DONE !

This is my first Platinum. I selected it to compare with other gold-nibbed pens. The 3776 medium is a bit stiffer than the (18K gold) Waterman Charleston medium, but it writes beautifully nonetheless. As a test, I used an "old" ink, Levenger Cobalt Blue, and it flows as well as the day I bought the bottle. (The Cobalt Blue is a good color-match for the pen, incidentally.) There was none of the "scratchiness" some other owners have described, writing on 24-lb. Champion (laid paper) stock. The appearance of the pen is not as artful (for those for whom this matters) as a Charleston or Cross Townsend, but the value and performance of the 3776 is first rate. I felt like this was a gamble over a Pilot 74 which I considered (I like Pilot FP's at all price points), but it turns out that I made a good decision with the 3776.

title: This is an amazing pen for the price
text: This is an amazing pen for the price. I own four of them, in black and gold tone, as well as many other pens. Their outward appearance is plain, a simple metal body, but their feel is well-balanced. The Japanese-medium nib delivers a line that is a step between what pen users would call fine and medium.  I reserve a 5-star rating for pens like the Waterman Charleston (with it's pliable, 18K gold nib), but this pen is well worth your attention. The only negative is the Pilot CON-20 converter that is needed to hold ink looks cheap, a rubber (?) bladder covered by a metal sheath that over time looks like it will deteriorate. It may be best to order several replacements. AMAZON sells them, but you can find them for less online if you look.

title: ABOUT THOSE PESKY BUMPS
text: The template is well-made, even if some of the other reviewers don't understand what the Inspector Clouseau-like "buermps" are for. Youngsters, the small protrusions elevate the template above the surface to be marked, so that someone using ANY sort of pen need not worry about smearing the ink and ruining the drawing. The feature is called an INK-RISER template, and makes it more valuable than a template without the bumps.

title: It works, after adjustments
text:
I came really close to returning this cutter because it shredded the corners when I first used it. The trick is to make sure the blade aligns perfectly against the bottom plate, so that there is no space in between the two pieces. I also had to adjust the guides in order to get just the right smoothness to the corner. The cutter may not be perfectly calibrated right out of the box, and the instructions aren't overly clear about this. I can see how some users got frustrated and sent it back but it does work well once you get everything aligned exactly right. The only problem I'm having is that the corners on the bottom sheet are rough and need to be trimmed with scissors. I'm currently using it to trim laminated postcards in stacks of 8, but I'm sure it will go through several more at a time.
The machine comes with a few spare parts but no explanation as to what they're for. Some are obvious, like the allen wrenches, blade and oil, but the others are a mystery to me. I'm also concerned about blade replacement, the instructions don't say where to get replacement parts.

title: Exceeds my wildest dreams!!
text: I am a note taker. Always have been and always will be. I HAVE to out the pen to the paper to be able to retain more and I just need that feeling of writing.. I have to be taking notes in a meeting or I get restless and bored.. just like in HS back in the day. But everything is moving to electronic.. Taking notes on a laptop just isn't the same. But I have to take meeting minutes daily and email take aways to the team and the bosses.. So I would have to handwrite notes and then retype them in an email.. May not seem like a huge deal but when you have 4 meetings a day, the time adds up.. I bought a Rocketbook thinking it would solve my problems but it didn't. It was a good concept but the execution.. not there for me. The writing experience wasn't the same, the paper too slick and pen skipped too much.. having to take pictures each time was tiresome especially when it wouldn't align right.. I just wanted it to capture what I wrote without all the hassle.. Enter bamoo slate! I can write on my own paper, be it a legal pads or even a notebook and then tap the button and get it on my phone.. better yet, I tap another button on my phone and it converts it to text that I can send in an email right away.. It's awesome! It recognizes my sloppy handwriting too. My only qualm with it is that the pen requires a bit of push which tires my hand out but first world problem right? It did run out of ink quickly but it might be because I bought mine used (it was in the original packaging though) and it didn't come with the nib remover. Honestly not bothered at all. I got a great deal on it being used and it works fabulously. I can get the refills for cheap and I think tweezers will work to remove the nib, I hope anyway. This is a solid pad and exceeded my expectations! Might be a novelty to some but for the people who write daily or still need the feel of pen and paper but want notes digitally too.. this is the real deal!

title: Only Pilot lovers understand..
text: I.. I am.. I am a pen snob.. There I said it.. I just HAVE to have nice pens in my office.. in my room, the kitchen, my purse.. Pretty much everywhere.. I need a pen that is smooth like buttah. I need a pen that has such a fine point, I can write in all caps on a spreadsheet that has cells with a .15 height. I need a pen that is effortless to hold because.. let's be honest.. my hand cramps easily and I just cannot deal with that kind of negativity in my life.. This pen.. this pen is so good that it spans generations.. Yes.. generations.. My father used these pens ALL the time when I was growing up.. In fact.. rare was the day I DIDNT see him without one. At the time.. my feeble little mind could not possibly comprehend the differences between a Pilot and a BIC. I thought a pen was a pen and that was that.. How could a pen be better or worse than the other.. Oh how naive I once was.. I am awoken now.. I have seen the light.. This is MY pen now.. not my father's. The torch has been passed to me and how honored I am to be in the presence of gods. Yes.. I said it.. The experience of using this pen is otherworldly.. Serene, peaceful, powerful, and bold all at once.. Anytime I see someone using this pen.. I just stare at them with a knowing look. Our eyes meet for but a moments glance... But in that moment.. when the world melts away.. I have seen their soul and they have seen mine. We are pen lovers.. bound by the ink and fine point tip.. So scandalous, I know.. but you wouldn't.. you just would NOT understand.. How could you? How could you possibly understand.. You use.. well.. you use.. a BIC.

title: Great concept.. Crappy execution
text: So these are super cool in concept but the execution is not on par..it just isnt quite there yet.. They are advertised as reusable. In my head.. that means I can wipe it off and rewrite on it.. This is not the case.. When you write on the colored side and try to erase it, the dry erase ink definitely comes off.. but it takes the coloring with it.. so you have white letters where the black ink just was.. If they mean reusable in the sense that you flip it over to write on the white part.. they get dirty and wrinkly pretty quickly.. and the ink still shows a black mess when you try to erase it which you don't want on your walls at work.. Then there's the static charge.. It definitely works super well in sticking to the wall.. for about a couple of days.. Then they start to curl and slide off the wall, falling on the floor.. This wouldn't be a HUGE deal if I hadn't made a GIANT diagram of the GTD workflow on my wall at work. Spent a good 2 hours writing everything, color coding it, putting it on the wall, and connecting everything.. I come back in after the weekend off and half of my hard work was on the floor, shriveled and curled. I would've used post-it notes if I had known they didn't hold up for longer than a couple of days.. I mean I guess static looses it's charge after a while but I didn't think it wouldn't last more than a weekend. This product is advertised as a better alternative to post it's.. Because you can reuse it and move it effortlessly.. I disagree. You can't really reuse it.. and you can move a post it just as easy as these.. and post-its will last longer and are FAR less expensive... I really hate writing negative reviews.. I rarely do honestly.. if a product isn't up to par with my expectations.. I usually just admit it was user error and move on with my life admitting defeat. But in this case.. it really isn't user error and if it was not advertised the way it was.. I probably would've skipped buying it. Either change the wording or invest time and money into making the product live up to it's advertising.. The concept is so cool and really inventive.. I see it being a big deal and being successful.. IF they fix these small but vital issues..

title: Large tags hold lots of information
text:
These are sold as shipping tags, but I'd think they'd have a number of uses, especially in a classroom or other group. I'm thinking young students could have their own tag on a cubby, and because they are colorful, you could use the colors to code different colors for the kids to match up. As with any printer-fed labels, you are cautioned to print your labels on blank paper first, making minute adjustments in the positioning to ensure you get nicely printed labels to stick on the tags.

That said, I didn't print labels. What I was thinking about using these for was to tag different garden beds (e.g., NB-1, NB-2, NB-3, BK-1, BK-2, etc.) for helping me track sophisticated crop rotations and succession plantings through the AWESOME Seedtime program. I'm in the middle of an experiment now, sacrificing one of the tags to see if (a) I could cut one in half, allowing me to have the tag affixed to the bed and a "chip" coinciding with that bed to sort and organize indoors; (b) which wears better outside for writing on the tags, a paint crayon or a Sharpie. The first test I did with a pair of poultry shears and was able to cut the tag in half, although the line wasn't terribly straight. I'll most likely cut the others using a straight edge to score the cuts with an Exacto knife; they should then just snap apart cleanly. My second test will not have a result until that test tag has been out in the weather between now (cold, wet winter) and the summer with its humidity and high heat, but initially I think the Sharpie is going to work better. If it does fade, I may try to see if a version of Herrick Kimball's no-fade label trick will work with this plastic.

It's very important to note that there are two different holes, one at the very top that's got a ridge around it and the other just a punched hole. The top hole results in a completely unremovable tag when you stick the little zip tie thing inside of it. However, if you stick the tie through the bottom hole and pull it fairly tight, the tab will stay on but you can remove the tag later.

I did knock off a star because, when snapping apart the tags, you're left with rough edges of plastic that have to be sanded off if you want them smooth.

text:

It's a thinner cushion than some of the memory foam ones I've tried, but I like that because my legs are short and it's hard to get a chair at a height that's both comfortable for working at a desk/keyboard and also have my feet touch the floor. title: If you don't have the requisite Nespresso machine, you can make these in a K-cup holder
text:
Look. I'm not going to turn down the chance to review coffee, I don't care how it's packaged. Coffee is like gold in this household. I grabbed this Bestpresso variety pack to review, then went on Amazon looking for how much the various business Nespresso PRO Professional machines they are designed to use with cost, and I did not find a single one of them for sale. These are made for higher end office machines., apparently.

But that did not stop me. I have these marvelous reuseable stainless steel permanent K-cups (https://www.amazon.com/Reusable-Universal-stainless-Refillable-Makers-brewers/dp/B09F8T7TBG) that work great with my coffee maker (not K-cup brand, but it can brew K-cups), and one of these pods makes a great American Long-style cup; I just cut along the circle of the pod at the top, dump it in the K-cup, set my coffee maker to brew 12 oz. (which comes out closer to 10), and voila! Perfect portion, perfect brewing, perfect flavor. Or I could brew with less water and wind up with espresso.

Of the three different types, the Espresso Dolce is one I'll drink black; it has an exquisite flavor but a milder intensity than the others. The Cremoso, at the highest intensity of 11, I liked a lot with a little cream; this is the one I'd probably buy if choosing between the three. The Intenso, for lack of a better way of saying it (I am not a coffee connoisseur), tastes more "Columbian" and was my least favorite of the three, but still quite good.

These pods are a whole heck of a lot less wasteful, speaking in terms of landfills and garbage, than your typical Nespresso pods are, and they are also easier to use at home if you don't have one of those PRO machines. I'll keep my eyes peeled for newer Nespresso machines available through Amazon that these pods are compatible with.

title: Be sure to watch the assembly video
text:
This table goes together very quickly and is very well built with an amply large surface. I wasn't sure about whether I was supposed to remove the bolt on the inside of the bottom end of the pedestal; a hex wrench that was too small for that nut was included, and I couldn't figure out what it was for. You have to get the pneumatic mechanism working so when you press down on the little black handle thing, it snaps back to its original position. Also, I kind of lucked into figuring out how to raise and lower the tabletop: you press and hold down the black handle thing, then manually lift up or push down on the tabletop, then release to lock it to that height.

This table does not extend over into the bedspace as far as a side-pedestaled table does, but it's a lot sturdier than that type of table and extends far enough. title: I needed a tidy, non-slip mouse pad for my lap desk, and this is it.
text: I didn’t like my squarish mouse pad on my lap desk (spanning my recliner arms) because it hung over the edge, and it was a light color that didn’t blend in. title: Using for Aerogarden spacer and seed pod labels
text:
After my destructive little chiweenie chewed up two of my new Aerogarden seed pod kits, I was looking for a way to replace them less expensively than buying all-new pod kits. I got the sponges in a 50-pack, but I read that you have to IRON on the labels—I don't even own an iron—and I wanted something that I could at least stick on those plastic pods that now (post-Bingo) have no ends to hold the sponges in so I can use them as spacers. There needs to be a cover on these pods so light doesn't get to the water and cause algae growth.

This 1-2/3" diameter label size is about as close as I could get to the Aerogarden labels—and I can print information on them! Planting and germination date, height and type of plant...there was room to code all of that information on the label. (I output a PDF of the 5293 template, then set up the labels in Affinity Designer.) I have three 7-pod Aerogardens and one 3-pod, so 3x7+3=24, exactly how many labels are on one sheet. I can print out a growing season's worth of labels without waste.

These labels are a tiny bit smaller in diameter than the Aerogarden labels, but they are still big enough to stick down on the outer edges of the pods. I bought an EZ Tools 3/8" circle punch (1/2" size would have been better) to punch holes in the center of the labels to allow me to cut slits like the labels should have to allow the widening trunk of the growing plant to push the opening wider. Now I just have to figure out the most efficient way of reducing the stickiness on the parts of the labels that face down toward the plant, exposed to air, so the seedlings don't stick to them. Seeds can be pretty aggressive little things, however, so this may be unnecessary. It may be I could just stick a 1" diameter label to the sticky side or use a 1" circle punch to cut out a stack of tissue paper rounds, then punch a center hole in those and place one on the sticky side of each of the labels. Or I could just give it a dusting of dirt through the open part of the pod.

So, anyway, now I'm set for growing my own seeds after the new seed pod kits I bought to fill in the destroyed ones are spent. I got four useable spacers out of those two kits, so I'll be able to plant three tomatoes without having to buy the tomato seed pod kit. I'll just have to be careful to keep the plastic part of the pods safe from the ****ed dog so I can use them over and over.

title: Great Customer Service
text: I ordered a pair of HP 63XL cartridges (one B&W, one color) for my HP 3830 OfficeJet in early Nov 2021. When they arrived, I still had a few days of ink left in the black cartridge that was installed, so I kept using it. When both were depleted about a week later, I attempted to install and align both cartridges. No problem with the color, but the black cartridge wasn't recognized by the printer. This happens occasionally with refilled cartridges. Seller had included some tips on how to deal with lack of recognition, and I tried them all. No success. I really didn't want to return the pair to Amazon, because the color was full and worked well, so I reached out to the seller via Amazon. They asked for some pics of the error message, but sent a replacement cartridge for the black out anyway. I did send them the pics of the error message. The replacement black cartridge arrived day after Thanksgiving, and works perfectly. Great customer service! My printer shows both cartridges (color and the replaced black) as full now that they are installed and fully aligned. The original shipment also included a bag to return cartridges for recycling, a good thing to do. Since the black cartridge that I first rec'd was defective, it will just go in the trash, as it can't really be refilled and expected to work at this point.

title: Great shredder, works well, but basket a bit hard to empty
text: We've had at least 3 shredders over the years, from the simple strip shredders of years ago, to the micro-cut shredder. Shred level is appropriate for home financial documents. Noise is not bad. Our previous Amazon shredder had a removable basket while the head stayed mounted to the frame; on this unit, the head sits atop the basket, so when you need to empty it, you have to remove the head off the basket, and find a place to put it temporarily. I know there are still versions with pull out baskets, but their price has increased. We don't have to empty ours all that often, so from a price point, this works just as well. The more difficult challenge is the closing cutter cover on top; it doesn't open beyond 45 degrees, which makes it more difficult to insert paper for shredding. Our previous unit didn't have that. I'm not sure that the cover makes it all that much safer, but it's there. For the price, an acceptable unit. If we get 2-3 years out of it, I'll declare success! Biggest issue across all shredders is keeping the cutters lubed. Scrap 8.5 x 11 paper lightly coated (not saturated!) with higher temp oils (olive or avocado) should be used periodically. You can spend more, buying those pre-lubed shredder sheets, but why?? Just search on how to do this on the web. It does extend cutter life. This is a good budget choice!

title: Great Value, Works Perfectly
text:
UPDATE 1-23-17: My refill finally ran low on ink. Installed the first one on 4/21/16, lasted until 1/23/17. We print a fair bit (home use, not office use), and it lasted 9 months. Great experience!! I've popped my 2nd one in (bought the two pack), and it aligns and works just fine, but I'll wait about 6-7 months before re-ordering because they last that long.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I inherited an HP 4480 All In One from my in-laws, and have been using it as a back up to my regular printer (which doesn't have a scanner bed). The 4480 does, and I decided to keep both printers hooked up. The primary one (an HP OfficeJet 6000) is only stocked with new paper, and the 4480 is stocked with previously used (so I print drafts or working copies for the house on the back side). To do this, I didn't want to pay HP full boat pricing for cartridges. My mother-in-law left behind an unopened HP 75 color cartridge, but the HP 74 installed had dried out. I tried to resuscitate it, but it was too far gone (there are plenty of you tube videos showing how to clean the dried out ink from an HP cartridge like this one, using boiling water and hydrogen peroxide), filled to a depth of 1/4" or so.

Anyway, I needed a low cost solution to provide straight black ink. I read all the reviews, and selected the Valuetoner remanufactured ink cartridge. I ordered the 2 pack of black for around $8, free shipping included, and the order was promptly filled by ValueToner. Each cartridge was individually sealed in a plastic pouch, with a yellow pull tab tape connected to a small sheet of clear mylar or plastic covering the critical ink jet orifices on the bottom of the cartridge. In addition, there's a snap fitting (removable black plastic) that clamps over the entire front and base of the cartridge, which provides full protection. If you didn't know better, you'd think you just received an HP cartridge!

I opened one bag, removed the cartridge, removed the snap protective cover, peeled off the yellow tab with clear plastic/mylar protection, opened the HP 4480 and installed the cartridge in the spot I removed the HP 74 from. Now I did have just the regular HP 74 (not the HP 74XL), so I realized the ValueToner cartridge was indeed the XL version. It fits within the space constraints with no problem. The HP 4480 was immediately satisfied and began the process of asking me to print an alignment page. I printed the alignment page, scanned it in when prompted, and the HP 4480 was perfectly happy, informing me that the new cartridge was aligned. I took the old HP 74 cartridge, placed the protective film over it, and placed the snap protective cover on it. This allows me to store the used cartridge; I will attempt another refill some time in the future, once my two "new" ValueToner cartridges are empty.

I've had this several weeks now, and printed probably 1/2 a ream of paper, with no degradation in print quality at all. ValueToner exceeded ALL of my expectations! If you don't refill yourself, this is the best available option (and probably better than refilling yourself).

I've attached two pics - one showing the length difference (side view) and one showing labels of the ValueToner and old HP cartridges.

Also I noticed as I finished applying three coats to one of the blues that it had a purple hue, and the same unusual hues on some of the other colors ..just really pretty. Red Brown is an unusual color, and viewing it on paper from the side, it's very shiny and has some orange, gold, and red hues.
Each pencil is marked with the color, and the outside of the picture is quite similar to the core color. They come pre sharpened, and they don't break off easily when you're using them like some brands. They also come in a really nice tin, but I like to put them in a zippered pencil case where I can group the colors together and make my choice easier when I'm looking for a certain color. They feel smooth when you color on sty paper and even more so on some of the adult coloring books that come with nice paper.
I also noticed when I was erasing the pencil marks from my sample sheet that they were easy to erase. so I had to reapply the colored pencil ...sometimes you need to erase or you want to. I used a pink eraser and then a white eraser and both easily erased these colored pencils from my Arteza 100 art paper book. If you can swing it you should probably get the biggest set you can because these are really good pencils for the price, and I'm sure they have even more colors when you get a bigger set if there is one. take a look at the colors on my sample sheet. I hope this helps you decide.

title: Fantastic Wheels for Hard Surfaces
text:
I bought a rolling stool [[ASIN:B00315B1JA Perch 360-Degree Rolling Massage Therapy Swivel Stool Adjustable Backless 20.5" - 28" (Hard Floor Casters/Black Vinyl)]] that supposedly came with urethane-tired wheels designed for hard floors. The wheels were so tight on their axles the stool would not roll well.

So I bought a set of these 3" urethane skate wheels and replaced the OEM wheels the stool arrived with.

These wheels rock. My garage floor is coated with Rust Bullet [[ASIN:B0167ZRGE4 Rust Bullet RBCONQ Metallic Gray Protective Floor Coating for Concrete, 1 quart]], which is a water curing polyurethane. These polyurethane skate wheels roll on the urethane floor like air bearings. There's virtually no friction at all. I think if I pushed myself on the stool I would roll clear across the garage. I'll actually have to be very careful when sitting down as the stool can move out from under me with the slightest nudge.

The 3" diameter casters also resist small bumps way better than standard 2" casters. They raise the stool up a bit more too and as the stool has an adjustable center column, I've got a bit more height.

The axles are supported by metal bearings. They may not be world-class skate bearings, but they are way better than plastic on plastic or even metal on plastic. Ball bearings around the stems "caster" effortlessly.

I used to think dual wheels with polyurethane tires were the best wheel for an office chair on a hard surface, but I've had the thin urethane tires fail after several years. These 3" skate wheels are so much more robust and durable, they should last a long time, even rolling over the inevitable garage debris. After all, skate wheels are designed for the street.

Be aware these work best on hard surfaces. They roll easily and silently. Carpet will slow them down seriously. Best solution if you have carpet is to get a tempered glass surface you put over the carpet. Don't get plastic. Tempered glass. [[ASIN:B0183GG3HQ Cleartex Glacier Mat Glass Chair Mat for Hard Floors/All Pile Carpets, 36"x48", Crystal Clear (FC123648EG)]]. A bit pricey but a dream to roll on and the carpet stays brand new.

title: The Hard Floor Casters Are Very Stiff
text:
I had not even finished assembling the seat onto the post onto the base when I realized this stool's wheels were lacking.

The first thing I did was push the five super-special "hard floor casters" into their sockets in the base. I flipped the base over to see how smoothly the wonderful special casters performed. The base hardly moved at all. Scratched and skidded along the floor and barely worked. I flipped it over again and tried to roll the wheels on their axles. They are all stuck. The wheels will not turn freely on their axles. The stool should glide over my hard floor like a cloud. It skids like there are furniture glides on the base.

$25 in casters like the [[ASIN:B01IL7ATFY (SET OF 5) Office Addiction - Rollerblade Office Chair Replacement Wheels - Hardwood Safe 3-Inch Heavy Duty Replacements - Ball Bearing Swivels - Floor Safe Design - Black/Clear]] improve the rolling, but almost too much. They roll like rollerblades. Slick.

The only reason I can come up with for the stiff casters is that this stool is listed for massage therapy. If you were pushing on someone's back, you might not want the stool to roll away from you easily.

Aside from the wheels, the stool works well, especially with the new wheels I purchased separately referenced above. The elevation ring works well. The seat is comfortable.

For the money, I expected it to roll easily. After adding good casters, it does.

text:

The display is colorful and large. Has an AC power supply or internal AA batteries. And the convenient storage case. It reliably feeds and cuts the tape and allows several different feed and cut options to save tape.

Only down side is that I appear not to be able to create a new block on the same label. title: Attractive, Strong Magnetic Stainless Doorstop
text:
Very strong magnet on a 3" post can be mounted vertically onto the floor or horizontally onto the base molding. Metal is non-magnetic brushed stainless. Fasteners include 3/4-8 Phillips head flat head sheetmetal screws for mounting into wood, plastic anchors for drywall and a wedge bolt for mounting into a hole drilled with a carbide drill into a tile floor.

All mounting screws are invisible after installation.

The strike plate is 15/16" in diameter and is nicely mounted via a spring so that it has several degrees of angular freedom should the magnet and door not line up precisely. Outside finished diameter of the strike plate is 2", and extends about 1/2" outward.

Arrived directly from China in 15 days, but that's nine days ahead of schedule. Allow enough time for delivery. (Since I ordered these April 24, 2016, they have become a stock item with Prime and available much faster, but at $2 more.)

I can see how if they were mounted vertically to the floor and a door were to slam into them the impact could shear the post off the spot-welded base. I plan to mount them horizontally to the baseboard (not the floor) so if the door hits them hard, the impact will be in line with the mount, not a shearing force. Hopefully they will survive.

Very pleased with the looks and build. Installing four of them.

title: (Updated review) Great desk with one major flaw
text:
1/29/21 Update
This is my third update after owning 9 month. During my first review, i gave 5 stars, then lowered to 2 stars on my second update, which, in hindsight was a bit harsh. Now I'm raising to 5 stars again because after only 1 minor cosmetic issue, this is still the cheapest option for this type of desk. So here's my quick thoughts after 9 months.
-Still love it, the motor works fine
-The desk material is not too durable, but as long as you are gentle, it should be fine. for everyday typing and writing.
-Some people seem to have issues with the motor burning out. This didn't happen to me, so I can't speak to that, looks like just unfortunate luck for some people
-some people complain about the desk wobbling when you type but this doesn't happen for me, but I'm also a light typer

-------------------------------------

7/1/20 Update, 3 months later - I'm leaving my original review below, because everything is still true. This is a great desk for the most part, however, there's one huge flaw that happened today. I was taping a package and left a piece of packing tape attached to the desk. It wasn't even attached that firmly. After a few minutes, I pulled the piece of tape up and it took the whole corner of the desk laminate with it. As mentioned below, I was ok with a laminate desk for the price, but was shocked by how outrageously thin the laminate is. It's like... thinner than a piece of paper (view photo). It makes Ikea quality look like West Elm. Otherwise great desk, but because of such a huge flaw, i'm bumping it from 5 to 2 stars since it's still usable. Just be really careful about putting anything with a slight adhesive against the surface
-----------------------------------------------------
As a tech employee who has used many standing desks, I really like this, especially for the low cost. Instead of pros-cons, I though I'd address all the complaints in other reviews and give some insight to help buyers make a decision. The only thing I can't speak to is the longevity since I've only had it about a month or the customer service since I haven't needed to contact them.

Concerns found in other reviews:
Desk is cheap material - Ok, please be realistic. for sub-$300 you are NOT going to find a sit/stand desk made out of solid wood. You're not even going to find a standard desk made out of solid wood. Get over it. As of May 2020, my color doesn't appear available anymore, but it's a white frame with a ashy grayish beechwood that looks good for being synthetic. Yes, there are a lot of 1 star reviews of the outer layer arriving damaged. I mean, if your desk arrives damaged, not really the companies fault. And unfortunately, once particle board is damaged, it's looks pretty bad. Just return yours if it's damaged and be extra careful not to scratch it once it's built. You should be using this desk for computer work, not home improvement projects.

The edges of the desk are sharp - yes that's true, but it only hurts if you rest your arm for like 30 seconds or more. But for real, it's really bad posture to rest your arm on the corner of a desk so maybe don't do that.

Parts missing/difficult to assemble - Missing parts are unfortunate but it happens sometimes with Amazon orders. As far as difficult to assemble, if you've put together a piece of ikea furniture, you'll be fine. 95% of it can be assembled with included allen wrench. I did it alone in about 40 minutes.

Exposed motor - Some of the more expensive desks do a better job at hiding the motor. but who cares. Nobody has mentioned anything on mine.

It's loud - I've used several sit/stand desks. Most of them make noise. This one is not loud. Not sure how I can describe it. Maybe like an electric toothbrush while it's adjusting.

Programmable settings don't work - as of 5/1/20 the instructions on the listing appear to be incorrect, but after you create a setting, you have to double-tap the number to make it adjust. pressing it once won't do anything.

Desktop comes in two pieces and looks cheap - Yes, the desk comes in two pieces, but no one has noticed at all and it doesn't bother me. Would prefer one piece, but hey, this is by far the least expensive sit/stand desk so it's not really a big deal. Besides, most of your monitors or other equipment should be covering the crease.
